text: **Transmission and hearing-loss numbers**: Congenital CMV affects roughly 0.4-2.3% of newborns. A primary maternal infection in pregnancy infects the fetus about 40% of the time, compared with about 2% for a reactivation. Transmission rises with gestational age (about 25%, 50% and 75% by trimester), but first-trimester infection causes the worst neurologic sequelae. About 90% of infected infants look well at birth, and 10-15% of these develop hearing loss, compared with 65-70% of symptomatic infants. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 517)

**Congenital syphilis**: Late congenital syphilis has the Hutchinson triad: interstitial keratitis, notched (Hutchinson) incisors and SNHL. Clutton joints (painless symmetric knee effusions) and mulberry molars may also be present. Syphilis acquired after birth can cause sudden or fluctuating SNHL and vertigo, which often improve with penicillin plus steroids. Consider it in any sexually active adolescent with new SNHL or vertigo. It is uncommon but treatable, so FTA testing is justified when it is suspected. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 518, 527)

**Postmeningitic hearing loss**: About a third of children (33.6% in a meta-analysis) have hearing loss after bacterial meningitis. The risk is highest after pneumococcal meningitis, even though Hib was historically the most common cause. Bacteria probably reach the labyrinth through the cochlear aqueduct or the IAC, causing suppurative labyrinthitis or eighth-nerve neuritis. The loss starts early in the illness, and no antibiotic choice has been shown to prevent it. If audiometry is normal after the first few days of treatment, significant SNHL later is unlikely. The benefit of dexamethasone for preventing hearing loss in children remains unproven, although some meta-analyses show benefit in high-income settings. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 519-520)

**Mumps and measles**: Mumps hearing loss is typically *unilateral* and moderate to profound (about 0.1% of cases). It can come before or after the parotitis, or occur with no parotitis at all. Hearing loss after MMR vaccination is reported very rarely (roughly one case per 6-8 million doses), and causation is unproven. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 519)

**NICU risk factors (JCIH)**: The JCIH risk indicators for congenital, delayed-onset or progressive loss include: NICU stay longer than 5 days, ECMO, assisted ventilation, ototoxic drugs, loop diuretics, and hyperbilirubinemia requiring exchange transfusion. Infants under 1500 g (VLBW) have the highest rates. Oxygen beyond 36 weeks was the strongest risk marker in one large cohort. Loop diuretics and noise both potentiate aminoglycoside ototoxicity. Delayed-onset and progressive losses are common in NICU graduates, so a passed screen does not end follow-up. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 522-523)

**Diagnostic yield of tests**: In a series of 270 children with severe-to-profound SNHL, the yields were: MRI abnormal in 24%, CT in 18%, biallelic GJB2 in 15%, genetics consultation 25%, ophthalmology 8%, renal ultrasound 4%, ECG (long QT) 1%, FTA 0.5%. CT and MRI do not always detect the same lesions, and only MRI shows brain malformations and CMV-type changes. Biallelic GJB2 patients seldom have abnormal temporal-bone imaging, so normal imaging makes GJB2 more likely. Overall, a cause is found in 50-60% of children. Always test for the treatable causes (CMV, syphilis) and the dangerous one (long QT in bilateral severe-to-profound loss). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 526-527)

**Membranous-only malformations (normal CT)**: *Scheibe (cochleosaccular) dysplasia* is the most common inner-ear malformation in children with profound SNHL. It affects only the pars inferior (cochlea and saccule), and the utricle and semicircular canals are normal. It is linked to Usher, Jervell and Lange-Nielsen, Waardenburg, Refsum, trisomy 18 and congenital rubella. *Bing-Siebenmann* is dysplasia of the entire membranous labyrinth inside a normal bony capsule, seen with Usher and retinitis pigmentosa. *Alexander* dysplasia is confined to the basal turn and causes high-frequency SNHL. Imaging is normal in all three, which helps explain why CT/MRI is abnormal in only about 20% of children with SNHL. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 531-534)

**Michel aplasia vs labyrinthitis ossificans on CT**: Both can look like an absent labyrinth. In labyrinthitis ossificans the promontory is still convex and the middle ear is normal-sized. In Michel aplasia the promontory is flat or concave and the middle-ear space looks enlarged because there is no cochlea. MRI also helps. The distinction matters in a postmeningitic child being evaluated for a cochlear implant. Michel aplasia is associated with thalidomide exposure and Klippel-Feil. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 534)

**EVA natural history**: In the Jackler and De La Cruz series, EVA was bilateral in 94%. Hearing progressed stepwise in about 65%, often after minor head trauma, averaging about 25 dB over 6 years. Nearly a third had a conductive component even though the middle ear was normal (a third-window effect), and a mixed loss in a child strongly suggests EVA. The size of the aqueduct does not predict how severe the loss is or whether it will progress. Endolymphatic sac decompression, shunt or occlusion worsened hearing in 50-100% of patients and is contraindicated. Counsel avoidance of head trauma and barotrauma, and monitor with serial audiograms. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 525) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 538)

**Pendred testing**: Pendrin (SLC26A4, chromosome 7) is a chloride/iodide transporter. Pendred syndrome is euthyroid goiter with SNHL and is diagnosed classically by an abnormal *potassium perchlorate discharge test* (an organification defect). It is the most common syndromic cause of SNHL, at about 10% of syndromic cases. Up to 80% of patients have inner-ear anomalies (EVA with or without IP-II). The goiter usually appears in adolescence, so a child can have SLC26A4-related EVA (DFNB4) with normal thyroid function. Many experts screen SLC26A4 in every patient with EVA. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Nongenetic Hearing Loss", p 525) (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Inner Ear Anomalies", p 537-538)

**Craniofacial syndromes and their ear findings**: *Treacher Collins* (TCOF1, autosomal dominant, about 60% new mutations; a neural-crest migration defect of the first and second arches) gives bilateral, symmetric moderate-to-severe conductive loss. It comes from ossicular deformity in a small, fibrous epitympanum, and the inner ear is usually normal. *Crouzon* and *Apert* (FGFR2): about a third of Crouzon patients have a nonprogressive conductive loss, and Apert classically has congenital stapes footplate fixation. Both have eustachian tube dysfunction and OME. *Osteogenesis imperfecta* (COL1A1/COL1A2, type I with blue sclerae): conductive loss from thin, fragile stapes crura and from otosclerosis that is often aggressive. *Osteopetrosis* (malignant recessive form): mixed loss, facial palsy, optic atrophy and choanal atresia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 570, 572, 575-577)

**Chromosomal and other syndromes**: *Turner* (45,X, about 1 in 5000 females) has persistent OME that often progresses to chronic otitis media. A characteristic midfrequency ('cookie-bite') SNHL can progress in the teens, so these children need lifelong audiometry. *Noonan* (PTPN11 and others; normal karyotype; males and females; pulmonary stenosis) has a Turner-like phenotype with conductive or sensorineural loss. *Wildervanck (cervico-oculo-acoustic) syndrome* is Klippel-Feil fusion plus Duane retraction plus congenital SNHL, almost entirely in females. *Möbius* is congenital bilateral facial (and abducens) palsy, with hearing loss in 15-25%. *Hurler* (mucopolysaccharidosis I) causes mixed loss from mesenchyme filling the middle ear, plus OME. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 563, 567, 571, 572, 574, 576)

**CHARGE audiogram and BOR numbers**: The hearing loss in CHARGE is typically mixed, with a 'wedge-shaped' audiogram: the bone-conduction curve slopes down and meets a flat air-conduction curve in the low frequencies. Chronic OME and ossicular anomalies add a conductive component, and cochlear-nerve aplasia can cause profound loss. In BOR (about 1 in 40,000, autosomal dominant), the loss is mixed in about 50%, conductive in 30% and sensorineural in 20%, and may begin in childhood. Cervical sinuses open anterior to the SCM below the hyoid, and severe renal dysplasia occurs in about 6%, so renal ultrasound is required. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Anomalies of the External and Middle Ears", p 564, 570)

**Jahrsdoerfer cutoffs and outcomes**: On the 10-point scale (stapes 2 points, 1 point each for oval window, middle-ear space, facial nerve, malleus-incus complex, mastoid pneumatization, incus-stapes connection, round window, external ear), a score *below 6* means the patient is not a candidate. In one series, a score of 6 or less gave only a 45% chance of a postoperative SRT of 30 dB or better, compared with 89% for a score of 7 or more. Exclusions include *any* inner-ear anomaly (higher risk of SNHL), a temporomandibular joint lying lateral to the middle-ear cleft, a severely low tegmen, or a facial nerve covering the oval window. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 609-611)

**Atresiaplasty complications and results**: *Meatal or canal stenosis* is the most common complication and the most common reason for revision (0-25%). Triamcinolone injection and lining the meatus with a pedicled full-thickness flap reduce it. TM lateralization occurs in 0-18%, facial nerve injury in 0-7% (more often with low Jahrsdoerfer scores, and transient palsies usually recover), and SNHL in 0-7.5% (from drill energy or stapes work, and mild high-frequency loss is common). About 70% reach 25-30 dB or better in experienced hands, revision results are worse, and hearing can decline over time. The new canal is not self-cleaning and needs periodic debridement. Do not fenestrate the lateral semicircular canal. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 614-615)

**Pediatric percutaneous bone-conduction implant**: FDA labeling allows implantation from age 5 (earlier abroad). Before that, use a softband, ideally started at 6-12 months because toddlers often refuse it later, with aided thresholds around 25-30 dB, compared with about 15-18 dB once implanted. In young children with skull bone only about 2.5 mm thick, use a two-stage procedure with about 6 months for osseointegration, accepting that dura or sigmoid may be exposed. The usual site is about 5.5 cm posterosuperior to the canal. In microtia, move it to about 6.5-7 cm from the planned meatus so it does not compromise the future auricle. Skin-thinning flaps are kept about 0.6 mm thick, and revision rates in children are high (about 40%, with about 9% fixture loss). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Surgical Management of Microtia and Congenital Aural Atresia", p 616-617)

**Pediatric NOE is different**: Children with NOE are rarely diabetic, except adolescents with type 1 diabetes. They are immunocompromised from leukemia, solid tumors, malnutrition, anemia, HIV, neutropenia or immunoglobulin deficiency. In infants the bone-cartilage junction sits more medially and the tympanic ring and mastoid are undeveloped. As a result, the infection reaches the tympanic membrane, middle ear and mastoid early, and *complete facial paralysis is an early presenting sign that often does not recover*. Overall survival is better than in adults, but healing often leaves canal stenosis and cartilage deformity. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 626-627)

**Other canal infections and dermatoses**: *Otomycosis* itches more than it hurts. Aspergillus niger causes about 90% of cases and looks like cottony hyphae dusted with gray-black spores, while Candida is white. Risk factors are mastoid cavities, occlusive hearing aids, diabetes and overuse of antibiotic drops. Treat with debridement plus acidifying or antifungal agents (clotrimazole), and avoid ototoxic acetic acid, boric acid, gentian violet and cresylate if the TM is not intact. *Furunculosis* is a staphylococcal infection of a hair follicle in the lateral canal: a dry canal with focal swelling, treated with an antistaphylococcal antibiotic and incision and drainage if it forms an abscess. *Bullous myringitis* causes blebs on the TM and bony canal. It is classically linked to Mycoplasma, though ruptured bullae can also grow Pseudomonas, and it needs systemic antibiotics when the middle ear is involved. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the External Ear", p 624-625)

**AOM antibiotic choices**: First line is high-dose amoxicillin, 80-90 mg/kg/day in two doses. It has the longest time above MIC against nonsusceptible pneumococci, and the high dose overcomes most intermediate resistance. The book also uses high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate (90 mg/kg/day amoxicillin with 6.4 mg/kg/day clavulanate) for severe disease (temperature of 39 C or more, or severe otalgia), which reflects the 2004 AAP approach. Under the current AAP 2013 guideline, amoxicillin-clavulanate is chosen for amoxicillin use in the past 30 days, concurrent purulent conjunctivitis, recurrent AOM unresponsive to amoxicillin, or failure at 48-72 hours, not for severity alone. About 35% of NTHi and about 90% of Moraxella produce beta-lactamase. For penicillin allergy use cefdinir, cefuroxime, cefpodoxime or ceftriaxone. The book offers azithromycin or clarithromycin for type I allergy, but AAP 2013 notes that macrolides have limited efficacy against pneumococcus and H. influenzae. TMP-SMX is unreliable because of pneumococcal resistance. IM ceftriaxone (50 mg/kg) is given once, or as 3 daily doses for treatment failure. Clindamycin covers pneumococcus only. Give a 10-day course to children under 2 years and to those with severe or recurrent disease, and shorter courses to older children with mild illness. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 693-694, 703-705)

**CONFLICT -- observation criteria**: The book's text (built on the 2004 AAP table) states that every child under 2 years with AOM should get antibiotics. The *current* AAP/AAFP 2013 guideline allows observation with assured 48-72-hour follow-up in two groups: children 6-23 months with *nonsevere unilateral* AOM, and children 24 months or older with nonsevere AOM (unilateral or bilateral). Nonsevere means mild otalgia for less than 48 hours and temperature below 39 C. Always treat infants under 6 months, anyone with otorrhea or severe symptoms, and children 6-23 months with bilateral AOM. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 693, 708-709)

**CONFLICT -- antibiotic prophylaxis**: The site (in line with AAP 2013) says not to use prophylactic antibiotics for recurrent AOM, and that is the current guideline position. The book still presents low-dose amoxicillin prophylaxis as a shared-decision option for children with 3 or more episodes in 6 months or 4 in 12 months. In the Casselbrant trial of effusion-free children, prophylaxis cut new AOM episodes more than tubes did, but tubes gave the least total time with otitis media (6.6% vs 10% vs 15% with placebo). The book also notes that prolonged low-dose amoxicillin selects resistant pneumococci. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696, 727-729)

**CONFLICT -- antibiotics for OME**: The book recommends a 10-day amoxicillin trial as a shared-decision option before tubes for chronic OME, citing a modest benefit in a Pittsburgh trial. The current AAO-HNSF OME guideline (2016) recommends *against* antibiotics, steroids, antihistamines and decongestants for OME, which matches the site. Both sources agree that antihistamine/decongestant combinations fail (two trials in more than 1000 children), that systemic steroids clear fluid only briefly (benefit gone within 2 weeks), that intranasal steroids do not work, and that Politzer or Valsalva autoinflation was ineffective for chronic effusion in children. Antihistamines given with AOM treatment actually *prolonged* the effusion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696-698)

**Microbiology numbers**: S. pneumoniae and nontypeable H. influenzae are the leading pathogens, followed by M. catarrhalis. About a quarter to a third of AOM aspirates grow no bacteria. Since PCV7 (2000) and PCV13 (2010), pneumococcal AOM has fallen and NTHi has risen proportionally. PCV7 cut vaccine-type pneumococcal AOM by about 57%, and serotype 19A replacement disease prompted PCV13. NTHi is the main cause of the *otitis-conjunctivitis syndrome* (matched isolates in 18 of 20 episodes). The bacteriology is similar at all ages after the newborn period. Viruses are found in middle-ear fluid in about 16% (mainly RSV and rhinovirus), and viral coinfection predicts treatment failure. Spontaneous clearance without antibiotics occurs in about 20% of pneumococcal and about 50% of NTHi infections. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 672, 676, 679, 696, 701)

**CONFLICT -- water precautions**: The site, following the AAO-HNSF 2013/2022 guideline, says routine water precautions are not recommended. The book still advises keeping water out of ears with tubes: earplugs or petroleum-jelly cotton for bathing and surface-only swimming. It acknowledges a meta-analysis showing no significant increase in otorrhea without protection. Current guidance is no routine precautions, with plugs reserved for children with recurrent otorrhea or for deep/lake swimming. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 732)

**Tube sequelae numbers**: Tubes usually stay in 6-12 months (in the Pittsburgh trials, 50% had extruded at 12 months and 75% at 18 months). In meta-analysis, otorrhea occurred early after surgery in about 16%, later in 26%, was recurrent in 7.4% and chronic in 3.8%. Otorrhea occurs in two-thirds of infants with unrepaired cleft palate. Tympanosclerosis is about 50% more common after tubes but is usually cosmetic. Persistent perforation ranges from 0.5% to 25% depending on tube type (highest with long-term/T-tubes and repeat insertions), and about 3% in a series of 2604 tubes. Cholesteatoma at the insertion site occurs in about 1%. Rare intraoperative disasters are injury to a high jugular bulb or an aberrant carotid. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 730-731)

**Adenoidectomy trial evidence**: In Paradise's trial of children who had already had tubes, adenoidectomy gave 47% less time with otitis media in year 1 and 37% less in year 2. In children who had never had tubes, adenoidectomy or adenotonsillectomy for recurrent AOM helped only modestly and only in the first year, so it is not a first procedure. Casselbrant found no added benefit of adenoidectomy in 2-3-year-olds with chronic OME. A Finnish trial in 10-24-month-olds and a Canadian trial in children under 2 found no benefit either. Adding tonsillectomy gives nothing more than adenoidectomy alone (Maw, Gates). A Cochrane review found that adenoidectomy helps OME but not recurrent AOM. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 696, 698, 732-734)

**Infant vs adult tube**: The infant tube is shorter, has a smaller lumen and more compliant (floppy) cartilage with less elastin at the hinge, and runs about 10 degrees from the horizontal compared with about 45 degrees in adults. Its tensor veli palatini muscle vector is less effective, so active opening fails; that, more than the angle itself, drives underventilation. The narrowest point (isthmus) lies *within the cartilaginous portion*, not at the bony-cartilaginous junction. This narrowing creates the protective 'flask effect', which is lost when the drum is perforated or a tube is in place, allowing reflux otitis. Mucosal folds and Ostmann's fat pad are relatively larger in infants. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Otitis Media and Eustachian Tube Dysfunction", p 636-637, 728)

**Stage-based management**: For mastoiditis with periosteitis only, give IV antibiotics (cefuroxime, ampicillin-sulbactam, or piperacillin-tazobactam in place of the book's ticarcillin-clavulanate, which is no longer marketed in the US, plus vancomycin if resistant pneumococcus is possible) and perform tympanocentesis, myringotomy and usually a tube. Periosteal signs should improve within 24-48 hours. About 75% of children were cured this way without mastoidectomy. Do cortical mastoidectomy for a subperiosteal abscess (regardless of CT), CT-proven osteitis, failure to improve, or any other intratemporal or intracranial complication. Some series use needle aspiration of the abscess plus myringotomy. Erosion of the cortical plate over the sigmoid sinus was the most sensitive and specific CT sign of osteitis. CT is not required for a nontoxic child who improves quickly after drainage and IV therapy. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 789-795)

**Masked (subacute) and chronic mastoiditis**: *Subacute mastoiditis* is AOM that persists after 10 days of antibiotics, with milder but persistent fever and otalgia. In one series it was caused by H. influenzae 28%, Pseudomonas 23% and pneumococcus 16%, and 19% needed mastoidectomy, though tube placement and culture-directed therapy usually work. *Masked mastoiditis* is occult mastoid infection with a near-normal drum. It can present as fever of unknown origin or as an intracranial complication, so CT of the temporal bones belongs in the workup of any otogenic-looking intracranial infection even when otoscopy is normal. In older children, recurrent postauricular pain with a clear middle ear may be an aditus block. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 795-796)

**Facial palsy complicating AOM in children**: Half of the cases occur at age 3 or younger, often with a dehiscent tympanic segment. In acute otitis without osteitis, treat with tympanocentesis or myringotomy (a tube if there is recurrent AOM, underlying chronic OME, or prolonged drainage is needed) plus IV antibiotics covering pneumococcus and H. influenzae. Recovery is usually rapid without mastoidectomy or decompression. Perform mastoidectomy only for coalescent osteitis, CSOM or cholesteatoma. Decompression is considered for complete paralysis with electrophysiologic degeneration. In contrast, facial palsy with *CSOM or cholesteatoma* needs immediate surgical exploration. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 802-803)

**Pediatric cholesteatoma behavior**: Childhood cholesteatoma is more extensive (22% filled the middle ear and mastoid vs 6% of adults, because children's mastoids are more pneumatized). It has higher residual and recurrence rates and more ossicular necrosis. Children rarely report unilateral hearing loss, and fever is not a feature of cholesteatoma: fever plus otalgia means look for a complication. About 70% arise from retraction pockets (posterosuperior or attic), and fewer from a central perforation or atelectasis. Cleft palate carries a 7-10% cholesteatoma rate, whereas Alaska Natives, American Indians and Aboriginal Australians have heavy otitis media but rarely cholesteatoma. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 811, 814-815)

**Retraction pocket staging**: Classify atelectasis as partial or total, acute (under 3 months) or chronic (3 months or more). The posterosuperior pars tensa and the pars flaccida are the most compliant parts of the drum and carry the most risk, as does the site of an extruded tube or a healed perforation. A pocket progresses from stage 1 to stage 4 based on four features: whether it touches or adheres to an ossicle or the promontory, whether it lifts with negative pneumatic pressure (or under nitrous oxide), whether its full extent is visible, and whether it is self-cleaning and dry. Sadé (posterosuperior) and Tos (attic) grades are the eponymous systems. Tympanometry cannot diagnose atelectasis; only visual inspection can. A pocket lying on the incus or stapes warrants an early tube to prevent ossicular erosion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Complications and Sequelae of Otitis Media", p 805-806, 822)

**Recovery timing, recurrence and tumor red flags**: Bell palsy in children recovers completely in about 90% (adults: 71% complete, 84% HB I-II). If recovery begins before 3 weeks it is almost always complete. If it begins at 3 weeks to 2 months it is usually satisfactory. If it is delayed to 2-4 months, fewer than 30% reach HB I-II. Progression from paresis to complete paralysis over 3-10 days predicts degeneration in about 75%. Bell palsy recurs in about 10%, two-thirds on the opposite side. About 10% of *ipsilateral* recurrences are tumors, mostly facial neuromas. Suspect a tumor with no recovery by 6 months, slow progression beyond 3 weeks, ipsilateral recurrence, twitching before the weakness, or other neurologic signs. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Facial Paralysis in Children", p 858, 860-861, 864)

**Juvenile otosclerosis**: Children make up fewer than 15% of otosclerosis cases, and clinical disease before age 9 is rare and usually familial. Pediatric disease tends to be more aggressive, bilateral and sometimes obliterative. Autopsy studies find subclinical foci in about 4% of people aged 5-19. The air-bone gap starts in the low frequencies and widens, but its size does not predict how much of the footplate is involved. High-resolution CT may show fenestral spongiotic foci (fissula ante fenestram). In a child with a conductive loss and normal drum, congenital ossicular anomalies are more common than otosclerosis, so palpate the whole chain at exploration. GWAS loci include 7q22.1 (RELN). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 870)

**Bone dysplasias of the otic capsule**: *Osteogenesis imperfecta* (COL1A1/COL1A2 in about 90%, Sillence types I-IV and beyond, type I is van der Hoeve with blue sclerae, present in about 95% of those with CHL) causes hearing loss in about 20% of children by age 5 and about 90% of adults. The loss is mostly conductive from stapes involvement, and CT shows thickened, undermineralized capsule. *Osteopetrosis*: the infantile malignant recessive form (TCIRG1 in more than half, CLCN7) causes marrow failure, cranial nerve palsies, optic atrophy and foraminal stenosis of the carotid and jugular. It is treated with stem-cell transplant (5-year survival about 30-36%). The hearing loss is mainly conductive, and about a quarter develop SNHL from IAC narrowing. The dominant (Albers-Schönberg) form is milder. *Fibrous dysplasia* of the temporal bone causes CHL in about 80%, mostly from EAC narrowing, which carries a risk of canal cholesteatoma, and SNHL in about 17% from capsule or IAC involvement. Look for café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy (McCune-Albright). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 871-873)

**Metabolic and vascular causes in children**: *Alport syndrome* (X-linked COL4A5 in most cases, autosomal recessive COL4A3/COL4A4) is nephritis with progressive SNHL from basement membrane defects of the stria and spiral ligament. *Fabry disease* (X-linked alpha-galactosidase A deficiency) causes SNHL in about 73% of those evaluated, often high-frequency and strial, with more sudden SNHL. Enzyme replacement can partly reverse it in adults. *Mucopolysaccharidoses* most often cause chronic OME, but progressive SNHL also occurs, so monitor hearing. *Sickle cell disease* is mostly associated with middle-ear effusion, but SNHL occurs in about 3.5%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Diseases of the Labyrinthine Capsule", p 872-874)

**Traumatic CSF otorrhea**: Most traumatic CSF otorrhea stops within about 2 weeks with bed rest, head elevation of 15-25 degrees and avoiding straining. Use a lumbar drain for a persistent leak or raised ICP. Operate for a leak lasting more than 2 weeks, a large petrous defect, a late-onset leak, brain herniation or recurrent meningitis. The subtemporal (middle fossa extradural) route preserves hearing and gives direct dural access. The transmastoid route avoids a craniotomy. Diagnosis: the halo sign is suggestive only. Glucose testing is unreliable (false positives in 45-75% of nasal secretions). Beta-2 transferrin needs only a tiny sample and is highly specific. With an intact drum, CSF looks like OME and may drain from the nose when the head is lowered. High-resolution CT shows the bony defect in about 70%. Intrathecal fluorescein and MR cisternography can localize the leak. The otic capsule heals by fibrous union, so it remains a lifelong route for meningitis. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 888)

**Hearing after head trauma in children**: The most common pattern is SNHL, reported in 13-83% after head or temporal bone trauma. Labyrinthine concussion gives a 4-8 kHz noise-like notch with good discrimination. A retrocochlear pattern (poor discrimination, tone decay) comes from eighth-nerve stretch. Low-frequency losses tend to recover. Suspect ossicular disruption, and consider exploration, when the air-bone gap is more than 50 dB initially or still more than 30 dB at 6 weeks. The usual injury is incus dislocation or incudostapedial separation. The malleus is the least often injured. Children rarely report a unilateral loss, so get an audiogram after any ear trauma and repeat it every 3-6 months until stable. Avoid cortical bone grafts in children because they tend to ankylose. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 889-891, 883)

**Temporal bone rhabdomyosarcoma and LCH masquerade as otitis**: RMS is the most common pediatric temporal bone malignancy, usually embryonal, with a mean age of about 4 years. It presents as an aural polyp (54%), discharge that is often bloody, a periauricular mass, or facial palsy (in up to 64% in one series, about 30% are found because of a nerve palsy). Diagnosis is delayed about 8 weeks, and up to 50% are misread on the first biopsy. As a parameningeal site it is at least IRSG stage II, and it is treated with chemoradiation (fewer than 5% are resected). *LCH* involves the temporal bone in 15-61% of cases. It typically presents in a child under 3 with otorrhea or a polyp refractory to antibiotics, postauricular swelling and a high ESR. CT shows a punched-out lytic lesion that spares the otic capsule. Diagnosis rests on S-100/CD1a and Birbeck granules. Get a skeletal survey and systemic workup. Treatment is curettage or low-dose RT (6-10 Gy) for unifocal disease, with a cure rate above 90%, or vinblastine-prednisone for multifocal disease. Biopsy any granulation tissue in a child's ear that does not respond to treatment. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 895-902)

**Congenital cholesteatoma staging (Potsic)**: Congenital cholesteatoma accounts for 2-5% of cholesteatomas. It is a white mass behind an intact drum, most often anterosuperior, with a 3:1 male predominance and a peak age around 4. It likely arises from a persistent epidermoid formation, which normally involutes by 33 weeks. Prior AOM, OME or tubes no longer exclude the diagnosis. Potsic stages: I, a single quadrant; II, multiple quadrants; III, ossicular involvement; IV, mastoid extension. Residual disease rises with stage. A closed cyst removed intact needs no second look. An open (ruptured) cholesteatoma needs tympanomastoidectomy and staged surgery. Petrous apex congenital cholesteatoma presents in the teens or twenties with headache, hearing loss and facial twitching or palsy; it is hypodense on CT, low on T1, high on T2 and DWI-bright, unlike cholesterol granuloma, which is bright on T1. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Tumors of the Ear and Temporal Bone", p 902-905)

**Airway-fire numbers**: keep inspired oxygen at 30% or less during laser use and avoid nitrous oxide, which also supports combustion. Have a basin of water and a fire extinguisher ready, and use a laser-resistant tube matched to the wavelength in the oral cavity, oropharynx, and glottis. Tubeless alternatives when a tube blocks exposure are jet ventilation, spontaneous ventilation, or the intermittent apneic technique with saturation monitoring. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Laser Surgery", p 1659)

**Eye and field protection by wavelength**: for the patient, lubricate the eyes with a water-soluble (not oil-based, which can ignite) ointment, tape them shut, and cover with saline-soaked pads. This suffices for CO2, but visible lasers and Nd:YAG pass through water, so add aluminum foil over the pads. Staff goggles must be printed with the optical density for the wavelength in use and have side shields. Ordinary window glass stops CO2 but visible-wavelength lasers require covered windows. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Laser Surgery", p 1658–1659)

**Malignancy risk numbers**: about 11% of pediatric neck masses evaluated are malignant, and 29% of biopsied masses that looked benign proved malignant. Growth over days suggests infection. Steady growth over 4–8 weeks is the classic malignant tempo. An asymptomatic mass is the typical presentation, and systemic B symptoms are usually absent when lymphoma is confined to the neck. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1717, 1731)

**Rank order of pediatric head and neck malignancy**: lymphoma first (about 55–59%), soft-tissue sarcoma (mostly rhabdomyosarcoma) second, thyroid carcinoma third. Non-Hodgkin lymphoma is more common overall in children, but Hodgkin disease more often presents as a neck mass. Non-Hodgkin more often shows extranodal Waldeyer ring involvement and disseminated disease at presentation. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1731)

**Ectopic (lingual) thyroid**: most often at the tongue base, far more common in females, and usually the only functioning thyroid tissue. Patients may be euthyroid, so normal TSH does not exclude it. This is why some surgeons add scintigraphy when ultrasound cannot document an orthotopic gland. Technetium-99m tests iodine trapping only (same-day, low dose), whereas I-123 tests trapping and organification but costs more, carries more radiation, and takes two days. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1723, 1729)

**Branchio-oto-renal (Melnick–Fraser) syndrome**: autosomal dominant (EYA1), with bilateral preauricular pits/sinuses, cervical branchial fistulas or cysts, auricular malformation up to microtia, inner-ear anomalies such as Mondini dysplasia, and hearing loss that may be conductive, sensorineural, mixed, or sudden, plus renal anomalies ranging from mild to severe. An isolated preauricular pit carries only about a 1-in-200 chance of hearing loss, but a pit or branchial anomaly plus hearing loss is a strong indication for renal ultrasound and EYA1 testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Congenital Cysts and Sinuses of the Head and Neck", p 1740)

**First cleft types**: type I is ectoderm-only, a duplication of the membranous EAC, and does not present as a neck mass; type II contains ectoderm and mesoderm (cartilage) and can run from the EAC floor to the submandibular area, passing near (often medial to) the facial nerve. A myringeal web—a fibrous band from a fistula opening in the canal floor to the umbo—is pathognomonic of type II. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1728–1729)

**Thyroid abscess rule**: a child with a thyroid abscess or suppurative thyroiditis should be assumed to have a lower (third/fourth) branchial anomaly and undergo esophagram and direct pharyngoscopy to find the piriform sinus opening; third-cleft tracts open in the lateral piriform sinus and fourth-cleft tracts at the piriform apex. First-cleft fistulas are mapped with a catheter fistulagram followed by CT to plan facial nerve dissection. A second-cleft cyst can also sit in the parapharyngeal space lateral to the tonsil. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Imaging of Pediatric Neck Masses", p 1695)

**Cervical thymic cyst**: a rare, predominantly left-sided lateral cyst along the third-pouch thymic descent path, usually misdiagnosed preoperatively as a branchial cyst or lymphatic malformation. About 50% extend into the mediastinum (directly or via a fibrous cord), which matters for surgical planning; Hassall corpuscles in the wall are diagnostic. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Neck Masses", p 1729)

**Infectious mononucleosis**: EBV spread by saliva (incubation up to 8 weeks) causes fever, exudative tonsillitis, and cervical adenopathy in about 95%, typically nontender, 5–25 mm, and more posterior than anterior, often with generalized nodes and hepatosplenomegaly. Atypical lymphocytes are suggestive. The heterophile/monospot test is specific but not sensitive, so EBV IgM/IgG titers are used when negative. CMV and HHV-6 cause most heterophile-negative mononucleosis-like illness. Older reports say up to 95% of EBV patients given amoxicillin or ampicillin develop a pruritic maculopapular rash, but recent series put the rate nearer 30%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cervical Adenopathy", p 1751–1753)

**Airway obstruction from mononucleosis**: treat supportively, but for obstructing adenotonsillar hypertrophy give IV corticosteroids (e.g., dexamethasone every 6 hours) with pulse oximetry; nasopharyngeal airway or intubation may be needed, acute tonsillectomy for refractory obstruction is generally well tolerated despite concurrent hepatitis, and severe cases may need tracheotomy under local anesthesia. Recovery usually takes 2–4 weeks. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cervical Adenopathy", p 1751–1752)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Tuberculous cervical adenitis (scrofula due to M. tuberculosis)**: older children, often with a TB contact, bilateral nodes, and abnormal chest film. Unlike NTM it is treated medically—isoniazid and rifampin with pyrazinamide for the first 2 months, completing 6 months when culture confirms—not by excision alone. AFB stains are positive in under 50%, three early-morning gastric aspirates yield organisms in up to 70% of young children, residual nodes over 10 mm persist in 30% after therapy, and all children with TB should be offered HIV testing. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Cervical Adenopathy", p 1755)

**Radiograph cutoffs**: on a properly positioned lateral neck film (extension, inspiration), a retropharyngeal soft-tissue width over 7 mm or a retrotracheal width over 13 mm makes infection likely. Loss of cervical lordosis, gas, or an air-fluid level supports abscess. If a young child cannot be positioned, airway fluoroscopy separates real thickening from artifact. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Head and Neck Space Infections", p 1769)

**Medical trial and its limits**: uncomplicated cellulitis/adenitis without airway signs responds to antibiotics, and some small abscesses resolve on IV antibiotics alone, but up to 50% of children given a trial of IV antibiotics ultimately need drainage. Drain if there is airway compromise, no rapid improvement within 24–72 hours, an obvious abscess, or a suspected unusual organism (immunocompromise). One or two needle aspirations plus antibiotics cured about 56% in older children, best for small unilocular collections. A child afebrile and nontoxic 24 hours after drainage can switch to oral therapy and go home. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Head and Neck Space Infections", p 1785)

**Quinsy tonsillectomy data and indications**: hemorrhage after quinsy (abscess) tonsillectomy was about 1% (0–7%) in over 1,000 patients, similar to interval tonsillectomy. Recurrent PTA after a first abscess averages about 17% (6–36%) and recurrent tonsillitis about 29%. Choose quinsy tonsillectomy for airway obstruction, extension to the lateral pharyngeal space, failed aspiration/drainage, or a prior history meeting tonsillectomy criteria. Otherwise interval tonsillectomy at 4–12 weeks or aspiration alone (90% success in one series) are acceptable, and aspiration suits older cooperative children or those who cannot have anesthesia or transfusion. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Head and Neck Space Infections", p 1774–1776)

**Pediatric Ludwig technique**: Ludwig angina is by definition bilateral submandibular (supra- and inframylohyoid) cellulitis with firm floor-of-mouth induration and posterior tongue displacement, with or without abscess. Release of tissue tension is the core principle, so open decompression is advised in all but very mild early cases even without imaged pus, with early airway control (tracheotomy preferred). Make a generous horizontal incision about 1 cm above the hyoid, split the deep fascia vertically from symphysis to hyoid, divide the digastric, mylohyoid, and part of the tongue musculature in the midline, finger-dissect laterally for pockets, and pack with iodoform gauze. Mortality in reported pediatric cases was 17%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Head and Neck Space Infections", p 1783–1784, 1786)

**Why biopsy bleeds and how it spreads**: JNA is biphasic, with fibrous stroma containing slit-like 'staghorn' vascular channels that lack smooth muscle, so they cannot contract after injury. It enlarges by expansion and pressure remodeling of bone rather than infiltrative destruction; intracranial spread is usually extradural via the infratemporal fossa roof or superior orbital fissure into the cavernous sinus, producing superior orbital fissure syndrome (ophthalmoplegia, proptosis, ptosis). Supply is chiefly internal maxillary, plus ascending pharyngeal and palatine branches. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Benign Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1794–1795)

**Pediatric adjuncts**: radiation, once used for extensive intracranial disease, is no longer recommended in children because of radiation-induced malignancy risk; interferon has been used for unresectable or extensive intracranial tumors. Endoscopic resection now reaches stage IIC (partial middle turbinate or vomer removal for circumferential access, clip the sphenopalatine artery, drill tumor off the pterygoid root and sphenoid face); orbital or intracranial extension generally needs open or combined approaches (lateral rhinotomy, midfacial degloving, posterior maxillary wall removal, neurosurgical team). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Benign Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1796–1797)

**Rhabdomyosarcoma by site**: about 35% of pediatric RMS arises in the head and neck, 70% before age 12 and 43% before age 5. Orbit (most common orbital malignancy of childhood) presents as rapidly progressive unilateral proptosis. Nasopharyngeal and sinonasal tumors in preschoolers mimic otitis media with effusion, rhinorrhea, obstruction, or 'sinusitis' headache with months of delay. Aural RMS presents as unilateral bloody otorrhea with a soft polyp in the canal or middle ear mistaken for otitis, and about 50% already have neurologic deficits, most often facial palsy. Multiple cranial neuropathies imply skull-base/CNS spread. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1812)

**RMS staging workup**: parameningeal primaries (nasopharynx, sinuses, middle ear, infratemporal fossa) need CT plus MRI and lumbar puncture with CSF cytology. Systemic workup includes chest imaging, bone scan, and bone marrow aspirate/biopsy (lung, bone, and marrow are the common metastatic sites). Clinically positive neck nodes occur in about 7% of non-orbital head and neck primaries but essentially never with orbital primaries. Distant metastases are present in about 13% overall versus about 4% for orbit. Staging uses the postsurgical IRS clinical group (I complete resection, II microscopic residual or resected nodes, III gross residual/biopsy only, IV distant metastases) plus pretreatment TNM in which orbit and nonparameningeal head and neck are favorable sites. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1812–1813)

**RMS treatment principles**: all children get multiagent chemotherapy. Resection is done only when it causes no major functional loss and would let radiation be omitted or reduced (often superficial nonparameningeal sites). Orbital RMS is treated with biopsy plus chemoradiation (3-year relapse-free survival about 91% in IRS I, versus 46% parameningeal and 75% other sites). For IRS group III disease, debulking adds nothing over biopsy. A clinically negative neck needs no treatment beyond chemotherapy. A positive neck gets neck dissection plus radiation. Radiation late effects include facial hypoplasia, malocclusion, dental disease, xerostomia, osteoradionecrosis, and second sarcomas. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1813–1814)

**Burkitt lymphoma**: a highly proliferative B-cell NHL with c-myc translocation and a 'starry sky' pattern. Endemic (African) BL (mean age about 9) is EBV-positive in 80–90% and presents as a jaw mass, maxilla more than mandible, with loose teeth, trismus, or proptosis. Sporadic (US) BL (mean age about 12) is EBV-associated in only 15–20%, usually abdominal (ileocecal), with about one-quarter in the head and neck as asymptomatic nodes or Waldeyer ring masses. Treatment is urgent multiagent chemotherapy. Surgery is for diagnosis. Localized head and neck disease has about 90% long-term survival. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1811–1812)

**Pediatric neuroblastoma in the neck**: neuroblastoma is the most common extracranial solid malignancy under age 5 (40% diagnosed before age 1), but only 2–5% of primaries are cervical sympathetic. Most neck disease is metastatic from below the diaphragm (also skull, orbit, jaw). A primary cervical tumor can present with Horner syndrome or heterochromia iridis, airway or feeding compromise, or lower cranial neuropathies. Calcification is seen in about 50% on CT, urine catecholamines (VMA/HVA) are elevated in 70–90%, and MIBG, bone scan, and marrow biopsy complete staging. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1823)

**Pediatric NPC numbers**: nasopharyngeal malignancy is about 1% of childhood cancers (mostly RMS and NPC). Pediatric NPC is mostly WHO type IIb undifferentiated nonkeratinizing, nearly always EBV-positive, more common in Black adolescents in US series, and over 80% present at AJCC stage IV with neck nodes after a median 4–5 months of symptoms mistaken for URI. Workup adds bone scan, chest/abdominal CT, marrow biopsy for advanced disease, and CSF cytology with skull-base invasion. Treatment combines chemotherapy with radiation (IMRT/proton to spare growth), yet 20–50% relapse, mostly within 1–2 years. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1825–1826)

**Pediatric DTC presentation**: solitary thyroid nodules are uncommon in children (0.2–2%) but 14–40% are malignant; the female predominance is weaker (about 1:1.3). Children usually present with a firm painless mass and normal thyroid function, yet 45–75% have palpable nodal metastases and about 15% lung and 5% bone metastases at diagnosis—more with radiation history. Despite this, mortality is about 2.4% over 12–33 years though recurrence is 10–35%. Childhood thyroid cancer rose 62-fold near Chernobyl; this chapter suggests thyroid ultrasound 5 years after head/neck or chest radiation and every 3 years thereafter. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1818–1820)

**Pediatric DTC surgery**: this chapter advises lobectomy with frozen section for diagnosis, total or near-total thyroidectomy for bilobar, nodal, metastatic, or locally invasive disease (to enable I-131 ablation), modified neck dissection only for clinically or radiologically positive nodes, no elective neck dissection, and avoiding laryngectomy or tracheoesophageal resection even with infiltration. Current 2015 ATA pediatric guidelines go further, recommending total thyroidectomy for most children with DTC, therapeutic central (and lateral) neck dissection for evident nodes, selective prophylactic central dissection, and risk-adapted rather than routine RAI. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1820)

**Prophylactic thyroidectomy timing**: this chapter uses the older three-level scheme—level 3 (MEN2B, codon M918T) before 6 months, level 2 (codons 611, 618, 620, 634) before 5 years, level 1 (609, 768, 790, 791, 804, 891) without consensus. The current 2015 ATA scheme instead groups M918T as highest risk (thyroidectomy in the first year), C634/A883F as high risk (by about age 5, guided by calcitonin), and the rest as moderate risk (timed by calcitonin surveillance). MEN2B MTC can appear before age 1. Cause-specific mortality is about 7% for familial versus 23% for sporadic MTC at 18 years. Hirschsprung disease is associated with RET mutations. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Malignant Tumors of the Head and Neck", p 1820–1821)

**Pediatric Graves therapy**: antithyroid drugs control over 95% but relapse is frequent after stopping and drug toxicity (rash, arthralgia, agranulocytosis) occurs in 5–45%; RAI is used sparingly in children; surgery is for drug failure, noncompliance, or toxicity, and total thyroidectomy is preferred because subtotal resection leaves persistent hyperthyroidism in 25–50% and recurrences can appear 10–25 years later. This chapter lists PTU and methimazole interchangeably and favors PTU for severe disease and neonates; current practice avoids PTU in children because of its boxed warning for severe hepatotoxicity, making methimazole the drug of choice (PTU reserved for first-trimester pregnancy or thyroid storm). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Thyroid", p 1843)

**Pediatric nodule workup**: nodules are present in only 1–2% of children but about one-quarter to one-third are malignant (ATA pediatric guidance cites about 22-26%, vs about 5% in adults). Follicular adenoma is the most common cause of a solitary pediatric nodule, and multinodular goiter carries only 1–7% malignancy. Start with TSH, calcitonin, and ultrasound (microcalcification, indistinct margins, heterogeneous echogenicity are suspicious). A suppressed TSH prompts scintigraphy for a hot nodule. Up to 50% of cancers have a cystic component and about 8% of cystic lesions are malignant. Ultrasound-guided FNA is now recommended in children (ATA pediatric guidance). (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Thyroid", p 1843–1845)

**Why no medullary TGDC carcinoma**: thyroid cell nests are found in about 62% of TGDC specimens. TGDC carcinoma (about 1.5%) is 92% papillary, with follicular and Hurthle cell types, but medullary carcinoma never arises there because parafollicular C cells derive from the ultimobranchial body (fourth pouch) rather than the median anlage—supporting a de novo origin. Up to 30% have a synchronous carcinoma in the orthotopic gland. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Thyroid", p 1841)

**Pediatric ATLS points**: jaw thrust (never chin tilt) and orotracheal intubation with in-line stabilization. Needle rather than surgical cricothyroidotomy below about age 11–12 because the cricothyroid membrane is tiny, and tracheotomy in an unintubated child is hard because soft cartilage is difficult to palpate. Hypoventilation is the leading cause of pediatric cardiac arrest (infants breathe 40–60/min). Blood pressure stays normal until 25–30% of blood volume is lost, so tachycardia, delayed capillary refill, and weak pulses are the early shock signs. Use two large-bore IVs or intraosseous access, warm all fluids, and grade neurologic status with the pediatric GCS or AVPU. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Neck", p 1852)

**Cord injury without fracture**: because the pediatric spine is flexible, significant spinal cord injury can occur with a normal bony CT (SCIWORA), so a complete neurologic exam and MRI—not CT alone—clear the cord. MRI also clears the neck for positioning in children who cannot cooperate. Concomitant cord injury accompanies about 25% of severe cervical spine injuries, and nerve root injury another 25%. Confusion or combativeness may be hypoxia rather than brain injury, so check oximetry before sedating. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Injuries of the Neck", p 1853, 1858)

**Treacher Collins vs craniofacial microsomia**: Treacher Collins (mandibulofacial dysostosis, TCOF1/treacle on chromosome 5, autosomal dominant, about 60% new mutations) is bilateral and symmetric—downslanting palpebral fissures, lower-lid colobomas with absent medial lashes, malar/zygomatic and mandibular hypoplasia, bilateral microtia with canal atresia and conductive loss, sometimes cleft palate and choanal atresia, often needing tracheostomy. Craniofacial (hemifacial) microsomia/oculoauriculovertebral spectrum, including Goldenhar, is usually sporadic and asymmetric—ramus/TMJ hypoplasia with chin deviation to the affected side and upward occlusal cant, ipsilateral microtia and ossicular malformation, possible facial nerve dysfunction, and cleft palate in about 25%. Isolated microtia may be its microform. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Craniofacial Development and Congenital Anomaly: A Contemporary Review of Processes and Pathogenesis", p 1875)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Syndromic cleft genes to know**: Van der Woude syndrome (autosomal dominant, IRF6) is the classic syndromic CL/P with lower-lip pits—examine the lower lip of every cleft child and counsel 50% recurrence; X-linked cleft palate with ankyloglossia (CPX) is due to TBX22; EEC syndrome (ectrodactyly, ectodermal dysplasia, clefting; p63) combines cleft hand and abnormal skin, teeth, and hair with CL/P; Apert syndrome clefts are linked to the FGFR2 Ser252Trp mutation; velocardiofacial (22q11.2 deletion, TBX1) classically causes submucous cleft palate with conotruncal heart defects. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Craniofacial Development and Congenital Anomaly: A Contemporary Review of Processes and Pathogenesis", p 1872, 1874)

**Stepwise airway algorithm**: prone positioning, then high-flow nasal cannula or nasal CPAP (to 'break the seal' of the tongue on the posterior pharyngeal wall), then a correctly sized and secured nasopharyngeal tube (the infant larynx is high, so length matters), then intubation and surgery—tongue-lip adhesion, subperiosteal floor-of-mouth release, glossopexy, mandibular distraction, or tracheotomy. Watch for columellar/alar pressure necrosis from nasal interfaces and humidify gases. Isolated PRS 'catches up' with mandibular growth and neuromotor maturation, whereas Treacher Collins or craniofacial microsomia often needs long-term tracheotomy. Obtain polysomnography and echocardiography because chronic partial obstruction causes cor pulmonale. Mortality is mostly from OSA and failure to thrive. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Primary Care of Infants and Children With Cleft Palate", p 1879–1881)

**Pediatric facial fracture patterns**: children have a small face-to-cranium ratio, elastic bone, cartilaginous sutures, and unerupted teeth, so they sustain more skull and greenstick fractures and fewer classic Le Fort patterns (oblique craniofacial fractures through the skull base, frontal bone, orbit, and maxilla are typical). About 10% have associated cervical spine injury, and intracranial injury is common. Before the frontal sinus develops (begins about age 6, complete about 20), forehead/orbital roof fractures are skull-base fractures and can become 'growing skull fractures' (dural tear with leptomeningeal cyst) presenting with pulsatile exophthalmos or vertical dystopia. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Pediatric Plastic Surgery of the Head and Neck", p 1895)

**Epidemiology and natural history**: infantile hemangioma affects about 1 in 10 white infants (less often Black or Asian infants), with a 3:1 female predominance and higher risk in low-birth-weight and preterm infants; 60% are in the head and neck. Proliferation runs about 4–10 months (deep lesions up to 2 years), involution begins around 12–18 months, and 20–40% leave residual laxity, telangiectasia, fibrofatty tissue, or scarring. This chapter quotes the classic rule of maximal involution in 50% by age 5 and 90% by age 9; more recent data show most growth is finished by about 5 months and most involution by about age 4, which is why the AAP 2019 guideline urges early referral (by about 1 month) for high-risk lesions. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1901–1902)

**Multiple and segmental hemangiomas**: up to 20% of infants have multiple lesions. The book uses six or more cutaneous hemangiomas, and current AAP 2019 guidance uses five or more, as the trigger for screening for visceral (especially hepatic) hemangiomas with abdominal ultrasound and thyroid tests. Hepatic lesions can cause hepatomegaly, GI bleeding, high-output heart failure, anemia or profound consumptive hypothyroidism. Segmental lesions are plaque-like, proliferate up to about 18 months, ulcerate more, rarely involute completely, and carry PHACE risk (posterior fossa anomalies such as Dandy–Walker, hemangioma, arterial anomalies, cardiac/aortic arch defects, eye anomalies, sternal cleft or supraumbilical raphe), with neurologic sequelae in over 50%. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1901, 1904–1905)

**High-risk sites**: about 65% of beard-distribution hemangiomas (chin, jawline, preauricular) have airway involvement, usually supraglottic or subglottic, and they often involve the parotid and parapharyngeal space with a 12–16 month proliferative phase, airway compression, and recurrent otitis media. Periocular lesions cause astigmatic, strabismic, or deprivation amblyopia (deprivation can occur after as little as 1 week; untreated children over age 1 reach 75% amblyopia), so refer to ophthalmology immediately. Nasal tip lesions (about 16% of facial hemangiomas) splay the medial crura and are often excised before school age; ear lesions can occlude the canal, and lip lesions ulcerate and impair feeding. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1905–1906)

**Ulceration and older therapies**: ulceration is the most common complication (nose, lips, periorbital, during rapid growth)—treat with analgesia, gentle cleansing, topical antibiotic, occlusive dressings, oral antibiotics for cellulitis, and PDL or excision for refractory ulcers. This 2014 chapter still lists corticosteroids as first line (oral prednisolone 2–3 mg/kg/day for 4–6 weeks then taper; intralesional triamcinolone/betamethasone up to about 2.5 mL with a 70–90% response but risk of retinal artery embolization in periocular injection; topical clobetasol for small lesions), with vincristine and interferon (spastic diplegia in 10–30%) as salvage and propranolol described as an emerging option. Current AAP 2019 guidance makes oral propranolol first-line systemic therapy (and topical timolol for small superficial lesions), with steroids second line. (Bluestone & Stool 5e, Ch "Hemangiomas and Vascular Malformations", p 1909–1910)

**Choosing the statistical test**: pick by independent vs paired samples and data scale. Independent numeric data use the t test (Mann-Whitney U if nonparametric); paired numeric data use the paired t test (Wilcoxon signed rank); dichotomous independent data use chi-squared or Fisher exact; paired dichotomous data use McNemar; three or more groups use ANOVA (Kruskal-Wallis if nonparametric); censored time-to-event data use log-rank with Cox regression for predictors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 2, p 14)

**Non-treatment explanations for improvement**: regression to the mean, natural history, placebo, Hawthorne (being observed) and halo (novelty and attention) effects can all produce apparent benefit in an uncontrolled study, which is why an uncontrolled series cannot show efficacy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 2, p 10)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Local anesthetic maximum doses**: lidocaine is about 4.5-5 mg/kg plain and 7 mg/kg with epinephrine (2% lidocaine = 20 mg/mL, so about 17.5 mL plain for 70 kg); bupivacaine is 2-3 mg/kg. Topical, infiltrated and IV lidocaine doses add together. Toxicity starts with CNS excitation and seizures, then arrhythmias and cardiovascular collapse, which may not respond to ACLS; give IV lipid emulsion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 5, p 53-54) (Cummings 7e, Ch 19, p 271)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Neuromuscular blockers**: succinylcholine works in 45-60 s and lasts 5-8 min. It is contraindicated with malignant hyperthermia risk, hyperkalemia, raised intracranial or intraocular pressure, and recent burns, stroke or denervation, where receptor upregulation causes a dangerous potassium rise. Pseudocholinesterase deficiency (about 1:2800; diagnosed by dibucaine number) prolongs paralysis. Rocuronium is the rapid-sequence alternative (onset 60-75 s, lasts 30-40 min). Sugammadex reverses it at 2, 4 or 16 mg/kg for moderate, deep or immediate reversal; it is renally cleared and reduces hormonal contraceptive effect for 1 week. (Cummings 7e, Ch 5, p 52-53)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Induction and inhaled agents**: etomidate keeps hemodynamics stable but suppresses the adrenal glands and causes myoclonus. Dexmedetomidine (an alpha-2 agonist) sedates with little respiratory depression; its main side effect is bradycardia. Sevoflurane is the agent of choice for mask induction. Nitrous oxide expands closed gas spaces, so avoid it in middle ear surgery; it also supports combustion, so lower FiO2 with air, not N2O. MAC is the inhaled concentration at which 50% of patients do not move to incision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 5, p 51-52)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Malignant hyperthermia**: triggered by volatile agents or succinylcholine, even in a patient with prior uneventful anesthetics. The earliest sign is rising end-tidal CO2 that does not correct with hyperventilation, then tachycardia, mixed acidosis, hyperkalemia and myoglobinuria; fever is late. Stop triggers, give dantrolene, switch to TIVA and support the circulation (MHAUS hotline available). (Cummings 7e, Ch 5, p 71)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Difficult-airway prediction**: unanticipated difficult intubation occurs in 1-3% of cases. Combining Mallampati class with thyromental distance predicts better than either alone, but neither is fully sensitive. Mallampati must be scored without a tongue blade. Higher-risk groups include angioedema, active airway bleeding, head and neck tumor, prior difficult airway, limited cervical mobility, prior tracheotomy or laryngectomy, and BMI over 30. Cummings cites the 2013 ASA guideline, now replaced by the current 2022 ASA guideline, which likewise favors video laryngoscopy and supraglottic airways for rescue. The Vortex aid allows no more than 3 attempts per noninvasive technique before moving to front-of-neck access. (Cummings 7e, Ch 5, p 54-60)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Emergency cricothyrotomy**: the cricothyroid membrane is about 6-8 mm tall and 2 cm wide, with the cords 0.5-1 cm above it. Steps: stabilize the larynx with the nondominant hand, make a vertical skin incision, make a horizontal incision through the lower membrane, spread with a clamp or hook, then place a 5.0 cuffed tube. Relative contraindications are age under 10, unpalpable landmarks or expanding hematoma, and laryngeal disease with subglottic extension. Convert to a tracheotomy once stable. Transtracheal needle ventilation (14-gauge, angled 30 degrees caudally) oxygenates for only 30-60 min because CO2 builds up. (Cummings 7e, Ch 6, p 77-79)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Awake fiberoptic intubation setup**: give glycopyrrolate about 30 min before (a drying agent that does not cross the blood-brain barrier) and little or no sedation if the airway is compromised. Topicalize with benzocaine spray, nebulized 2% lidocaine and a transtracheal 2 mL 2% lidocaine injection (or superior laryngeal nerve blocks), plus a nasal decongestant and 4% lidocaine. Sit the patient up. Fixed stenosis, heavy bleeding and an uncooperative patient are contraindications. If the tube catches, rotate it 90 degrees. (Cummings 7e, Ch 6, p 74-76)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Coronary stents and bridging**: delay elective surgery at least 1 month after a bare-metal stent and ideally 6 months after a drug-eluting stent, and current ACC/AHA guidance waits about 12 months after stenting for an acute coronary syndrome (Cummings says 6 months after stenting for MI). Reserve heparin bridging for high thrombotic risk: mechanical valve, active cancer, stroke or TIA within 3 months, venous thromboembolism within 3 months, atrial fibrillation with CHADS2 5-6, or a severe clotting disorder. Low-bleeding-risk procedures such as endoscopy and biopsy can continue anticoagulation. Platelets should be above 50,000-70,000 before surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 4, p 44, 47)

**Preoperative endocrine and pulmonary red flags**: assume adrenal suppression after more than 3 weeks of glucocorticoids and give stress-dose steroids. Pheochromocytoma requires alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine, at least 10 days) before any beta-blocker. PaO2 below 60 or PaCO2 above 50, or FEV1/FVC below 50%, mark high pulmonary risk; heavy smokers have 3 times the pulmonary complications. Order labs according to the history and exam, not routinely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 4, p 45-47)

**First tube change**: by AAO-HNS consensus, an open tracheotomy may first be changed on days 3-5, but a percutaneous tracheostomy should not be changed before day 10 because of false-passage risk. If a percutaneous tube dislodges before day 7, intubate from above rather than recannulate blindly. (Cummings 7e, Ch 7, p 88)

**Late complications**: tracheoinnominate fistula (about 0.7%, 78% occur 3-4 weeks after surgery) is linked to a low stoma, malnutrition, radiation, steroids and neck hyperextension. Treat with cuff overinflation or tamponade, then sternotomy and innominate ligation (about 50% mortality) or an endovascular stent. Keep cuff pressure below the 25-30 mm Hg mucosal perfusion pressure to prevent stenosis. After more than 4 months of cannulation, 70% leave a tracheocutaneous fistula. Radiation and Björk flaps increase this risk. Routine post-tracheotomy chest radiographs are not needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 7, p 86-88)

**Nodal size and morphology**: most normal cervical nodes are 5-10 mm; the jugulodigastric node can reach 15 mm. Retropharyngeal nodes are abnormal above 5 mm in adults and 10 mm in children. Nodes over 10-15 mm are suspicious and over 20 mm frequently malignant. Central low density (a focal defect) or rim enhancement means metastasis even in a normal-sized node. Occult nodal disease occurs in 15-40% of HNSCC. CT staging accuracy is 87-93%, vs 70-82% for palpation. Tumor contact over 75% of the carotid circumference suggests invasion; under 25% makes it unlikely. (Cummings 7e, Ch 8, p 129-131)

**Parapharyngeal fat displacement localizes the space of origin**: pharyngeal mucosal space masses push it laterally; deep-lobe parotid masses push it medially; masticator space masses push it posteromedially; carotid space masses push it anteriorly; retropharyngeal masses push it anterolaterally. Because the parapharyngeal space itself contains few structures, most lesions there arise from a neighboring space. (Cummings 7e, Ch 8, p 108-115)

**PET timing and DWI**: wait at least 2-3 months after surgery or radiation before FDG-PET (12 weeks is common practice) to avoid inflammatory false positives. FDG half-life is about 110 minutes. On DWI, malignant tumors have lower ADC than benign ones, lymphoma lower than carcinoma, and pleomorphic adenoma high ADC. (Cummings 7e, Ch 8, p 97-98, 105)

**Who can avoid drainage**: about 60% of deep neck infections resolve on IV antibiotics alone. A stable, healthy patient whose abscess is under 2.5 cm and in a single space can have a 48-72 hour antibiotic trial. A trial is reasonable in almost all stable children. Do not withhold steroids for airway edema. Airway narrowing under 50% often responds to medical therapy; over 50% needs urgent airway control, and awake fiberoptic intubation is feasible if a 5-6 mm scope can pass. (Cummings 7e, Ch 9, p 149, 151)

**Workup pearls**: exam alone misjudges the involved spaces in 70% of cases, so obtain contrast CT, which still cannot reliably separate phlegmon from abscess. On a lateral film, prevertebral soft tissue at C2 over 7 mm in adults or 5 mm in children suggests retropharyngeal infection. About 5% of deep neck infections in adults over 40 involve a necrotic malignant node. Congenital cysts cause 10-15% of pediatric cases, so suspect one when infection recurs. (Cummings 7e, Ch 9, p 141, 148)

**Vascular complications**: suspect carotid pseudoaneurysm or rupture with a pulsatile mass, Horner syndrome, palsies of CN IX-XII, an expanding hematoma or a sentinel oronasal bleed. Cavernous sinus thrombosis (30-40% mortality) spreads through the valveless ophthalmic veins and causes proptosis, ophthalmoplegia and a sluggish dilated pupil. Diagnose it with contrast MRI and treat with antibiotics plus anticoagulation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 9, p 153)

**Drainage route for descending mediastinitis**: if collections are confined to the anterosuperior mediastinum above the carina, bilateral transcervical drainage along the prevertebral plane is often enough. If disease extends below the upper mediastinum or into multiple compartments, thoracotomy or thoracic surgery is needed. In children, risk factors are age under 2, retropharyngeal involvement and MRSA. (Cummings 7e, Ch 9, p 153-154)

**MRSA in infants**: MRSA is now the most common community isolate in deep neck infections in children under 2, and S. aureus from the Waldeyer ring is more common in children than adults. Clindamycin is first-line, but 5-10% of pediatric MRSA isolates resist it. Switch to TMP-SMX or vancomycin if there is no response in 24-48 hours. (Cummings 7e, Ch 9, p 141, 150)

**PTLD**: EBV-driven, mostly B-cell lymphoproliferation that is the second most common malignancy after skin cancer in transplant recipients. Incidence is about 2-3% in adults and about 8% in children (EBV-naive). It is highest after intestinal or multiorgan transplant and lowest after renal transplant, and most cases occur within 2 years. About 40% present in the head and neck, often as adenotonsillar hypertrophy with mononucleosis-like illness and airway obstruction. First-line treatment is to reduce immunosuppression, which works in up to half of patients, then rituximab or chemotherapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 10, p 165)

**Skin cancer after transplant**: transplant recipients have the highest nonmelanoma skin cancer risk and develop SCC about twice as often as BCC, reversing the usual ratio. Kaposi sarcoma also occurs in transplant recipients; switching from cyclosporine to sirolimus may make lesions regress. (Cummings 7e, Ch 10, p 163, 166)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Laryngeal amyloidosis**: usually localized light-chain disease. It most often involves the true and false folds and ventricles, causing hoarseness and sometimes stridor. Diagnose with biopsy showing apple-green birefringence with Congo red. Screen for myeloma (CBC, renal and liver tests, urine Bence Jones protein). Treat with microdebrider or CO2 laser excision. Recurrence is common, so follow long term. Survival matches the general population. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 181-182)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Laryngeal granulomatous and autoimmune disease**: GPA presents with subglottic stenosis in 10-20% and can be ANCA-negative in up to 20% with airway disease. Sarcoidosis favors the supraglottis (epiglottis first) with pale, turban-like thickening and spares the cords. Rheumatoid arthritis involves the larynx in 25-30%, causing cricoarytenoid ankylosis that can fix both cords or submucosal rheumatoid nodules. In pemphigus of the larynx, bullae are rarely seen. Look for tan fibrinous erosions with an erythematous halo on the supraglottis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 180-182)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Infectious laryngitis that mimics cancer**: laryngeal TB now usually occurs without pulmonary symptoms (the PPD is usually positive). Test these patients for HIV. Histoplasmosis and blastomycosis (Ohio and Mississippi valleys) form exophytic or ulcerative lesions. Blastomycosis shows pseudoepitheliomatous hyperplasia and broad-based budding yeast. Cryptococcus affects the true folds in immunocompromised hosts. Biopsy with fungal and AFB stains before calling SCC. (Cummings 7e, Ch 11, p 183-184)

**Immune-mediated mucosal disease**: lichen planus shows Wickham striae (reticular) or erosive lesions on the buccal mucosa, gingiva and tongue. It carries a small malignant-transformation risk, so recheck erosive lesions. Pemphigus vulgaris is caused by anti-desmoglein 3 antibodies with suprabasal acantholysis and a positive Nikolsky sign. Mucous membrane pemphigoid is subepithelial, causes desquamative gingivitis and can scar the conjunctiva to blindness. Erythema multiforme (often HSV-triggered) causes target skin lesions and crusted lips. Stevens-Johnson syndrome is usually drug-induced. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 193)

**Systemic clues in the mouth**: Addison disease causes diffuse mucocutaneous pigmentation (not seen in secondary adrenal insufficiency). Crohn disease causes cobblestoning and deep granulomatous ulcers. Ulcerative colitis can cause pyostomatitis. Dialysis patients get uremic stomatitis and brown tumors (giant cell lesions) from hyperparathyroidism. Pregnancy gingivitis affects about two-thirds of pregnancies, and pyogenic granuloma (pregnancy tumor) under 10%. Leukemia can first present with gingival hyperplasia, bleeding or petechiae. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 190-197)

**MRONJ risk**: Cummings quotes about 0.4% with oral bisphosphonates for osteoporosis and 5-20% with IV antiresorptive therapy. **Current view**: the AAOMS 2022 position paper gives much lower estimates, under about 0.05% at osteoporosis doses and roughly 1-5% for cancer patients on zoledronic acid or denosumab. Treatment ranges from local debridement to resection, and nonvascularized bone grafts are not recommended. Head and neck cancer patients need dental evaluation and treatment before surgery or radiation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 12, p 189)

**Fourth Schuknecht type, cochlear (inner ear) conductive presbycusis**: caused by stiffening or atrophy of the spiral ligament, mainly in the apical turn. It gives a bilateral sloping loss with preserved word recognition. Sensory type gives a steep high-frequency loss with lipofuscin; strial type gives a flat loss in the 3rd-6th decades with good discrimination and good aid benefit; neural type gives discrimination worse than thresholds and poor aid benefit. (Cummings 7e, Ch 13, p 199)

topic: Pain Management in the Head & Neck Patient
text: **Opioid-sparing evidence**: about 6% of opioid-naive surgical patients still fill opioids 3-6 months later, and over 60% of those on 90 days of continuous opioids stay on them. A meta-analysis of NSAIDs after tonsillectomy found no increase in bleeding, reoperation or readmission. Preoperative gabapentin (for example 1200 mg) reduces pain and opioid use after thyroidectomy and septoplasty. Low-dose ketamine is antihyperalgesic and helps opioid-tolerant patients. Chronic opioids cause tolerance, opioid-induced hyperalgesia and dose-dependent hypogonadism. (Cummings 7e, Ch 14, p 207-212)

**ICSD-3 diagnosis and screening**: OSA requires either 5 or more obstructive events per hour (apneas, hypopneas or RERAs) with symptoms or a comorbidity, or 15 or more per hour regardless of symptoms. UARS is now classified within OSA. STOP-BANG 3 or more means high risk and 5-8 means high probability of moderate-to-severe OSA (sensitive but not specific). Epworth above 10 suggests excessive sleepiness. Women more often report insomnia, palpitations and ankle edema. (Cummings 7e, Ch 15, p 216-218)

**Four OSA endotypes**: (1) a narrow or collapsible airway (Pcrit above atmospheric pressure); (2) poor dilator (genioglossus) responsiveness; (3) a low arousal threshold; and (4) high loop gain (an unstable ventilatory controller). Fujita types: I = retropalatal only, II = retropalatal plus retrolingual, III = retrolingual only. (Cummings 7e, Ch 15, p 217)

**More profile norms**: nasofacial angle 30-40 degrees (ideal 36); nasomental angle 120-132 degrees, with lips about 4 mm (upper) and 2 mm (lower) behind the nasomental line; Goode projection ratio 0.55-0.60; Simons tip projection about equal to upper lip length (1:1); columellar show 3-5 mm; upper-to-lower lip height 1:2; mentocervical angle 80-95 degrees. Ideal chin per Gonzalez-Ulloa is on the zero meridian (nasion perpendicular to Frankfort). The upper lid crease is about 11 mm (7-15) from the lash line, and the brow peaks above the lateral limbus. (Cummings 7e, Ch 16, p 240-244)

topic: Basal Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Aggressive features and syndromes**: Cummings lists these higher-risk features: size over 6 mm on the face or over 10 mm on the forehead, scalp or neck, perineural invasion, non-nodular or non-superficial subtype, prior radiation and ill-defined borders. These size cutoffs come from the older area-based NCCN scheme. Current NCCN guidelines (since 2022) treat a BCC of any size on the head or neck as high risk by location. About 20% are infiltrative. Gorlin syndrome is autosomal dominant (PTCH1) with hundreds of BCCs from adolescence. Xeroderma pigmentosum is autosomal recessive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 17, p 254-256)

topic: Cutaneous Squamous Cell Carcinoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Precursors and mimics**: an actinic keratosis progresses at about 0.24% per lesion per year (about 10% chance over 10 years that at least one becomes SCC). Bowen disease (SCC in situ) progresses at about 5% per lesion per year. Keratoacanthoma grows to about 2.5 cm in 3-8 weeks and may involute, but it mimics SCC; excise it with adequate depth (punch biopsy is not diagnostic) or use intralesional 5-FU. Multiple KAs suggest Muir-Torre or Ferguson-Smith syndrome. PDT is FDA-approved only for actinic keratoses. (Cummings 7e, Ch 17, p 257-258)

**Revision technique and timing**: many unfavorable scars can be revised after the first 60-90 days, and early realignment may speed maturation. Scars otherwise keep improving for 12-36 months. Dermabrasion works best 6-8 weeks after injury or revision. Z-plasty lengthens by about 25%, 50% and 75% at 30, 45 and 60 degrees. W-plasty and geometric broken-line limbs should be 5-7 mm and do not lengthen the scar. Wait 6-12 months after isotretinoin before dermabrasion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 18, p 260-264)

**Keloid regimen numbers**: excision alone recurs in 45-100% of keloids, so always add an adjuvant (steroid, 5-FU, radiation or pressure).
