Intralesional triamcinolone 10-40 mg/mL every 2-4 weeks, then monthly. Triamcinolone with 5-FU beats either alone. Silicone sheeting should be worn 8-12 hours a day for 6-12 months. Keloids are up to 15 times more common in darker skin. Imiquimod helps only ear keloids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 18, p 264-267)

**Facial burns**: the head and neck make up about 10% of total body surface area. Combined facial and inhalation burns most often need airway control, and edema peaks over hours. With anterior neck burns, intubate rather than perform an early tracheotomy. Use topical agents (silver sulfadiazine, mafenide, bacitracin) rather than prophylactic systemic antibiotics. Excise and graft wounds not healed by 7-14 days; do not mesh facial split-thickness grafts. A child's electrical-cord oral commissure burn is managed conservatively with a splint at about 3 weeks; labial artery bleeding can occur when the eschar separates. (Cummings 7e, Ch 19, p 282-284)

**Auricular hematoma and frostbite**: incise and drain an auricular hematoma promptly and bolster it with through-and-through mattress sutures to prevent cauliflower ear. Treat frostbite of the nose and ears with rapid rewarming in 40-42 °C water for 15-30 min, no early debridement, aloe vera and ibuprofen, plus tetanus prophylaxis. For a near-total auricular avulsion, replant on the pedicle; options for a total avulsion include the pocket principle (Baudet) or a TPF flap. (Cummings 7e, Ch 19, p 277-278, 284-285)

**Angle fracture fixation data**: Champy described a single 2.0-mm miniplate along the external oblique line (tension zone) with no chewing on that side for 6 weeks. Because the tension zone shifts, others place two miniplates. In one comparison the infection rate was 3.1% with two angle miniplates vs 26.3% with one, while a 2.4-mm mandibular reconstruction plate is the most dependable (load-bearing) angle repair. Oblique fractures whose fragments overlap suit lag-screw fixation (two screws, about 2 mm). (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 308)

**Tooth in the fracture line**: since routine antibiotics, extracting a healthy tooth in the fracture line no longer lowers infection, so keep it unless it blocks reduction. At the angle, the third molar adds cross-sectional bone. Extracting it at repair destabilizes the fracture and raised complication rates in one series. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 309)

**Zide and Kent (1983) condylar ORIF indications (classic board list)**: absolute indications are displacement into the middle cranial fossa, inability to achieve reduction/occlusion, lateral extracapsular displacement, and a foreign body. Relative indications include bilateral condylar fractures in an edentulous patient without a splint, bilateral condylar fractures with comminuted midface fractures, and cases where splinting is contraindicated. Recent prospective studies suggest open reduction may outperform closed treatment, but the trade-off is facial nerve risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 308)

**Subcondylar fracture signs**: on the injured side, the ramus is shortened, the jaw deviates toward the fracture, and the molars contact early. The result is an open bite toward the opposite side. Bilateral subcondylar fractures may show only an anterior open bite with premature contact of the molars on both sides. A central blow to the chin can cause bilateral subcondylar fractures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, pp 291, 293)

**Entrapment adjuncts**: on applanation tonometry, a rise in intraocular pressure of 4 mm Hg or more when the patient looks toward the limited gaze suggests entrapment. Globe position is measured with an exophthalmometer. If the lateral rim is displaced, use a device referenced to the external auditory canal (such as the Naugle) instead of the Hertel, which rests on the lateral rim. Parasagittal CT reconstruction along the optic nerve axis helps judge orbital floor defects and predict enophthalmos. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, pp 292, 294)

**Lower-lid approach and orbital details**: avoid injuring the orbital septum during lower-lid (subciliary/transconjunctival) approaches, since septal scarring causes lower-lid malposition. A Frost traction suture taped to the forehead for 24 to 48 hours, plus lid massage starting after week 1, reduces ectropion risk. Release trapped tissue and do forced ductions before and after each orbital maneuver. Overcorrect enophthalmos slightly to allow for intraoperative swelling. Over the superior rim, elevate superiorly first because the orbital roof overhangs by 3 to 7 mm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, pp 297-298, 306, 310)

**Canthal exam**: normally the intercanthal distance is about the width of each palpebral fissure, or about half the interpupillary distance. Other signs of NOE injury are loss of dorsal height and new epicanthal folds. Test the tendon by pulling the medial canthus laterally. The Paskert-Manson bimanual exam presses an intranasal instrument against a finger over the medial canthus to detect a mobile central fragment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, p 292)

**Predicting outflow injury**: in the Stanley-Becker classification, a nasoethmoid or supraorbital rim fracture combined with comminution of the anterior or posterior table predicted frontal outflow duct injury. For skull base trauma, more central and more severe fractures carry a higher CSF leak risk (Sakas), and the longer a leak persists the higher the meningitis risk, which argues for earlier repair. A leak that stops may only be plugged by herniated brain, so late meningitis remains possible. (Cummings 7e, Ch 20, pp 295, 303)

**Internal lining options**: for full-thickness alar or tip defects up to 1.5 cm in vertical height, a bipedicle vestibular skin flap advanced from the remaining vestibule can line the defect, with cartilage grafts sutured to it. Larger defects use a septal mucoperichondrial hinge flap (Burget-Menick). The ipsilateral flap is based anteriorly on the caudal septum and fed by the septal branch of the superior labial artery. The contralateral flap is hinged on the dorsal septum and fed by the anterior ethmoid artery. Defects taller than about 2.5 cm need both flaps. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, pp 316-319)

**Subunit principle and alar options**: when a defect covers more than 50% of a convex nasal subunit (tip or ala), excise the rest and resurface the whole subunit so scars fall at subunit borders (Burget-Menick). Repair nasal and adjacent cheek/lip parts of a defect with separate flaps. A superiorly based interpolated melolabial flap on a subcutaneous pedicle is a key option for alar resurfacing. It is divided and thinned at about 3 weeks. If lateral crus is missing, replace it with a free cartilage graft placed along the nostril margin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 21, pp 316-317)

**Patterns and classification**: androgenetic alopecia is the most common hair loss in adults. It affects more than half of men and up to 40% of older women. Men lose hair frontotemporally and at the crown, graded by the Norwood classification (I to VII; VII leaves a narrow horseshoe fringe). Women typically keep the frontal hairline with diffuse central thinning, graded by Ludwig (I to III). Polygenic inheritance with variable penetrance makes family history a poor predictor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, pp 331, 333)

**Rule out non-androgenetic causes**: alopecia areata is T-cell autoimmune, with round smooth patches (totalis = whole scalp, universalis = whole body). Exclamation-point hairs are its most specific dermoscopic sign, and first-line treatment is potent topical or intralesional steroid. Telogen effluvium is diffuse shedding 3 to 6 months after a stressor (illness, childbirth, surgery, drugs) and is self-limited. Also consider thyroid disease, iron/zinc/protein deficiency, tinea capitis (KOH), and traction. The pull test grasps 30 to 40 hairs. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, pp 332-333, 335)

**Medical therapy facts**: topical minoxidil (2% or 5% solution, 5% foam) and oral finasteride 1 mg daily are the only FDA-approved drugs for androgenetic alopecia. Finasteride is a type II 5-alpha-reductase inhibitor and the most effective of the two; it stabilized loss in about half of men and regrew hair in about half. Side effects are decreased libido (about 2%), erectile dysfunction (about 1.4%) and less ejaculate, which reverse on stopping. It roughly halves PSA, so men over 45 need adjusted PSA interpretation. The propylene glycol-free 5% foam helps patients with irritant dermatitis. Oral minoxidil, PRP and low-level laser (630 to 680 nm) remain off-label or unproven. (Cummings 7e, Ch 22, pp 334-335)

**Fitzpatrick and Glogau**: Fitzpatrick types run from I (always burns, never tans) to VI (never burns). Types I to III are the safest for peels and lasers. Types III and IV often show lines of demarcation, and types V and VI tend to develop hyperpigmentation lasting 18 to 24 months, so most surgeons avoid deep peeling there. The Glogau scale grades photoaging: I mild (little wrinkling, no keratoses, about 28 to 35 years); II moderate (early wrinkling, sallow color, early actinic keratoses, about 35 to 50); III advanced; IV severe. The ideal resurfacing patient is a fair, thin-skinned woman with fine rhytids. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 351-352, 359)

**Peel agents and frost levels**: in Cummings' depth scheme, superficial reaches the papillary dermis, medium the upper reticular dermis, and deep the midreticular dermis. 50% TCA alone was abandoned because of scarring and pigment change; Jessner + 35% TCA (Monheit) is the standard medium peel and clears actinic keratoses about as well as topical 5-FU. Frost levels: I = erythema with streaky white, II = white frost with erythema showing through, III = solid enamel-white frost (reticular dermis). Phenol under 50% acts as a keratolytic and paradoxically penetrates deeper. In Baker-Gordon solution, croton oil drives depth. 88% phenol alone gives only a medium-depth peel. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 354-356)

**Phenol toxicity numbers**: toxic doses are about 8 to 15 g in adults, with cardiac, hepatic and renal effects. Phenol is cleared by the kidneys (largely within about 20 minutes), so renal disease contraindicates it. Before a deep peel, get CBC, liver and renal panels, electrolytes and a baseline ECG. Run IV fluids (500 to 1000 mL), wait at least 15 to 30 minutes between facial units, and treat no more than half the face at once. Monitor the heart for at least 30 minutes afterward with ACLS staff present. Arrhythmia is the main danger. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 357-358)

**Dermabrasion**: it is best for acne, traumatic and surgical scars, and is the treatment of choice for rhinophyma. Perioral dermabrasion matches CO2 laser results but heals in about half the time. Expect only 50% to 80% improvement of rhytids and 30% to 40% of severe acne scars. Healing takes 10 to 14 days, and erythema lasts 8 to 12 weeks. Wait 12 months before repeating. Treat to the jawline, hairline and orbital rims but not across them, and never dermabrade the neck. Pinpoint bleeding marks the papillary dermis. Milia and acne flares are common afterward. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 359-362)

**Ablative lasers**: CO2 (10,600 nm) is photothermal and leaves a wide coagulation zone, which gives hemostasis and immediate collagen shrinkage (up to about 25%) and true tightening. Do not overlap its pulses. Er:YAG (2940 nm) sits near water's absorption peak and is photomechanical. It leaves a narrow thermal zone, allows about 10% pulse overlap, causes pinpoint bleeding at the papillary dermis, and heals in 4 to 5 days rather than 7 to 10. CO2 erythema can last 3 to 4 months. Fractional delivery lowers hypopigmentation risk and can be used more safely in darker skin. Use only one pass on eyelid skin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 23, pp 362-365)

**Normal eyelid numbers**: palpebral fissure about 28 to 30 mm wide by 9 to 10 mm tall. The upper lid crease sits 10 to 12 mm above the margin in women and 7 to 8 mm in men. The upper margin covers 1 to 2 mm of the superior limbus, and the lower margin rests at the inferior limbus. The lateral canthus sits 2 to 4 mm above the medial canthus. MRD1 (corneal light reflex to upper margin) is normally about 3 to 4.5 mm, and levator excursion is normally more than 12 mm. Tarsus height is about 10 to 12 mm in the upper lid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, pp 405, 407-409)

**Preoperative tests**: check for brow ptosis, because the brow must be corrected first or too much lid skin will be removed. A snap-back/distraction test showing lower-lid laxity calls for a lid-shortening procedure at blepharoplasty to prevent ectropion. Schirmer testing with anesthetic showing under 5 mm of wetting at 5 minutes signals dry-eye risk. A ptotic lacrimal gland (mobile, about 5 mm, superolateral) should be resuspended. True ptosis is often hidden by dermatochalasis and is most often involutional. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, pp 408-410)

**Blepharoplasty complications**: orbital (retrobulbar) hemorrhage is most common after lower-lid surgery and presents with pain, proptosis and ecchymosis. With intact vision and stable swelling, observe with ophthalmology. With vision loss or optic neuropathy, perform immediate lateral canthotomy and cantholysis plus mannitol and IV steroids, then orbital decompression if needed. Delay beyond about 90 minutes risks permanent loss. Early lagophthalmos is common; if it persists beyond 6 to 8 weeks, suspect overresection. Cicatricial lower-lid retraction needs scar lysis and a spacer graft such as hard-palate mucosa. Excess skin can be revised after 4 to 6 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 26, pp 413-414)

**Epidemiology**: prominent ears occur in about 5% of white people. Inheritance is autosomal dominant with variable penetrance. The usual causes are an underfolded antihelix and a deep conchal bowl with a high conchal wall. The antihelix normally folds at about weeks 12 to 16 of gestation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 433)

**Neonatal molding**: newborn cartilage is pliable, likely because of circulating maternal estrogen, so taping or splinting in the first weeks (ideally within about 6 weeks) can correct prominent, lop and Stahl ears without surgery. Treatment usually lasts 4 to 6 weeks, and as little as 2 weeks if started in the nursery. In one cohort, about 57% of newborns had an ear deformity at 1 week. Many deformities self-corrected, but protruding ears did not. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, p 435)

**Otoplasty complications**: early complications are hematoma (which can progress to infection, chondritis or cauliflower ear), pain, infection and cartilage necrosis. Late complications are suture extrusion or granuloma, keloid, numbness (great auricular nerve) and cold sensitivity. Loss of correction is more common with suture-only techniques and usually occurs in the first 3 months. It can reach about 40%, so mild overcorrection is advised. Telephone ear comes from overcorrecting the middle third. Reverse telephone ear and vertical-post deformity come from technical errors. Asymmetry up to 2 to 3 mm is acceptable. Cutting techniques relapse less but cause more irregularities. (Cummings 7e, Ch 28, pp 435-438)

**Paradoxical nasal obstruction**: a patient with a unilateral septal deviation may feel blocked on the open, nondeviated side. Compensatory mucosal and bony turbinate hypertrophy fills that side, and the nasal cycle accentuates it during the congested phase. The nasal cycle alternates turbinate engorgement in about 80% of people, averaging about 2.5 hours, under autonomic control. Surgery may need to address the compensatory turbinate as well as the septum. (Cummings 7e, Ch 29, pp 442, 444)

**Stranc-Robertson classification**: injuries are lateral (more common, less severe, better prognosis) or frontal. Frontal injuries are graded by plane. Plane 1 involves the anterior nasal spine, anterior septum or lower nasal bones. Plane 2 involves the nasal bones and frontal process of the maxilla, with significant septal deviation, but spares the orbital rims. Plane 3 disrupts the NOE complex and often cannot be fully restored unless the NOE component is treated. Descriptors include unilateral, bilateral, comminuted, depressed, open-book (splayed), impacted (telescoped) and greenstick. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, pp 459-460)

**Closed reduction details**: measure the elevator against the external nose and insert it about 1 cm less than that depth to protect the cribriform plate. Reduce the septum (Asch forceps) before the nasal bones. Medially displaced upper lateral cartilage avulsions may need 10 to 14 days of internal packing to maintain the keystone. Internal packing, when used, stays 3 to 5 days, up to a week if unstable. Septal splints stay about 1 week. The external splint stays 7 to 10 days, and patients avoid contact activity for 6 to 8 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, pp 464-466)

**Pediatric nasal fractures**: children's softer noses favor greenstick fractures, which are hard to feel, and septal cartilage injury can stunt nasal and midfacial growth. Because children heal faster, Cummings advises reduction within about 4 days, usually under general anesthesia. Packing and splints generally add discomfort without benefit, except possibly in obligate nasal breathers under 6 months. After septal loss from hematoma or abscess, immediate cartilage grafting at drainage is recommended and graft loss is uncommon. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, pp 467-468)

**Timeline**: a subperichondrial clot cuts the cartilage off from its blood supply, and necrosis begins within about 3 days. An undrained hematoma becomes infected and forms an abscess at about 6 to 7 days. Contiguous spread can cause osteomyelitis, orbital or intracranial abscess, meningitis and cavernous sinus thrombosis. Late results are saddle nose, perforation, columellar retraction, a widened nasal base and, in children, midface growth disturbance. After drainage, leave small openings and use quilting sutures or splints to prevent reaccumulation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 30, p 468)

**Complete vs interrupted strip**: conservative cephalic trim preserving a complete, uninterrupted lateral crural strip of at least about 6 to 10 mm (often 7 to 9 mm) keeps long-term support and natural contour. Interrupted-strip (dome division) techniques, reserved for severe asymmetry or overprojection, always cost some support. They tend to rotate the tip cephalically, so use them with a columellar strut and only when rotation is wanted. Avoid a complete transfixion incision when possible, because it destroys the medial crural-caudal septal attachment, a major support. Postoperative tip ptosis from lost support is one of the most common rhinoplasty errors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, pp 483-486, 499)

**Osteotomies**: do medial osteotomies first, angled about 15 to 20 degrees laterally (medial oblique) to set the back-fracture point. Do an intermediate osteotomy next if planned, and the lateral osteotomy last. A low-curved lateral osteotomy starts at the piriform aperture at or just above the inferior turbinate. Perforating 2- to 3-mm micro-osteotomies spaced 2 to 3 mm apart reduce trauma. A complete osteotomy to the radix is often needed for a twisted nose. Low cuts protect the airway better than high cuts in deviated noses. An unnoticed deviated perpendicular plate can block the airway after infracture. (Cummings 7e, Ch 31, pp 474, 506-508) (Cummings 7e, Ch 32, pp 517-518)

**Spreader graft threshold and dorsal options**: when the dorsum is lowered more than about 3 mm, the middle vault roof is disrupted. Spreader grafts or flaps are advised to prevent an inverted-V deformity and internal valve collapse. For dorsal augmentation without a structural need, diced cartilage wrapped in temporalis fascia (DCF) is useful. Temporalis fascia alone camouflages irregularities and resorbs little. Gore-Tex has limited ingrowth, so it stays stable but can be removed. Extended spreader grafts fixed to a caudal septal extension graft or columellar strut control projection and rotation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 32, pp 519-521)

**Gell-Coombs hypersensitivity types**: Type I is mast cell-mediated. It can be IgE-dependent (allergic rhinitis, anaphylaxis) or IgE-independent (reactions to iodinated contrast). Type II is cytotoxic, with IgG/IgM against cell-surface antigens (e.g., penicillin-induced hemolytic anemia). Type III is immune-complex disease (serum sickness, lupus vasculitis). Type IV is delayed, T-cell-mediated (PPD reaction, contact dermatitis). (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 567)

**Classification definitions**: traditionally, perennial allergic rhinitis means symptoms more than 2 hours a day for more than 9 months a year (dust mite, indoor mold, dander, cockroach). In ARIA, intermittent means symptoms on fewer than 4 days a week or for fewer than 4 consecutive weeks; persistent means more than 4 days a week and more than 4 consecutive weeks. Each is graded mild or moderate-severe by effects on sleep, daily activities, work/school and troublesome symptoms. ARIA guides the treatment algorithm. Heritability of allergic rhinitis may be as high as 80%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, pp 567, 576)

**Medications that blunt skin tests**: stop oral H1 antihistamines 2 to 7 days before testing, depending on half-life. Topical azelastine, H2 blockers (e.g., ranitidine) and some tricyclic antidepressants also suppress the wheal and flare. Omalizumab must be stopped about 8 weeks before. Montelukast does not affect skin tests and can be continued. Contraindications to skin-prick testing include severe cardiopulmonary disease, including poorly controlled asthma. Do not test over active dermatitis. A large reaction at the negative control (dermatographism) makes results unreliable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 577)

**Contraindications**: poorly controlled asthma, active autoimmune disease and malignancy contraindicate SCIT in some guidelines. Relative contraindications are cardiovascular disease, partly controlled asthma, autoimmune disease in remission and current beta-blocker use (beta-blockers worsen anaphylaxis and blunt epinephrine). Do not start immunotherapy during pregnancy, but established maintenance doses can continue. Patients at high risk of asthma or new sensitizations may especially benefit. (Cummings 7e, Ch 35, p 582)

**Congenital anosmia and Kallmann syndrome**: Kallmann syndrome is hypogonadotropic hypogonadism with anosmia caused by failed migration of GnRH neurons, linked to several genes. It is usually diagnosed at age 12 to 16, is 3 to 5 times more common in males, and may include midline craniofacial defects, sensorineural hearing loss and renal anomalies. MRI shows absent olfactory bulbs and tracts. Hormone replacement does not restore smell. Isolated congenital anosmia (hypoplastic bulbs, short olfactory sulci) is more common than the syndromic form and often comes to attention around puberty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 594)

**Foster Kennedy syndrome and central causes**: an olfactory groove or other frontal mass can cause ipsilateral anosmia and optic atrophy with contralateral papilledema (Foster Kennedy). Pituitary tumors, suprasellar meningiomas and frontal gliomas can also impair smell. Smell loss from frontal masses may improve after resection. Depression and schizophrenia are the psychiatric conditions most linked to olfactory loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 36, p 595)

topic: CF / Primary Ciliary Dyskinesia Sinonasal Disease
text: **Mucociliary and PCD testing (Cummings)**: each ciliated cell has about 200 cilia (9+2 axoneme with dynein arms) beating at 8 to 20 Hz; in vitro the beat frequency is about 8 Hz at room temperature and 12 Hz at 37°C. On the saccharin test (particle on the inferior turbinate), normal transit is about 10 minutes; over 30 minutes is abnormal, and normal transport effectively excludes PCD. Nasal nitric oxide is about 10-fold lower in PCD and is a useful screen from about age 5, but cannot prove or exclude PCD. A beat frequency under about 11 Hz on high-speed video prompts electron microscopy. An abnormal EM is diagnostic, but a normal EM does not exclude PCD. Air-liquid interface culture separates inherited from acquired defects. PCD is mostly autosomal recessive (X-linked forms: RPGR, PIH1D3); more than 30 genes are known, so next-generation sequencing is preferred. (Cummings 7e, Ch 37, pp 603-606)

**Imaging predictors**: smooth dural thickening over 5 mm, or any nodular dural thickening and enhancement, predicts dural invasion with 100% positive predictive value. Imaging judges periorbital invasion with only about 60% to 70% accuracy, mainly because its negative predictive value is low. Spread into the posterior sphenoid wall usually means the tumor is unresectable. Loss of fat in the pterygopalatine fossa signals perineural spread toward the foramen rotundum, the vidian canal and the cavernous sinus. Most malignancies are darker than retained secretions on T2 and enhance diffusely. ADC is about 1.5 × 10⁻³ mm²/s or higher in benign lesions and about 0.98 or lower in malignant ones. Nodal metastases occur in about 25% of cases. (Cummings 7e, Ch 38, pp 617, 628-630)

**NARES specifics**: defined by nasal cytology eosinophils above 10% with negative skin/serum IgE testing. Symptoms are more severe than in AR or other NAR subtypes, and NARES is associated with olfactory loss, obstructive sleep apnea, later nasal polyposis and aspirin sensitivity (it may precede the AERD triad). Intranasal steroids are the mainstay (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 637, 641).

**Three mechanisms of drug-induced rhinitis**: (1) local inflammatory: aspirin/NSAIDs (AERD) (2) neurogenic: sympatholytics such as clonidine, methyldopa, guanethidine, prazosin/doxazosin, and PDE-5 inhibitors (sildenafil), which leave parasympathetic tone unopposed. (3) idiopathic: beta-blockers (including ophthalmic drops), ACE inhibitors, calcium channel blockers, exogenous estrogens/oral contraceptives, some psychotropics and gabapentin. In rhinitis medicamentosa the mucosa is beefy red with scant mucus, whereas other drug-induced rhinitis usually shows normal-looking mucosa (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, pp 638–639).

**Drug details**: beclomethasone and fluticasone propionate are the only intranasal steroids FDA-approved for NAR, and weather-sensitive idiopathic rhinitis may respond poorly to them. Azelastine helps (bitter taste is the classic side effect) and olopatadine works off-label. Azelastine plus fluticasone beats fluticasone alone. Ipratropium 0.03% is approved for AR/NAR rhinorrhea (0.06% for viral colds), helps only rhinorrhea, and needs caution in glaucoma and prostatic hypertrophy (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 641).

**Vidian neurectomy vs posterior nasal nerve procedures**: the vidian nerve is formed by the greater superficial petrosal nerve (preganglionic parasympathetic) and the deep petrosal nerve (sympathetic). Endoscopic vidian neurectomy controls rhinitis in up to about 91% but risks dry eye and palatal numbness because lacrimal and palatal fibers run in the canal. Cutting or cryoablating the postganglionic posterior nasal nerve at the sphenopalatine foramen/posterior middle meatus spares lacrimal fibers, and office nitrous-oxide cryoablation improved NAR symptoms to 1 year (Cummings 7e, Ch 39, p 642).

**IDSA's three entry criteria (vs AAO-HNSF)**: (1) persistent symptoms for 10 or more days without improvement; (2) severe onset, meaning fever of 39°C or higher with purulent discharge or facial pain for at least 3–4 consecutive days at the start; (3) worsening ('double sickening'): new fever, headache or more discharge after a typical viral URI of 5–6 days that had been improving. The severe-onset arm is IDSA-specific and is not part of the AAO-HNSF adult definition (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, pp 645–646).

**IDSA antibiotic rules**: empiric amoxicillin-clavulanate for adults and children. High-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate is used for (1) regions with high penicillin-nonsusceptible S. pneumoniae, (2) severe infection, (3) recent hospitalization or antibiotics within the past month, or (4) immunocompromise. Macrolides (about 30% pneumococcal resistance) and TMP-SMX (30–40% resistance) are not for empiric use, nor is second- or third-generation oral cephalosporin monotherapy. Doxycycline is the adult alternative (not for children) (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646).

**Penicillin allergy, duration and failure**: for type I allergy in adults use doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin or moxifloxacin); in children with type I allergy use levofloxacin; for non-type I allergy in children use a third-generation cephalosporin (cefixime or cefpodoxime) plus clindamycin. Routine MRSA coverage is not recommended. Treat 5–7 days in adults and 10–14 days in children. Change therapy if the patient worsens after 72 hours or fails to improve after 3–5 days; failure on high-dose amoxicillin-clavulanate or a fluoroquinolone should prompt a search for another diagnosis such as CRS, allergy or a facial pain disorder (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 646).

**Cummings thresholds**: Chandler I (preseptal) can be treated with oral antibiotics and close follow-up, while Chandler II–V need IV broad-spectrum antibiotics on admission. Get a CT if preseptal disease progresses after 24–48 hours of antibiotics. Operate for reduced visual acuity, an afferent pupillary defect, or no improvement after 48 hours of IV therapy. Most abscesses are drained, but a small subperiosteal abscess with normal vision can get a 48-hour medical trial. For cavernous sinus thrombosis, drain every involved sinus including the sphenoid. Anticoagulation is controversial (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, pp 648).

**Histology and stains**: Aspergillus shows septate hyphae branching at acute (about 45°) angles, while Mucorales (Zygomycetes; Rhizopus oryzae is the most virulent) show broad, ribbon-like, nonseptate hyphae with irregular branching. Calcofluor white and Grocott methenamine silver stains, plus permanent sections, help tell them apart; Fusarium and Alternaria are less common. The middle turbinate is the most common site of pallor or necrosis to biopsy for frozen section. Check nasal sensation at endoscopy (Cummings 7e, Ch 40, p 648).

**Tissue eosinophilia cutoffs**: in research, eosinophilic CRSwNP is defined by more than 5 eosinophils per high-power field, or by a tissue ECP/MPO ratio above 1. A cutoff of more than 10 eosinophils/HPF is the clinically meaningful threshold for quality-of-life impact. Higher tissue or blood eosinophils and comorbid asthma predict worse quality of life, more severe disease and polyp recurrence after surgery; IgE, ECP and IL-5 also predict recurrence (Cummings 7e, Ch 41, p 657).

**Macrolide pearl**: low-dose macrolides (erythromycin, clarithromycin, azithromycin) work through immunomodulation (less IL-8, NF-κB inhibition, reduced neutrophil activity) and are an ICAR 'option' (Grade B) for CRS. CRSsNP responds better than CRSwNP, and patients with allergy, tissue/blood eosinophilia or high IgE respond less well. They inhibit CYP450 (erythromycin and clarithromycin most strongly), so hold statins (rhabdomyolysis risk) and take a cardiac history (QT prolongation, ventricular arrhythmia). Azithromycin has the least CYP450 inhibition but still carries an FDA warning for QT prolongation and fatal arrhythmia (Cummings 7e, Ch 42, p 664).

**ICAR recommendations against**: routine oral non-macrolide antibiotics without an acute infection (Grade B; C. difficile colitis carries about 5% mortality); IV antibiotics (Grade C; complications in 16–29%, including neutropenia, line thrombophlebitis/DVT and sepsis), though IV therapy is still needed for complicated ABRS; topical antibiotic irrigations (Grade B); oral antifungals (terbinafine, itraconazole; Grade B); and topical amphotericin or fluconazole irrigations (Grade A). Oral steroids have no recommendation in CRSsNP (Grade D) (Cummings 7e, Ch 42, pp 664–665).

**SNOT-22 numbers for counseling**: the SNOT-22 runs from 0 to 110, and its minimal clinically important difference is about 8.9 points. In a 40-study meta-analysis, ESS improved SNOT-22 by a mean of about 24 points (range 12.7–44.8) at roughly 11 months, and about 75% of primary ESS patients achieve a clinically meaningful improvement. Patients with a baseline SNOT-22 below about 20 seldom reach an MCID, while a baseline of 31 or more gives over a 70% chance; low preoperative severity is the only consistent predictor of a poor outcome (Cummings 7e, Ch 43, pp 669–673).

**Antrochoanal polyp**: a solitary, unilateral polyp that arises in the maxillary antrum and passes, usually through the posterior fontanelle or an accessory ostium, back to the choana, causing one-sided obstruction (classically in adolescents and young adults). Image or biopsy it to exclude neoplasm before 'polypectomy.' Recurrence is unlikely only if the antral attachment is fully removed (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 687).

**Complication numbers to quote**: in a 3,128-patient English/Welsh prospective audit, major complications were 0.4% and minor 6.6% (mostly bleeding). Rates tracked disease extent (polyps, CT opacity, comorbidity), not surgeon grade or instruments. In a US database of about 62,800 ESS cases, major complications were 1.0%: CSF leak 0.17%, orbital injury 0.07%, transfusion 0.76%. Children had fewer CSF leaks but more orbital injuries. Orbital complications overall run about 0.12%. Synechiae are the most common minor complication (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 706).

**Orbital injury details**: arterial (anterior/posterior ethmoidal) orbital hematoma expands rapidly, while venous bleeding from lamina papyracea veins expands slowly and may show only in recovery or at home; treat both the same way. Raised orbital pressure can cause blindness within 60–90 minutes. Diplopia most often comes from medial rectus, then superior oblique, injury when a microdebrider pulls fat through a dehiscence, so keep the blade tangential to the lamina. Keep the eyes in the field and ballot the globe while watching the lamina. Subcutaneous/orbital emphysema from a small lamina fracture usually resolves in 7–10 days without treatment (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 707).

**Nonallergic eosinophilic fungal rhinosinusitis**: patients whose histopathology looks like AFRS (eosinophilic mucin with fungal hyphae) but who lack elevated fungus-specific IgE are classified as nonallergic (eosinophilic) fungal rhinosinusitis rather than AFRS (Cummings 7e, Ch 44, p 687).

**Medial rectus injury management**: the patterns are (1) entrapment, contusion or intramuscular hematoma, (2) partial or complete transection, and (3) injury to oculomotor branches on the muscle's lateral surface. Treatment should start within 3–4 weeks to prevent fibrosis, but suspected entrapment is the only indication for immediate re-exploration. Direct reanastomosis is advised for complete transection if the posterior 20 mm of muscle is intact and functional. The prognosis is poor, and the realistic goal is single binocular vision in primary gaze (Cummings 7e, Ch 45, pp 716–717).

**'All or none' drilling rule**: drilling in the frontal recess causes unavoidable circumferential mucosal injury and stenosis. Once the drill is needed for inflammatory disease, proceed to a full Draf III rather than stopping at a Draf IIb. Reserve Draf IIb for healthy-mucosa conditions such as benign tumors (e.g., inverted papilloma attachment) or mucoceles that have already eroded the medial recess ('auto-Draf IIb'). In Draf IIa, keep at least 50% of the recess mucosa (ideally all) (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 723, 726).

**Draf III restenosis**: neo-ostial stenosis occurs in 10–30% and is linked to asthma, allergy, CF and prior frontal surgery. Inject steroid into an early thick web at the beak within the first 3 months. Excise bridging scar, with optional intraoperative mitomycin C 0.5 mg/mL for 5 minutes; final patency exceeds 90%. Frontal restenosis after mucocele drainage is about 23% after Draf IIb vs 3.6% after Draf IIa. Draf IIa also works less well for CRSwNP with polyps inside the frontal sinus, especially with asthma or AERD (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 726–728).

**Frontal osteoma (Chiu grading)**: grade I attaches posteroinferiorly in the recess, lies medial to a sagittal plane through the lamina papyracea, and is less than 75% of the recess AP diameter. Grade II is the same but more than 75%. Grade III attaches anteriorly or superiorly in the sinus and/or extends lateral to the lamina plane. Grade IV fills the sinus. Grades I–II were the classic endoscopic limit, but many grade III lesions can now be drilled out, often with a Draf III; the frontal floor lateral to the mid-orbit stays hardest to reach. Osteomas occur in about 3–4% of people, and most are incidental and wrongly blamed for headache (Cummings 7e, Ch 46, pp 728–729).

**Compression time (book vs guideline)**: Cummings advises 15–20 minutes of uninterrupted pressure on the soft lower nose, chin to chest with no peeking, because platelet plugs take up to about 20 minutes to mature; tilting the head back causes swallowed or aspirated blood. The 2020 AAO-HNSF epistaxis guideline specifies at least 5 minutes, which is the current guideline minimum. Limit oxymetazoline to 3 days or less (rebound risk); tranexamic acid (topical or oral) may help (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, pp 736–737).

**ESPAL landmarks and results**: the crista ethmoidalis lies just anterior/anteroinferior to the sphenopalatine foramen, and in 95% the foramen is within 1 mm of it. Raise a mucosal flap, remove the crista with a Kerrison and control every branch (posterior septal and posterior lateral nasal; branching is highly variable and missed branches cause failure). No packing is needed. Long-term control exceeds 90%; in one series posterior packing worked in 62% vs surgery in 97%, and ESPAL is cheaper with a shorter stay (3 vs 6 days). Transient crusting and palatal numbness are the usual complaints (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, p 740).

**Embolization facts**: success is 75–92%, with stroke reported in about 1.1–1.5%, and it costs more than surgery. The internal maxillary artery is the usual target; never embolize ICA/ophthalmic territory (blindness, stroke). Other risks are groin hematoma and contrast nephropathy. It is preferred for tumor bleeding (nasopharyngeal carcinoma), preoperative JNA devascularization, craniofacial trauma with distorted anatomy, and carotid injury or blowout (after local packing control) (Cummings 7e, Ch 47, p 742).

**Marker and tracer pitfalls**: β2-transferrin also appears in aqueous humor and in serum in alcoholic liver disease. β-trace protein (prostaglandin D2 synthase) is unreliable in renal insufficiency (serum levels rise) and bacterial meningitis (CSF levels fall). Intrathecal fluorescein is off-label: use 0.1 mL of 10% IV (not ophthalmic) fluorescein diluted in 10 mL of the patient's CSF, infused slowly (Cummings says over 30 minutes, the sinus atlas about 10 minutes), and doses of 50 mg or less rarely cause adverse events such as seizures. CT cisternography confirms about 80% of leaks. MR cisternography has sensitivity 0.87 and specificity 0.57. Radionuclide pledget studies have too many false positives to stand alone (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 749–751).

**Traumatic leaks and meningitis**: meningitis risk after posttraumatic fistula ranges from 2% to 50%, and leaks lasting more than 7 days carry at least an 8- to 10-fold higher risk. Repair is advised for posttraumatic leaks persisting beyond about 7 days despite conservative care, or immediately with massive head injury needing exploration. Prophylactic antibiotic data conflict (one review found 14% vs 5% meningitis with vs without antibiotics, and a meta-analysis found 2.5% vs 10%), and a Cochrane review found no evidence that they prevent meningitis. Pneumococcal, H. influenzae and meningococcal immunization may be considered. Postoperative leaks recognized weeks later respond poorly to conservative care and favor early repair (Cummings 7e, Ch 48, pp 753, 756–757).

**Diplopia-sparing options and outcomes**: an inferomedial bony strut (first feasible in 71% of orbits, now about 100% with angled instruments), a medial periorbital 'sling' along the medial rectus borders, and balanced medial plus lateral decompression (postoperative diplopia still 10–33%). Medial plus inferior decompression reduces proptosis by about 3.2 mm, and adding the lateral wall gives about 5.6 mm total. Sling preservation in balanced decompression costs little (about 5.1 mm), but strut preservation lowers reduction (about 3.6 mm). For compressive optic neuropathy, remove the walls and periorbita completely rather than sparing them (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 766–768).

**Imaging pitfall**: get a noncontrast CT of orbits and sinuses (also usable for navigation) before decompression. Avoid iodinated IV contrast, which has caused severe acute exacerbations of Graves disease. MRI is usually unnecessary when the diagnosis is clear. Indications for decompression are disfigurement, exposure keratopathy and compressive optic neuropathy (dyschromatopsia, RAPD, falling acuity), the last being urgent (Cummings 7e, Ch 49, pp 765–766).

**Risk factors and molecular split**: organic solvent exposure raises IP risk in a dose-dependent way, while smoking and alcohol do not cause IP. Smoking does, however, raise the risk of recurrence and of malignant transformation (about 12-fold in one cohort: 26% of smokers vs 3% of nonsmokers transformed). Transformation overall is 5–15% and is more often synchronous than metachronous. IP carries EGFR mutations, whereas oncocytic papilloma carries KRAS mutations, so these are separate entities. The HPV role is unclear: high-risk types appear in dysplasia/carcinoma, but transcriptionally active HPV is usually absent (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 774–775).

**Recurrence and surveillance numbers**: in a meta-analysis recurrence was 13.8% after endoscopic, 18.7% after external and 12.9% after combined approaches (under 10% in large expert series). Endoscopic resection cuts recurrence risk by one-third to one-half. Risk factors are incomplete resection, higher stage (Krouse T3 about 51% higher risk than T2), recurrent tumor, smoking and dysplasia (3- to 10-fold). Most attachments are on the medial maxillary wall/fontanelle region, with multisite involvement in about 30%. A suggested schedule is endoscopy every 4 months for 2 years, every 6 months to year 5, then yearly to year 10. Image only for inaccessible cavities, symptoms or proven recurrence (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 774, 777).

**Other sinonasal papillomas**: exophytic (fungiform) papilloma is the second most common type. It has a 10:1 male predominance, occurs in the 3rd–5th decades, arises from the anterior-inferior septum without sinus involvement, is driven by low-risk HPV 6/11 and almost never becomes malignant; excise it with the underlying septal perichondrium. Separate it from keratinizing vestibular skin lesions. Oncocytic papilloma is the rarest type. It occurs in the 5th–6th decades in the lateral wall/maxillary sinus, is HPV-negative, KRAS-mutated, and shows intraepithelial mucin/neutrophil microcysts, with 4–17% malignant transformation (usually SCC); manage it like IP (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, p 777).

**Residual vs recurrent disease**: JNA is thought to persist (residual) rather than truly recur. Residual rates are 6–39% overall and 0–17% with planned endoscopic surgery, and are higher with skull base involvement and residual ICA vascularity after embolization. Get an early (e.g., postoperative day 3) gadolinium MRI before inflammation sets in, continue surveillance for at least 3 years, and watch residual disease with serial MRI. Treat only growth, since many residuals stay stable or regress after adolescence. Low-dose radiotherapy (30–36 Gy) or radiosurgery is for unresectable advanced or recurrent disease, and aggressive surgery with major morbidity for small residuals in critical areas is not justified (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, p 780).

**Osteoma specifics**: the most common benign sinonasal tumor, seen in 1% of sinus radiographs and 3% of sinus CTs. Classically 80% are frontal, but a large CT series found ethmoid 55% vs frontal 37.5%. Histologic types are ivory/eburnated, mature (spongiosum) and mixed. Multiple osteomas suggest Gardner syndrome (APC; colon polyposis), so screen with colonoscopy. Observe with imaging if asymptomatic and away from skull base, optic nerve and orbit. Endoscopic resection uses cavitation: drill the core and fracture the thin shell, being ready for a CSF leak when it abuts dura. Recurrence is rare, so one CT at 1 year is enough (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 780–782).

**Fibrous dysplasia vs ossifying fibroma**: FD is a developmental anomaly (monostotic, or polyostotic with café-au-lait spots and endocrinopathy in McCune-Albright; polyostotic is 6–10 times rarer), found in the first two decades. On CT it ranges from lytic to ground-glass/sclerotic with no capsule. Ossifying fibroma is a true neoplasm (juvenile psammomatoid type in the fronto-orbital and ethmoid bones), more common in Black women in the 2nd–3rd decades, and appears well-defined and multiloculated with an eggshell rim. OF needs complete resection (high, aggressive recurrence, especially ethmoid). FD surgery is for symptoms (optic compression, deformity) and is delayed until skeletal maturity; prophylactic optic canal decompression is not indicated, radiation is contraindicated, and bisphosphonates (pamidronate) help pain and extensive disease (Cummings 7e, Ch 50, pp 785–786).

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **GPA test performance**: c-ANCA (PR3) is positive in about 95% of active systemic GPA but only about 60% of localized disease over its course, and about 10% are p-ANCA positive instead. Nasal biopsy has low yield: only about 24% (12 of 51) showed histology suggestive of GPA in one study, so a negative biopsy does not exclude it. CT may show bony erosion with neo-osteogenesis (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 789).

topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Cocaine-induced midline destructive lesion vs GPA**: CIMDL mimics GPA clinically, radiographically and histologically (leukocytoclastic vasculitis, fibrinoid necrosis). About half of ANCA-positive CIMDL patients have PR3/c-ANCA, but human neutrophil elastase (HNE) ANCA is common in CIMDL and not in GPA, so it is the discriminating test, along with urine/hair toxicology. Isolated septal perforation occurs in about 4.8% of habitual users, and destruction can extend to the palate, orbit and skull base. Immunosuppression has no role. Abstinence is the treatment, and reconstruction (rib cartilage) waits for proven abstinence (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 791).

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Relapsing polychondritis (McAdam criteria)**: diagnose with 3 of 6 criteria: bilateral auricular chondritis, nonerosive seronegative polyarthritis, nasal chondritis, audiovestibular damage, respiratory tract chondritis and ocular inflammation. Alternatively, 1 criterion plus positive histology, or chondritis at 2 or more separate sites that responds to steroids or dapsone, is enough (Damiani). Auricular chondritis is the most common presentation (40%). Saddle nose is present in 24% at diagnosis and 53% later, airway involvement in about 25%, and eye disease in over 50%. HLA-DR4 doubles risk, and anti-type II collagen antibodies track flares. Five-year survival is 66–74%, or 45% with vasculitis. Treat with NSAIDs for mild disease and steroids (80–100 mg/day in severe flares) with dapsone, methotrexate or cyclosporine (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 792).

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Granulomatous infections of the nose**: rhinoscleroma (Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis) passes through catarrhal (atrophic, honey-colored crusts), granulomatous and sclerotic stages, mostly on the turbinates. Mikulicz cells (vacuolated macrophages containing bacilli) and Russell bodies are diagnostic, culture on MacConkey agar is positive in only 50–60%, and ciprofloxacin is first-line. Nasal TB favors the cartilaginous septum (caseating granulomas, AFB, lupus vulgaris). Test for HIV. Leprosy causes atrophy of the anterior nasal spine and premaxilla. Actinomycosis forms a hard mass with sinus tracts and sulfur granules (drainage plus prolonged penicillin-class therapy). Rhinosporidiosis (R. seeberi, from contaminated water) gives a polypoid mass treated by excision plus dapsone. Syphilis causes chancre or gumma (FTA-ABS, penicillin G) (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, pp 793–794).

**Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type**: EBV-associated, male-predominant (about 40 years in Asia, 5th decade in the West), and although Cummings cites Western series suggesting similar prevalence worldwide, it remains proportionally far more common in East Asia and Latin America. It progresses from obstruction and purulent bloody discharge to necrotic midline destruction of the nose, palate and orbit, with nodal spread in no more than about 25%. Histology shows angiocentric/angiodestructive polymorphous infiltrates with coagulative necrosis. The cells are CD2+, CD56+ and cytotoxic-marker positive, CD3 variable, and CD4/CD5/CD8 negative. Take deep, generous biopsies. First-line treatment for localized disease is radiotherapy combined with chemotherapy (concurrent platinum-based, or the asparaginase-based regimens favored by NCCN), with surgery limited to biopsy and debridement (Cummings 7e, Ch 51, p 792).

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Numbers against 'sinus headache'**: of nearly 3,000 patients with self- or physician-diagnosed 'sinus headache,' more than 80% met migraine criteria. Only 20–30% of patients with endoscopic or radiologic sinus disease report facial pain. CT mucosal thickening appears in 30–40% of asymptomatic people. Contact points are as common without pain as with it, and nearly 50% of facial-pain patients have their contact point on the opposite side (Cummings 7e, Ch 52, pp 795–796).

**Teflon (PTFE) paste**: now discouraged except when long-term survival is not expected, because PTFE granulomas cause late dysphonia and even airway obstruction from mass effect. Recognized overinjection is best treated immediately by incising the mucosa over the injection and suctioning out excess paste; late removal (microlaryngoscopy with cupped forceps or CO2 laser, or thyrotomy for persistent granuloma) is harder because the material migrates and scars. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 908–910)

**Medialization vs intracordal injection**: medialization injection goes into the paraglottic space lateral to the vocalis and leaves the mucosa untouched; intracordal injection for soft-tissue deficits (collagen, micronized dermis) is placed more superficially just deep to the lamina propria while avoiding Reinke space. PTFE must never be placed intracordally. Calcium hydroxylapatite has case reports of foreign-body granulomatous reaction requiring microflap excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 908–909)

**Window landmarks**: the vocal fold lies at a level roughly midway between the thyroid notch and the anterior inferior thyroid border, along a line parallel to the inferior border. A prefabricated hydroxyapatite (VoCoM) window is about 6 × 10 mm, with its anterior edge 5–8 mm (women) or 8–10 mm (men) behind the midline. Implants range 3–7 mm of displacement and more than 7 mm is rarely needed. For carved Silastic (Netterville), the window is about 6 × 13 mm, placed about 3 mm above the 'true inferior border' (line from the anterior inferior border to the notch in front of the inferior cornu). (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 911–913)

**Numbers**: overall complication rate is under 3%, but incomplete glottic closure from undercorrection or malposition occurs in about 10–15% and is more likely after early implantation because the denervated muscle keeps atrophying. Use the largest implant that preserves voice quality, since intraoperative edema makes the voice look better than it will be. Revision (reposition or larger implant through the same window), injection, arytenoid adduction or reinnervation salvage undercorrection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, pp 912–915)

**Prognosis groups**: recovery is likely after blunt trauma, intubation injury, idiopathic and viral (e.g., Ramsay Hunt) paralysis. It is unlikely after nerve section at tumor resection, tumor invasion of the nerve, thoracic aortic aneurysm, or progressive neurologic disease. High vagal lesions add cricothyroid paralysis and supraglottic sensory loss, leaving a lateralized, bowed, atrophic fold with worse dysphagia and aspiration. Early thyroplasty is warranted. Short life expectancy with aspiration favors simple injection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 62, p 907)

**Arytenoid abduction (lateralization) suture**: through the same lateral approach as adduction, a suture through the muscular process is pulled posteroinferiorly and tied to the inferior cornu of the thyroid cartilage, externally rotating the arytenoid and lifting the vocal process out of the airway. Unlike endoscopic arytenoidectomy it leaves no endolaryngeal wound to contract and does not abolish residual adductor tone, so voice is largely preserved; it can be done instead of emergency tracheotomy or to allow decannulation (general anesthesia preferred). Synkinetic inspiratory adduction limits success. (Cummings 7e, Ch 63, pp 918–921)

**Ansa–RLN transfer facts**: indicated for unilateral paralysis with little chance of recovery, usually after waiting about 12 months; needs an intact distal RLN stump and one ansa (ipsilateral or contralateral). Absolute contraindications: glottic airway compromise, bilateral paralysis, absent distal RLN, absent ansa bilaterally, poor health. Results are better when done within about 2 years of injury and in younger patients; voice begins improving at roughly 3–4 months and keeps improving beyond a year, so a temporary injection is often added at surgery. It eliminates any chance of spontaneous recovery, does not burn bridges for later thyroplasty, and works well in children because laryngeal growth does not alter the result. (Cummings 7e, Ch 64, pp 927–928)

**Side-check trap**: unlike thyroplasty, ansa–RLN transfer done on the wrong (mobile) side divides the only working RLN and produces bilateral immobility with airway obstruction. Lateral fixation of the arytenoid, scar, web or polyp limit the voice result; passive arytenoid mobility predicts success. (Cummings 7e, Ch 64, pp 927–928)

**Lindeman procedures**: tracheoesophageal diversion (TED) divides the trachea at about the 4th–5th rings, sews the proximal stump end-to-side into the anterior esophagus and brings the distal trachea out as an end stoma; laryngotracheal separation (LTS) is used when a prior high tracheotomy prevents TED — the trachea is divided at the 2nd–3rd rings (or the existing stoma), the proximal stump closed as a blind pouch buttressed with strap muscle, and the distal end matured as a stoma. Both control aspiration nearly uniformly, preserve the larynx and RLNs, and are reversible. (Cummings 7e, Ch 65, pp 936–937)

**LTS complications**: tracheocutaneous fistula from the proximal stump is the most common (about 11–38%), less common after TED, more likely with prior tracheotomy, and usually closes conservatively; skin-flap or strap reinforcement lowers the rate. Deaths from tracheoinnominate artery fistula have occurred, especially in children with chest-wall deformity or scoliosis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 65, p 937)

**Hyoid fractures**: seen in about 17% of strangulation victims and most often from strangulation; nearly all (about 89%) are managed nonoperatively because plating disrupts the muscular sling and can cause dysphagia. Operate only for fragment extrusion into the airway or significant supraglottic distortion; follow with early videofluoroscopy for aspiration. Homicidal strangulation is more likely than suicidal to cause laryngotracheal separation and neurovascular injury, and airway edema can progress hours after a benign first exam. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 940, 945)

**Arytenoid dislocation**: posterior dislocation usually follows extubation and leaves the fold higher; anterior dislocation usually results from the laryngoscope tip at intubation and leaves the fold lower. CT shows a reduced or absent cricoarytenoid joint space and EMG helps if paralysis is in question. Reduce under anesthesia — lift a posterior dislocation anterosuperiorly with a straight-blade laryngoscope (with external cricoid counterpressure), and push an anterior one back with the laryngoscope tip or a balloon. After trauma, wait about 6 months before permanent medialization for unilateral paralysis, and keep a tracheotomy rather than doing early arytenoidectomy for bilateral immobility. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 944–946)

**Intubation injury numbers**: about 10% of patients show laryngeal lesions a day after short surgical intubation, approaching 90% after prolonged ventilation, with lasting sequelae in about 11%. In adults the tube presses on the medial arytenoids/posterior commissure, causing ulceration, perichondritis and interarytenoid scar (posterior glottic stenosis) with poor prognosis. In children the subglottis is the narrowest site and is most often injured. Significant injuries seen at extubation (over 40%) mostly resolve by 6 months (under 5% remain). Early tracheotomy in prolonged ventilation is favored to prevent laryngeal (worse than tracheal) stenosis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 66, pp 946–947)

**Staging systems beyond Myer-Cotton**: McCaffrey stages laryngotracheal stenosis by site and length — I: subglottic or tracheal lesion under 1 cm. II: subglottic lesion over 1 cm, not reaching glottis or trachea. III: subglottic lesion extending into upper trachea but sparing glottis. IV: glottic involvement with fixation or paralysis of one or both folds — and predicts decannulation prognosis. Flow-volume loops: fixed obstruction flattens both limbs. Variable extrathoracic obstruction flattens the inspiratory limb (bilateral fold immobility shows mid-vital-capacity inspiratory flow under about 1.5 L/s). (Cummings 7e, Ch 67, pp 954–955)

**Resection numbers**: the adult trachea averages about 11 cm with 14–20 rings, and about half (5–7 cm) can be resected with primary anastomosis using mobilization. Success exceeds 90% when the glottis is normal, and subglottic involvement or impaired fold motion worsens outcome. For cricotracheal resection keep about 1 cm of normal lumen below the glottis and stay subperichondrial near the cricothyroid joints (RLN entry). Release maneuvers: annular-ligament incisions (up to about 2.5 cm, alternating sides), suprahyoid release (preferred, less dysphagia than infrahyoid, which risks the superior laryngeal nerve), and intrathoracic hilar mobilization. Older patients need release after shorter resections because ligament elasticity is lost. Keep the neck flexed with a chin-to-chest stitch for about 7–10 days. (Cummings 7e, Ch 67, pp 960–962)

**Rings and webs**: rings are circumferential (mucosal or muscular), usually distal; webs are partial, always mucosal, usually proximal (found in up to 5% of asymptomatic people). Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome = proximal web + iron deficiency anemia + dysphagia. The Schatzki (B) ring at the squamocolumnar junction is the most common cause of intermittent solid-food dysphagia and food impaction: under 13 mm almost always symptomatic, over 20 mm almost never; barium swallow is most sensitive; treat with bougienage ± acid suppression. The A ring is a muscular ring about 2 cm above, rarely symptomatic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 977–978)

**Infectious and pill esophagitis**: Candida, CMV and HSV are the three main infectious causes; odynophagia is the cardinal symptom. Candida: adherent white-yellow plaques, hyphae on brushing, fluconazole 100–200 mg/day for 10–14 days. CMV infects submucosal fibroblasts/endothelium, causing serpiginous deep ulcers — biopsy the ulcer base. HSV infects squamous epithelium, causing vesicles then raised-edge ulcers — biopsy the ulcer margin (multinucleated giant cells, ground-glass inclusions); IV acyclovir 5–10 mg/kg every 8 hours. Pill injury (potassium chloride, doxycycline, quinidine, NSAIDs, iron, alendronate) occurs at the aortic arch and distal narrowing; take pills upright with ample water and stay upright 15–30 minutes. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 983–985)

**Barrett esophagus**: intestinal (goblet-cell) metaplasia replacing distal squamous epithelium; long-segment is 3 cm or more. Found in 6–12% of GERD endoscopies, mainly older white men. Annual cancer risk about 0.12–0.5%. Surveillance: four-quadrant biopsies every 2 cm; no dysplasia every 3–5 years; low-grade dysplasia every 6–12 months or endoscopic eradication (preferred); high-grade dysplasia harbors occult carcinoma in about 40% of esophagectomy specimens and progresses about 6% per year, so it requires eradication. Do surveillance only after inflammation is controlled. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 981–982)

**pH testing numbers**: a reflux event is esophageal pH below 4.0 (pepsin is active below this); the key metric is percent time pH below 4, abnormal when over about 4.2% of the study. Distal probe sits 5 cm above the manometric LES; proximal esophageal probe 15–20 cm above the LES (normal under 1%); hypopharyngeal probe 2 cm above the UES (more than 2–3 events abnormal). Off-therapy testing requires stopping PPI for 1 week, H2 blockers 48 hours, antacids 2 hours. Wireless (Bravo) capsule is placed 6 cm above the GEJ and records 48–96 hours. Impedance-pH detects nonacid and gas reflux. Symptom index of 50% or more indicates good correlation. pH studies are normal in about 25% of erosive esophagitis and only about 50% of patients with laryngeal 'reflux' signs have abnormal acid exposure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 969–972, 980)

**Evidence pearls**: 87% of healthy volunteers had at least one 'reflux' laryngeal sign (interarytenoid bar, medial arytenoid erythema, posterior pharyngeal cobblestoning), so findings are nonspecific. Recommended approach: empiric twice-daily PPI, taper to daily on response; pH/impedance testing if no response. PPIs heal erosive esophagitis in about 90% and keep remission in 80% (H2 blockers about 50%). GERD is the third most common cause of chronic cough (after postnasal drip and asthma; about 21%), and 43–75% of such patients lack heartburn; a PPI trial for cough should last about 3 months. Antireflux surgery is not advised for PPI-unresponsive patients without objective acid or nonacid reflux. (Cummings 7e, Ch 68, pp 979–981)

**Outcome numbers**: complications/mortality — ESD about 2.6%/0.3%, other endoscopic techniques 7.4–8.1%/0.2%, external diverticulectomy about 11.8%/1.6%. Recurrence 0–19% external, 0–22% endoscopic (11.8% in one ESD cohort, complete early recurrence suggests incomplete myotomy or scar band, late partial recurrence suggests reformation), and revision ESD is not harder after prior surgery. Carcinoma in the sac occurs in roughly 0.25–0.5% (filling defect that persists on barium). If found, ESD is contraindicated and the pouch should be excised externally. (Cummings 7e, Ch 70, pp 1003–1005)

**Ang risk groups (RTOG 0129 secondary analysis, printed as 0219 in the text)**: HPV status was the strongest predictor of survival (3-year OS 82% vs 57%), followed by smoking (10 or fewer vs more than 10 pack-years), T stage and N stage. Low risk is HPV-positive with 10 or fewer pack-years, or HPV-positive with more than 10 pack-years and N0–N2a (3-year OS 93%). Intermediate risk is HPV-positive with more than 10 pack-years and N2b–N3, or HPV-negative with 10 or fewer pack-years and T2–T3 (71%). High risk is HPV-negative with T4 or more than 10 pack-years (46%). These N categories are AJCC 7. Risk of death rose about 1% per pack-year regardless of HPV status. Meta-analysis: HPV-positive OPSCC has about a 57% lower risk of death. (Cummings 7e, Ch 74, pp 1050–1051)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Physics basics**: 1 Gy = 1 joule absorbed per kilogram. Megavoltage photons spare the skin (dose builds up below the surface), whereas electrons deposit most of their dose superficially over a short, energy-dependent range, so they are used for skin and superficial targets. Protons deposit most energy at the end of their range (Bragg peak), lowering exit and integral dose (parotid mean dose reductions up to about 50% with intensity-modulated protons) but with limited prospective data and reports of skin toxicity and temporal lobe necrosis. Planning volumes: GTV (visible tumor), CTV (GTV plus microscopic extension and at-risk nodal basins), PTV (CTV plus margin for setup error and motion). (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1053–1057)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Linear-quadratic model**: survival S = e^-(αD + βD²). The α/β ratio is the dose at which linear and quadratic killing are equal. Early-responding tissues (mucosa, skin, most tumors) have high α/β (about 10) and are relatively insensitive to fraction size. Late-responding tissues (spinal cord, connective tissue) have low α/β (about 2–3) and are spared by small fractions. This is the rationale for hyperfractionation. Hypoxic cells are about 2.5–3 times more radioresistant. Cell-cycle sensitivity is greatest in M/G2 and least in late S. Radiotherapy works because normal tissues repair and repopulate better than tumor, not because tumors are intrinsically more sensitive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1058–1060)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Altered fractionation**: hyperfractionation (about 1.1–1.2 Gy twice daily to 74–80 Gy over the usual duration) and accelerated schedules (6–7 fractions/week or concomitant boost) improve 2-year locoregional control by about 8–20% over standard RT alone at the cost of more acute (and often late) toxicity. The original MARCH meta-analysis (2006, 15 trials, 6515 patients) showed about 6.4% absolute locoregional benefit and 3.4% 5-year survival benefit, mainly with hyperfractionation. Accelerated regimens with dose reduction gave no survival gain. Concurrent chemoradiation, not altered fractionation alone, is the modern standard. A 5-day prolongation costs about 3.5–8% local control in laryngeal cancer. SBRT (1–5 large fractions to gross tumor only) is used mainly for reirradiation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1060–1062, 1067)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Radiosensitizer and hypoxia trials**: chemotherapy adds about 4% absolute 5-year survival overall in the classic MACH-NC meta-analysis, with the benefit confined to concurrent delivery (about 6.5% absolute, hazard ratio about 0.81, in the update). Hyperbaric oxygen raised response rates but not survival. Hypoxic sensitizers (nimorazole, tirapazamine) and ARCON (carbogen + nicotinamide) have no proven survival benefit outside selected trials. Correcting anemia with erythropoietin actually worsened locoregional control and/or survival. Bonner trial: RT plus cetuximab (400 mg/m² load, then 250 mg/m² weekly) improved median survival 49 vs 29 months and 3-year survival 55% vs 45% over RT alone, but cisplatin-RT remains the standard because cetuximab-RT was inferior in HPV-positive oropharyngeal cancer (RTOG 1016, De-ESCALaTE). EORTC/RTOG pooled analysis: only extranodal extension and positive margins clearly benefit from adding cisplatin to postoperative RT. Two or more positive nodes without ENE did not. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1062–1066)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Normal-tissue tolerance numbers**: chronic myelopathy risk is under 0.5% at 50 Gy and about 5% at 5 years (TD 5/5) near 60 Gy in 1.8–2-Gy fractions, rising steeply above that (about 50% at 68–73 Gy). Lhermitte sign (electric shocks down the spine on neck flexion) 2–6 months after RT reflects transient posterior-column demyelination and does not predict progressive myelitis, which presents 6–12 months out with paresis, sensory loss, sphincter dysfunction or Brown-Séquard syndrome. Parotid permanent loss of function occurs above a mean dose of about 26 Gy (sparing one parotid preserves flow). Temporary loss occurs after about 10 Gy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1065, 1067–1069)

**Toxicity management numbers**: dermatitis appears as early as 2 weeks (worse with 5-FU); avoid lotions/ointments on treated skin before fractions (bolus effect). Mucositis begins at 2–3 weeks and is clinically significant in about 64%. Amifostine reduced acute xerostomia (78% to 51%) and chronic xerostomia at 12 months (57% to 34%) with RT alone but is seldom used because of toxicity, cost and conflicting chemoradiation data. Pilocarpine/cevimeline (muscarinic M3 agonists) help only if residual gland remains, need weeks, and cause sweating; gustatory (sour) stimuli are the strongest natural sialagogues. Hypothyroidism appears at a median of about 1.4–1.8 years (range 0.3–7 years) and is more common after combined surgery and RT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1067–1069)

**Numbers and risk factors**: mandibular ORN occurs in about 5–10% after conventional RT or HDR brachytherapy (severe in about 2%) and is more frequent with hyperfractionation (23% vs 9% in one oral cancer series). The mandible is affected far more than the maxilla because of its unilateral blood supply and dose exposure. Post-irradiation extraction raises ORN risk, and ORN after post-RT extraction more often needed radical resection (45% vs 12%). Remove nonrestorable teeth before RT but do not extract healthy or restorable teeth. In a randomized trial of established ORN, hyperbaric oxygen did not improve healing (19% vs 32% placebo). (Cummings 7e, Ch 75, pp 1068–1069)

**Trial numbers**: VA larynx trial (332 patients, stage III–IV) — induction cisplatin/5-FU then RT vs laryngectomy + PORT: identical 2-year survival (68%), 66% of survivors in the chemo arm kept the larynx; more local recurrence (20% vs 7%) but fewer distant metastases (11% vs 17%) with chemotherapy; salvage laryngectomy was needed in 56% of T4 vs 29% of smaller tumors and more often with fixed folds. RTOG 91-11 (547 patients, T4 largely excluded) 10-year update — larynx preservation 82% with concurrent cisplatin (100 mg/m² days 1, 22, 43) vs 68% induction vs 64% RT alone; laryngectomy-free survival similar for induction and concurrent arms; late deaths not from cancer trended higher with concurrent therapy (overall survival 38% induction vs 27% concurrent, p = .08). GORTEC (larynx/hypopharynx): induction TPF vs PF gave higher response (83% vs 61%) and larynx preservation (80% vs 58%). EORTC hypopharynx trial confirmed equivalent survival with induction-based preservation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 76, pp 1073–1075)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Concurrent and induction evidence**: MACH-NC meta-analyses show concurrent chemoradiation gives about a 6.5% absolute 5-year survival gain over RT alone (benefit confined to concurrent timing). Single-agent cisplatin 100 mg/m² on days 1, 22 and 43 is the reference arm, and multi-agent concurrent regimens have not proved superior. Adding cetuximab to cisplatin-RT (RTOG 0522, 891 patients) added toxicity without improving control or survival. Induction TPF beats PF (TAX 323: OS 18.8 vs 14.5 months, TAX 324: 3-year OS 62% vs 48%, 5-year 52% vs 42%), but induction followed by chemoradiation did not beat chemoradiation alone in DeCIDE (N2–N3) or PARADIGM (3-year OS 73% vs 78%), partly because HPV-positive patients improved control arms. Induction is reserved for selected high distant-metastasis risk (bulky/low neck nodes) or organ preservation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 76, pp 1075–1081)

**Adjuvant trial details**: Intergroup trial of sequential cisplatin/5-FU before PORT in margin-negative patients showed no survival benefit (fewer distant metastases only). RTOG 9501 and EORTC 22931 (cisplatin 100 mg/m² weeks 1, 4, 7 with PORT) — pooled analysis shows benefit for positive margins and/or extranodal extension: about 42% lower locoregional failure and about 10% absolute survival gain, with more acute but not more chronic toxicity; two or more nodes without ENE did not benefit. RTOG 0234 (phase II) tested PORT 60 Gy plus cetuximab with weekly cisplatin or docetaxel (docetaxel arm 2-year DFS 66%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 76, pp 1077–1078)

**Intergroup 0099**: in advanced nasopharyngeal carcinoma, RT with concurrent cisplatin 100 mg/m² (days 1, 22, 43) followed by three cycles of adjuvant cisplatin/5-FU improved 3-year overall survival (78% vs 47%) and progression-free survival (69% vs 24%) over RT alone, establishing chemoradiation as standard. IMRT is standard for NPC because it preserves salivary flow without loss of control (about 97% locoregional control in the UCSF series). (Cummings 7e, Ch 76, p 1076, Ch 75, p 1064)

**Historical cytotoxic benchmarks**: single agents (methotrexate, cisplatin, taxanes, 5-FU, cetuximab) give about 10–30% (mostly partial) responses lasting 2–4 months, with median survival 6–9 months. Cisplatin/5-FU gives about 30–40% responses without clear survival gain over single agents. Cisplatin–paclitaxel equals cisplatin–5-FU (26% vs 27%). EXTREME (platinum/5-FU ± cetuximab) raised median OS from 7.4 to 10.1 months. Panitumumab added to PF did not significantly improve OS. CheckMate 141 (nivolumab after platinum): median OS 7.5 vs 5.1 months, 1-year OS 36% vs 17%, fewer grade 3–4 events (13% vs 35%). RECIST partial response = 30% decrease in the largest dimension. Current first-line care is pembrolizumab-based (KEYNOTE-048): pembrolizumab alone for PD-L1 CPS 1 or more, or with platinum/5-FU, so EXTREME is now an alternative rather than the default. (Cummings 7e, Ch 76, pp 1082–1087)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Timeline and strength**: inflammatory (exudative) phase lasts about 4–5 days in a sutured wound (7–10 days if open), with neutrophils peaking around day 1 and macrophages (the key orchestrating cell, source of growth factors) dominant from about day 3. Proliferation runs from about day 3 for about 2 weeks (keratinocyte migration via MMP-1, granulation tissue at 3–4 days, fibroblasts dominant by the first week, TGF-β–driven myofibroblasts with α-smooth muscle actin causing contraction). Remodeling starts about week 3 and continues up to 12 months as type III collagen is replaced by type I. Tensile strength is about 3% of normal at 1 week, 20% at 3 weeks and 80% at 3 months (never 100%). Hypoxia drives VEGF-mediated angiogenesis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1100–1104)

topic: Wound Healing / Scar Biology in Head & Neck Surgery
text: **Impaired healing specifics**: a chronic wound is one that fails to heal within about 3 weeks. Infection = more than 10^5 organisms per gram of tissue. Biofilms exist in 60–80% of chronic wounds without classic signs of infection and are best removed by sharp debridement. Corticosteroids, immunosuppressants and chemotherapy disrupt the critical first 3 days. Ideally stop them about a month before and 1–2 weeks after surgery. Weight loss of 10% or more predicts poor healing. Diabetes slows collagen synthesis and tensile strength. Wound oxygenation is improved mainly by hydration, warmth and analgesia (relieving vasoconstriction). Topical PDGF (becaplermin) is approved for diabetic foot ulcers. Moist occlusive dressings speed epithelialization. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1104–1106)

**Delay phenomenon**: partially raising and replacing a flap increases total blood flow (not shunt fraction), reduces distal vasoconstriction, and develops collaterals through choke vessels. Benefit appears with as little as 24 hours, peaks around 4 days (no further gain to 14 days), lasts up to about 6 weeks, and still works in irradiated tissue. Nicotine impairs flap survival, an effect reversed experimentally by stopping 2 weeks before surgery. E-cigarettes appear similar. Hyperbaric oxygen helps compromised pedicled flaps only if started early (little benefit after 24 hours). A transcutaneous O2 rise of 50 mm Hg or more on a test dive predicts response. ICG angiography can show adequate perfusion for paramedian forehead flap division as early as about 2 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1094–1098)

**Ischemia tolerance**: tissue generally tolerates about 6 hours of complete ischemia; a first (primary) ischemia during transfer lowers tolerance of a later (secondary) ischemia from anastomotic thrombosis, and a longer reperfusion interval before secondary ischemia improves tolerance. Early complete venous occlusion is more damaging than arterial insufficiency, and venous thrombosis is the more common cause of failure (implantable venous flow couplers outperform arterial Doppler). No-reflow = restored pedicle (zone I) flow without capillary/interstitial perfusion. Venous couplers over 3 mm reduce revision about 40%; longer anesthesia time, hardware and congestive heart failure predict compromise, while age (even over 90) and BMI do not contraindicate free flaps. (Cummings 7e, Ch 77, pp 1092–1095)

**Timing numbers**: most anastomotic thromboses occur within the first 48–72 hours; after roughly 12 hours of ischemia a flap is usually not salvageable even if flow is restored. Collateral ingrowth can sustain a flap independent of the pedicle as early as about 8 days in animals, but surgeons should not rely on bed neovascularization for 3–4 weeks (longer in irradiated beds), and bone may remain pedicle-dependent. Clinical inspection and pinprick (slow bright-red bleeding) remain the gold standard; the best intraoperative confirmation of patency is bright red bleeding from the skin paddle edge (strip testing can injure endothelium). Fluid collections and dehiscence near the pedicle must be drained promptly because pus causes compression and thrombosis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 78, pp 1117–1120)

**Antithrombotics (no strong trial evidence)**: aspirin acetylates cyclooxygenase; about 100 mg suppresses thromboxane while sparing prostacyclin, and it is most effective given preoperatively or within 24 hours. Systemic heparin prevents both arterial and venous thrombi but raises hematoma risk; topical heparin irrigation (100 U/mL) showed no flap benefit. Dextran 40 interferes with fibrin and von Willebrand factor but did not improve outcome in a prospective trial and risks anaphylaxis (test dose), volume overload/pulmonary edema, renal injury and ARDS, so it is discouraged for routine free flaps, especially over age 50. (Cummings 7e, Ch 78, pp 1116–1117)

**Acute suppurative parotitis specifics**: About 75% of cases yield beta-lactamase-producing organisms, so empiric coverage must handle S. aureus and oral anaerobes (beta-lactamase-resistant agents), with MRSA coverage for nosocomial cases; response is expected within 48–72 hours and therapy continues about a week past resolution. An abscess that fails medical therapy is drained through radial incisions in the parotid fascia parallel to facial nerve branches, and sialendoscopy is avoided during acute infection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1162)

**Mumps**: Mumps (paramyxovirus) is the most common cause of acute nonsuppurative sialadenitis. After a 2–3 week incubation and viral prodrome, it causes painful, tense, nonerythematous parotid swelling that is bilateral in about 75% of cases and pushes the earlobe up. Confirm with serology: S (soluble) antibodies appear early and mark active infection, V antibodies persist for years, and a fourfold titer rise is diagnostic. Care is supportive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1164)

**Key epidemiology**: It is the second most common pediatric inflammatory salivary disorder after mumps. Boys are affected more than girls; episodes start by age 1–2 years, recur every 3–4 months, and the diagnosis is usually made at ages 3–6 years.
