Reported associations include IgA or IgG3 deficiency, early juvenile Sjögren syndrome, and HIV (about 20% of HIV-infected children). Glands can lose 50–80% of function, even though most cases resolve at puberty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1163)

**Radioiodine sialadenitis**: Salivary damage from radioiodine depends on dose: injury is generally reversible at about 20–30 Gy to the gland but may be permanent above about 50 Gy. Sialadenitis affects roughly 18–26% of thyroid cancer patients treated with RAI and is usually bilateral parotid swelling. Interventional sialendoscopy (washout, removal of mucus plugs, dilation, steroid irrigation) relieves symptoms in about 50–100% of reported series and is preferred over parotidectomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1164)

**Sjögren drug therapy**: Pilocarpine (a muscarinic agonist) is the main systemic sialogogue at about 5 mg three to four times daily; sweating, flushing, and urinary frequency are common. Rituximab (anti-CD20) depletes B cells and can improve sicca symptoms and systemic symptoms. Systemic steroids or cytotoxic drugs are reserved for severe extraglandular disease such as vasculitis or glomerulonephritis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1169)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Kimura and Rosai-Dorfman disease**: Kimura disease typically affects young Asian men: painless, often itchy cervicofacial and periauricular masses, sometimes in the parotid, with peripheral eosinophilia and high IgE that track disease activity. Treatment options include observation, excision, steroids, cyclosporine, or radiation. Rosai-Dorfman disease presents with massive painless bilateral cervical adenopathy. It involves the salivary glands in about 30% of cases, and its histiocytes are S-100-positive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1170)

**HIV salivary gland disease (BLEC/DILS)**: Parotid enlargement from benign lymphoepithelial cysts occurs in about 1–10% of HIV patients, can be the first sign of infection, is bilateral in about 80%, and is rare enough in HIV-negative people that finding it should prompt HIV testing. DILS (diffuse infiltrative lymphocytosis syndrome) mimics Sjögren but has circulating CD8 lymphocytosis, involves organs outside the glands (lung, GI tract, kidney), and lacks SSA/SSB antibodies. Management options are observation, repeat aspiration, antiretroviral therapy, sclerotherapy, or low-dose RT. Rapid growth calls for FNA to rule out lymphoma. (Cummings 7e, Ch 83, p 1164)

**Milan System for salivary cytology**: The Milan system is a Bethesda-like tiering for salivary FNA. The current 2nd edition (2023) gives these approximate malignancy risks: nondiagnostic about 15%, non-neoplastic about 11%, atypia of undetermined significance about 30% (repeat FNA or surgery), benign neoplasm under 3%, salivary neoplasm of uncertain malignant potential (SUMP) about 35%, suspicious for malignancy about 83%, and malignant about 98%. Older sources quote the 1st edition figures (about 25%, 10%, 20%, under 5%, 35%, 60% and 90%). The last two categories go to surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 84, p 1174)

**Metastasizing pleomorphic adenoma**: A histologically benign-appearing PA can metastasize, typically after multiple local recurrences. The mean interval from the primary to metastasis is about 12 years. Sites are bone (about 50%), lung (about 30%), and regional nodes (about 30%), and about 40% of patients die of the disease. This is a reason to remove PAs completely at the first operation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1200)

**Facial nerve landmarks and outcomes**: The main trunk lies about 1–1.5 cm deep and slightly inferior to the tragal pointer and about 6–8 mm deep to the tympanomastoid suture. It exits just anterior to the posterior belly of digastric at the mastoid, and the posterior auricular artery is met nearby. The pes anserinus is about 1–2 cm from the stylomastoid foramen. If the trunk cannot be reached, the marginal branch can be found along the retromandibular vein (or the buccal branch along Stensen duct) and traced back. In one large series, temporary weakness occurred in about 46% and permanent weakness in about 4%, with higher rates after revision and total parotidectomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 84, p 1183)

**FNA pitfalls**: In a College of American Pathologists dataset, salivary FNA had only about 68% sensitivity for malignancy (32% false negatives, worst for lymphoma, acinic cell carcinoma, and low-grade mucoepidermoid) and about 91% specificity. Basal cell adenoma was the most frequent false-positive (read as adenoid cystic carcinoma). Low-grade cancers such as polymorphous adenocarcinoma and myoepithelial carcinoma often cannot be called malignant without seeing invasion on the resection specimen. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1192)

**Mucoepidermoid carcinoma specifics**: MEC is the most common salivary cancer overall and in children. It contains mucous, epidermoid (squamoid), and intermediate cells. Grading systems (Auclair, Brandwein) score cystic component under 20–25%, PNI, necrosis, 4 or more mitoses per 10 hpf, and anaplasia. The CRTC1-MAML2 t(11,19) fusion is found in more than half of cases, mostly low and intermediate grade. Submandibular MECs, even low grade, recur and metastasize more often than parotid ones. True keratinization points to adenosquamous carcinoma instead. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1195)

topic: Salivary Adenoid Cystic Carcinoma and Perineural Spread
text: **Grading and molecular facts**: Grade I is tubular with or without cribriform areas and no solid areas. Grade II is mainly cribriform with less than 30% solid. Grade III has more than 30% solid component. Grade III tumors cause most of the rare nodal metastases. PNI is seen in about 70–75% of cases. The MYB-NFIB t(6,9) fusion is present in up to two-thirds. More than 90% of tumors express c-KIT, yet imatinib has failed. Bone metastasis carries about 30% 5-year survival, while slow lung metastases should not by themselves stop resection of the primary. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1196)

**Polymorphous adenocarcinoma**: Formerly called PLGA, this is almost only a minor salivary gland tumor and the second most common minor-gland carcinoma. It favors the hard–soft palate junction and women aged 40–60. It shows single-file 'eye of the storm' whorls and frequent PNI but bland cytology. Unlike pleomorphic adenoma, it is GFAP-negative, and unlike adenoid cystic carcinoma it is p63-positive and p40-negative. Treatment is conservative wide excision. Local recurrence is 10–15%, nodal metastasis is about 10% or less, and neck dissection is done only for clinical disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1196)

**Acinic cell carcinoma**: More than 90% arise in the parotid. It is the second most common pediatric salivary carcinoma. Cells contain PAS-positive serous zymogen granules, are DOG1-positive, and are often accompanied by dense lymphoid stroma. It has no benign counterpart. About one-third recur, 10–15% metastasize, recurrences can come a decade later (survival about 80% at 5 years and 70% at 10 years), and high-grade transformation behaves aggressively. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1198)

**Carcinoma ex pleomorphic adenoma invasion categories**: The invasion depth of the carcinoma beyond the PA capsule drives prognosis. Intracapsular (in situ) and minimally invasive (1.5 mm or less) tumors behave almost like benign PA when fully excised. Widely invasive (over 1.5 mm) high-grade tumors have 5-year survival of about 26–65% and need wide excision, neck dissection, and RT. The classic history is a long-standing mass that grows suddenly, often with facial palsy, in patients about a decade older than typical PA patients. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1198)

**Salivary duct carcinoma and secretory carcinoma**: Salivary duct carcinoma looks like high-grade ductal breast cancer with comedonecrosis. It is male-predominant (about 4:1) and AR-positive, a subset is HER2-positive, and it is ER/PR-negative. Half to three-quarters of patients develop distant metastases, so treat with wide excision, neck dissection, and PORT, with trastuzumab or androgen blockade for advanced disease. Secretory carcinoma (formerly mammary analogue) is S-100- and mammaglobin-positive and carries ETV6-NTRK3 t(12,15), making it a target for NTRK inhibitors. It is usually low grade, with a parotid predominance. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1200)

**Metastases and other primaries in the parotid**: The parotid holds about 20 intraglandular nodes that drain the scalp, face, ear, and EAC, so 80–90% of parotid metastases come from cutaneous SCC or melanoma (deep-lobe nodal disease is worse). In contrast, about 85% of submandibular metastases come from outside the head and neck (breast, kidney, lung). Primary salivary SCC is rare (under 1%) and requires excluding a skin primary. Salivary small cell carcinoma is CK20-positive and practically indistinguishable from metastatic Merkel cell carcinoma, while lung small cell is TTF-1-positive and CK20-negative. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1202)

**Elective neck: who and which levels**: Occult nodal metastasis is about 21% for submandibular versus 9% for parotid cancers. It is about 20% for tumors 4 cm or larger versus 4% for smaller ones, and about 49% for high-grade versus 7% for low/intermediate-grade tumors. Higher-risk histologies are high-grade MEC, SCC, undifferentiated carcinoma, adenocarcinoma NOS, salivary duct carcinoma, CXPA, and any high-grade transformation. Parotid primaries need at least levels I–IV, and submandibular/sublingual primaries need levels I–III. A clinically positive neck needs an ipsilateral comprehensive dissection because skip metastases occur. (Cummings 7e, Ch 85, p 1208)

**Lingual thyroid**: About 90% of ectopic thyroid lies at the tongue base near the foramen cecum. Up to about 70% of patients are hypothyroid, and in about 70% the lingual gland is the only functioning thyroid tissue. Symptoms (dysphagia, globus, airway obstruction, bleeding) often appear at times of high demand such as puberty or pregnancy. Thyroid hormone suppression is first-line and shrinks the mass. Excision (transoral/TORS or transcervical) is for symptomatic euthyroid patients, followed by lifelong replacement. (Cummings 7e, Ch 89, p 1282)

**DOI and occult metastasis data**: In a large series of early tongue cancers, occult nodal metastasis was 28% and multiplied disease-specific death risk about fivefold. Every occult metastasis had a DOI of 2 mm or more (92% had 4 mm or more), and none were seen in superficial (under 2 mm), well-differentiated tumors. A close margin cutoff of about 2.2 mm predicted local recurrence. SEER data support elective neck dissection when a moderately or poorly differentiated tumor exceeds 1 cm, or a well-differentiated tumor exceeds 2 cm. (Cummings 7e, Ch 91, p 1304)

**Skip metastases**: Byers found that about 16% of lateral tongue cancers skip levels I–II and metastasize first to level III or IV. That is why many surgeons dissect levels I–IV rather than a supraomohyoid (I–III) dissection for the N0 lateral tongue, and treat both sides when the tumor nears midline. (Cummings 7e, Ch 91, p 1304)

**DOI and survival**: For floor-of-mouth/oral SCC: DOI under 2 mm carries about 13% nodal metastasis and 95% 5-year survival; DOI 2–9 mm about 46% and 85%; DOI over 9 mm about 65% and 65%. About half of FOM patients have neck metastases (level Ib most often, and bilateral for anterior lesions). Five-year survival is about 90%, 80%, 65%, and 30% for stages I–IV. (Cummings 7e, Ch 91, p 1306)

**Oral cavity selective dissection details**: The supraomohyoid dissection (levels I–III) is standard for the N0 oral cavity, includes the submandibular gland, and should include level IIb (about 10% involvement). A yield under 18 nodes was linked to worse 5-year survival (about 51% vs 74%). Elective treatment is indicated whenever occult-node risk exceeds 20%. Debulking gross nodal disease does not improve survival. (Cummings 7e, Ch 91, p 1311)

**Timing and package time**: Adjuvant RT should start within about 6 weeks of surgery, at 60–66 Gy for high-risk and 50–60 Gy for lower-risk beds. A total package time (surgery to end of RT) under 100 days is associated with better locoregional control and survival. In one oral cavity series, chemoradiation helped when three or more of these were present: pT4, pN1, margin 4 mm or less, poor differentiation, PNI, LVI, or DOI 11 mm or more. (Cummings 7e, Ch 91, p 1312)

**Pre-radiation dental triage**: Teeth in fields expected to get more than 50 Gy are assessed for lifelong prognosis. Extract teeth with periodontal pockets of 5 mm or more, furcation involvement, active periapical disease, nonrestorable or unopposed teeth, or impactions. Ideally do this during the cancer operation so bone heals before RT, which usually starts about 6 weeks after surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 92, p 1332)

**Lifelong fluoride and post-RT surgery rules**: Dentate patients with xerostomia use custom trays daily for life with 1.1% neutral sodium fluoride or 0.4% stannous fluoride gel for 5–10 minutes. Bone-exposing oral surgery (extractions, implants) in areas that received more than about 50 Gy raises ORN risk. When it cannot be avoided, Cummings offers the Marx hyperbaric oxygen protocol (20 dives before and 10 after, 90 minutes at 2.4 atmospheres). **Current view**: the HOPON randomized trial found no meaningful reduction in ORN with HBO before extraction in irradiated jaws, so routine HBO for this purpose is no longer standard. Dosimetry should be obtained from radiation oncology, since field edges and contralateral teeth get far less dose. (Cummings 7e, Ch 93, p 1334)

**Esthesioneuroblastoma Kadish definitions**: Kadish A: confined to the nasal cavity. B: extends into the paranasal sinuses. C: beyond the nasal cavity and sinuses. D (modified): cervical or distant metastasis. About half present as Kadish C, with 5-year survival of 50–70%. Neck metastases eventually develop in 20–25%, which feeds the debate over elective neck treatment. Calcifications on CT are a clue. Follow-up should continue 15–20 years. (Cummings 7e, Ch 93, p 1364)

**Symptoms that localize spread**: Epiphora means nasolacrimal involvement. Diplopia means orbital, apex, or cavernous sinus disease. Trismus means pterygoid invasion. Cheek numbness means V2 perineural spread toward Meckel cave. Hearing loss from eustachian tube or prevertebral extension implies unresectability. Loose nonvital teeth or a widened alveolus means inferior/palatal bone involvement. The Ohngren line (medial canthus to mandibular angle) separates infrastructure tumors (earlier, more resectable) from suprastructure tumors (worse prognosis). (Cummings 7e, Ch 94, p 1366)

**Resectability and RT limits**: Open-surgery contraindications include gross brain invasion, invasion of both orbits, carotid encasement, cavernous sinus invasion, and nasopharyngeal/pterygoid extension. Endoscopic limits are dura lateral to the mid-pupillary line, anterior/lateral frontal sinus disease, facial or orbital soft-tissue spread, and palatal involvement. Surgery plus PORT outperforms RT alone (one series: 5-year OS about 60% vs 9%). PORT doses of 60–70 Gy exceed optic nerve tolerance (45–54 Gy), and conventional RT caused visual toxicity in about 35%, which IMRT and protons reduce. (Cummings 7e, Ch 94, p 1372)

**Orbit and craniofacial resection**: Orbital floor bone invasion requires total maxillectomy with orbital floor reconstruction. Exenteration is reserved for tumor through the periorbita into orbital fat, and only with curative intent. In the international craniofacial resection study (1334 patients), 5-year DFS and OS were 53% and 48%. Independent predictors were positive margins, intracranial extension (brain invasion about 28% 5-year DSS), and histology (mucosal melanoma worst). Craniofacial resection carries 30–54% complications and 0–8% mortality, versus about 4% CSF leak in endoscopic series. (Cummings 7e, Ch 94, p 1376)

**Rhabdomyosarcoma staging logic**: RMS is the most common pediatric sinonasal malignancy, with the orbit the most common head and neck subsite. Embryonal type (55–65%, including botryoid) has the best prognosis, alveolar (20–30%, teens) is worse, and anaplastic/undifferentiated types are worst. Risk group combines site-based TNM stage (orbit and non-parameningeal head and neck sites are favorable stage 1, while the nasopharynx, nasal cavity, sinuses, temporal bone, and infratemporal fossa are parameningeal), clinical group by completeness of resection, and histology. Biopsy plus chemoradiation is standard. Five-year survival is about 95% for orbital and 74% for parameningeal disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 94, p 1364)

**EBV serology and DNA**: In NPC, IgA (not IgG) antibodies to viral capsid antigen and early antigen are raised: IgA-VCA is more sensitive and IgA-EA more specific, and a negative IgA-EA makes NPC unlikely. Plasma EBV DNA rises with stage and predicts survival. In a screening study of over 20,000 people, persistently positive EBV DNA gave about 97% sensitivity and 99% specificity and shifted diagnoses to earlier stages. Serology never replaces nasopharyngeal biopsy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 95, p 1395)

**Presentation numbers**: About 60% present with a neck mass (upper level II/V), and imaging finds nodes in at least 80% overall. Other presentations: blood-stained saliva about 41%, conductive hearing loss from effusion about 30%, epistaxis about 23%, cranial nerve palsy about 10%. Cranial nerves are affected in the order V, VI, IX, X, XII, and an isolated CN VI palsy (via foramen lacerum) should prompt nasopharyngeal exam in endemic groups. About 10% of tumors are submucosal and look normal. Dermatomyositis carries about a 10% NPC risk, and about 15% of patients have an affected first-degree relative. (Cummings 7e, Ch 95, p 1396)

**Staging details**: Retropharyngeal nodes are N1 regardless of laterality. N3 means a node over 6 cm or extension below the caudal border of the cricoid. T0 is used for an EBV-positive node with no visible primary. Bone is the most common distant site. Cummings favors bone scan for distant staging, but FDG PET/CT is now the preferred study for advanced (T3-T4 or N2-N3) disease in NCCN guidance. Get a baseline audiogram and tympanogram before cisplatin-based treatment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 95, p 1398)

**Salvage surgery**: Local recurrence occurs in 5–10% of patients, and about half are surgically salvageable (best for rT1). Limits are ICA involvement, skull base erosion, and intracranial extension. Approaches include endoscopic/robotic nasopharyngectomy for small central lesions, lateral rhinotomy/medial maxillectomy, and the Wei maxillary swing for pterygopalatine extension. Regional recurrence (about 10%) is treated with a radical neck dissection, sacrificing the IJV, CN XI, and SCM, because recurrent nodes run along the jugular and accessory chains with frequent extracapsular spread. A pectoralis flap protects the carotid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 95, p 1400)

**Nasopharyngeal mass differential**: In a child, think adenoids. In a teenage boy, JNA. In an adult, carcinoma until proven otherwise. A Thornwaldt cyst is a smooth, yellowish, midline remnant of the notochord/pharyngeal bursa that may cause postnasal drip. It needs no biopsy or removal unless it is dark, which raises concern for melanoma. Meningoencephalocele must be excluded. Chordoma arises from the clivus/basisphenoid and erodes into the nasopharynx with cranial neuropathies. It is resected endoscopically or by a skull base approach, with proton therapy for residual tumor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 95, p 1391)

**Prognostic weight of p16**: In the Ang (RTOG 0129) secondary analysis of stage III–IV chemoradiated oropharyngeal SCC, p16 positivity cut the risk of relapse or death by about 58% (HR 0.42), and HPV ISH positivity by about 59%. This is why p16 IHC alone is accepted as the routine prognostic and staging marker. HPV-associated cases rose from about 40% of OPSCC before 2000 to about 72% by 2005–2009. (Cummings 7e, Ch 96, p 1419)

**Transoral candidacy and contraindications**: Use the eight T's to judge access: teeth, trismus, transverse mandibular width, tori, tongue bulk, tilt (neck extension), prior treatment (RT), and tumor. Absolute contraindications to transoral resection are skull base invasion, great-vessel encasement, mandible invasion, primary tumor confluent with neck disease, and any tumor that cannot confidently be cleared. Resections needing more than 50% of the tongue base or more than 75% of the soft palate are relative contraindications. Debulking with plans for RT to 'clean up' is unacceptable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 97, p 1430)

topic: Transoral Robotic Surgery (TORS) for Oropharyngeal Cancer
text: **Post-TORS/TLM bleeding protocol**: After transoral oropharyngeal cancer surgery, bleeding occurs in about 3–8% (1.4% in a 701-patient TLM series, including fatal cases) and is most common in the first week. Minor bleeds usually happen around days 9–14. Patients die from aspiration and asphyxia, not blood loss. Teach dependent head positioning with pressure on the neck on the resected side, place a cuffed tube through any tracheostomy stoma, and take major bleeds to the OR. Prevention: clip vessels 2 mm or larger with 2–3 clips and ligate lingual, facial, and superior thyroid branches (or the ECA for large defects) at neck dissection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 97, p 1442)

**Soft palate defects after cancer resection**: resection of 50% or more of the soft palate predictably causes VPI. The reconstruction must narrow the velopharyngeal aperture (folded radial forearm flap plus pharyngeal adhesion/pharyngoplasty, Gehanno posterior-lateral pharyngeal wall turnover, or superior-constrictor advancement-rotation flap [SCARF] for defects up to about 65%). Small marginal defects can use the uvulopalatal flap (requires intact uvula and contralateral palate), FAMM or buccinator flap. Isolated soft palate defects are the hardest to obturate because a prosthesis is not dynamic. (Cummings 7e, Ch 98, pp 1452–1455)

**Fluoroscopic cricopharyngeal findings**: failure to relax (cricopharyngeal 'achalasia') produces a smooth posterior bar at C6 that is under 1 cm tall, unlike most retropharyngeal masses; commonest cause is cerebrovascular disease. Absent impression between swallows (cricopharyngeal chalasia, an incompetent UES) is specific for myotonic dystrophy; delayed but complete opening occurs in familial dysautonomia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 100, pp 1481–1482)

**Esophagogram patterns**: achalasia – dilated aperistaltic esophagus with smooth 'bird-beak' tapering at the GE junction (Chagas disease and distal/cardia carcinoma mimic it; achalasia raises SCC risk); scleroderma – aperistalsis of the distal two-thirds (smooth muscle) with an incompetent LES and reflux (opposite of achalasia); diffuse esophageal spasm – corkscrew/rosary esophagus, diagnosed only with chest pain; nutcracker esophagus – normal esophagogram, diagnosed by manometry; dermatomyositis targets striated pharyngeal/upper esophageal muscle. (Cummings 7e, Ch 100, pp 1482–1483)

**Imaging criteria for nodes and carotid invasion**: nodes >1 cm (>1.5 cm jugulodigastric) are abnormal. Round shape and central necrosis favor metastasis while a reniform shape with fatty hilum favors benign. Tumor contact with the carotid over >270 degrees of circumference or >4 cm length predicts arterial invasion. <180 degrees predicts no invasion. If sacrifice is considered, balloon test occlusion with perfusion imaging predicts tolerance. Radiologic level boundaries: hyoid separates II/III, lower cricoid separates III/IV. (Cummings 7e, Ch 100, pp 1497–1498)

**AJCC 8 hypopharynx T stage**: T1 one subsite and ≤2 cm; T2 >1 subsite or adjacent site, or >2–4 cm, without hemilarynx fixation; T3 >4 cm or hemilarynx fixation or extension to esophageal mucosa; T4a thyroid/cricoid cartilage, hyoid, thyroid gland, esophageal muscle, or central compartment soft tissue (prelaryngeal straps, subcutaneous fat); T4b prevertebral fascia, carotid encasement, or mediastinal structures. Note that unlike the larynx, size cutoffs (2 and 4 cm) drive T1–T3. (Cummings 7e, Ch 101, p 1508)

**Submucosal spread and margins**: in serial sections, 58% of specimens had submucosal extension (type 1 visible, type 2 histologic only, type 3 true skip lesion—rare), greatest inferiorly, then laterally, then superiorly. Recommended margins in unirradiated patients are about 3 cm inferior, 2 cm lateral, and 1.5 cm superior (4, 3, 2 cm after radiation). Piriform apex involvement predicted laryngeal framework invasion in every case in Kirchner's whole-organ study, which is why apex disease excludes conservation surgery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 101, p 1507)

**Conservation operations and contraindications**: partial (lateral) pharyngectomy suits T1–T2 tumors limited to the posterior or lateral piriform wall—contraindicated by >1 wall, apex, or any laryngeal involvement. Partial laryngopharyngectomy (medial wall/marginal tumors) and supracricoid hemilaryngopharyngectomy (Laccourreye; T1–T3) are contraindicated by piriform apex involvement, postcricoid extension, ipsilateral cord fixation/paralysis, posterior wall invasion, or cricopharyngeus encroachment; they require good pulmonary reserve. Anterior transhyoid pharyngotomy reaches small posterior-wall tumors, with prevertebral fascia as the deep margin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 101, pp 1510–1514)

**Neck management**: occult metastasis is common (about 55% for T3/T4 cN0 piriform tumors); treat both sides of the N0 neck for all but very early tumors, selective levels II–IV for N0 and comprehensive dissection for N+. Address level VI/paratracheal nodes (positive in about 71% of cervical esophageal and 8% of hypopharyngeal primaries in one series) with ipsilateral thyroidectomy for apex/postcricoid/esophageal extension; retropharyngeal nodes are positive in about 20% (more with posterior wall tumors) and are covered by radiation fields. Medial piriform wall tumors carry higher contralateral risk than lateral wall tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 101, pp 1516–1517)

**Larynx-preservation trials specific to hypopharynx**: EORTC 24891 (piriform sinus; induction cisplatin/5-FU, complete responders irradiated, nonresponders operated) showed no survival detriment and about 50% larynx retention at 5 years. A trial without response-based selection (induction then RT for all) gave worse 5-year survival (19% vs 37%) than surgery, showing that bioselection is essential. GORTEC added docetaxel (TPF) to induction and improved larynx preservation without survival change; EORTC 24954 found alternating chemoradiation equivalent to sequential. RTOG 91-11 enrolled only larynx, not hypopharynx. (Cummings 7e, Ch 102, pp 1520–1521)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **MACH-NC meta-analysis**: adding concurrent chemotherapy to definitive locoregional treatment improves 5-year overall survival by about 6.5% (original 2000 analysis: 8% for concurrent, 4% for any chemotherapy). Induction and adjuvant chemotherapy give no consistent survival benefit, and the benefit of chemotherapy wanes with age (>70) and poor performance status. Site benefit for hypopharynx was smaller (about 4%). Concurrent chemotherapy mainly improves locoregional control. Induction mainly reduces distant failure, but adding induction to CRT (e.g., PARADIGM, DeCIDE) has not improved survival. (Cummings 7e, Ch 102, pp 1521–1522)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Altered fractionation**: hyperfractionation = smaller fractions twice daily to a higher total dose. Accelerated = similar dose in shorter overall time (e.g., concomitant boost, DAHANCA six fractions/week). RTOG 90-03 showed better locoregional control with hyperfractionation and concomitant boost (no chemotherapy). The updated MARCH meta-analysis (2017, 33 trials) showed a 3.1% 5-year survival gain overall, driven by hyperfractionation (8.1%), but altered fractionation alone is worse than standard-fraction CRT, and adding concomitant boost to CRT (RTOG 0129) gave no benefit—reserve it for patients who cannot receive chemotherapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 102, p 1522)

**Fistula recognition and conservative care**: most pharyngocutaneous fistulas declare around postoperative day 7 (1–6 weeks depending on prior radiation). Confirm with methylene blue or water-soluble contrast swallow. Manage with NPO, packing, antibiotics, reflux control, salivary bypass tube for high output, and a pedicled muscle flap if it does not close. Once the patient handles saliva, early oral feeding is reasonable in nonirradiated patients. Risk factors: prior (chemo)radiation, positive margins, diabetes, hypothyroidism, poor nutrition, salvage within 1 year of CRT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1586, Ch 109, pp 1668–1670)

**Hemithyroidectomy and paratracheal dissection indications**: include the ipsilateral thyroid lobe and paratracheal nodes for subglottic primaries, glottic tumors with >1 cm subglottic extension, transglottic or T4 tumors, anterior commissure/thyroid cartilage invasion or a palpable abnormality. Thyroid invasion is actually found in only about 8–20%. For stomal-recurrence prevention, irradiate the upper mediastinum when nodes or extralaryngeal spread are present. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1579, 1587, Ch 109, p 1663)

**CT/MRI thresholds that change surgery**: anterior commissure soft tissue >1 mm implies tumor; any measurable soft tissue between the cricoid and airway is abnormal (subglottic spread); subglottic extension >1 cm anteriorly or >6 mm posteriorly, contralateral cord involvement >30%, or thyroid cartilage invasion generally excludes vertical partial laryngectomy. The true cord level is where thyroid, arytenoid and cricoid cartilages appear on one axial slice. Image before biopsy or wait at least 48 hours to avoid post-biopsy edema. (Cummings 7e, Ch 104, pp 1550, 1554–1557)

**Cartilage invasion on imaging**: the most reliable signs are frank cartilage destruction by adjacent tumor and tumor in the medullary space (loss of T1 fat signal on MRI) or extralaryngeal extension; sclerosis alone has low specificity (about 40% in the thyroid cartilage) and often reflects perichondritis. Irregular normal ossification mimics invasion; MRI is more sensitive but less specific than CT; dual-energy CT iodine maps help. Cartilage invasion upstages to T3/T4a, predicts poorer RT response and chondroradionecrosis, and precludes most partial procedures. (Cummings 7e, Ch 104, p 1556; Ch 105, p 1576)

**Imaging the paralyzed cord**: image the entire vagus/RLN course from skull base to the aortopulmonary window/hila (MRI best for skull base, CT for neck and chest). Signs of paralysis on CT: paramedian cord, anteromedially displaced arytenoid, ipsilateral dilated piriform sinus and laryngeal ventricle, and thyroid cartilage tilt. Causes: neoplasm about 36%, postoperative (thyroid/parathyroid) about 25%, inflammatory 13%. About 90% of lesions are peripheral. (Cummings 7e, Ch 104, p 1547)

**Transglottic cancer**: tumors cross the ventricle by four routes—directly across the ventricle, via the anterior commissure, through the paraglottic space, or along the arytenoid (the last does not predict deep invasion). In Kirchner's series, framework invasion was present in over half of transglottic tumors >2 cm, nodal metastases in 30%, and in 55% when >4 cm. The anterior commissure tendon (Broyles, about 1 mm by 10 mm) is a strong barrier; deep invasion there requires supraglottic or subglottic extension. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1569)

**Nodal metastasis rates by subsite and T**: supraglottic pathologic nodes about 10% T1, 29% T2, 38% T3, 57% T4, with occult rates rising from 0–14% (T1) to 40–75% (T4); usually levels II–IV, I and V only with other levels involved. Glottic: about 0.1% T1, 5% T2, 18% T3, 32% T4 (overall 5.9%), drains to II–IV and VI, bilateral rare. Subglottic: paratracheal/level VI first (often bilateral), mediastinal nodes in up to 46% (counted as distant). Distant metastasis: glottic 3–9%, supraglottic 4–15%, lung most common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1575)

**Obstructing laryngeal tumor**: prefer transoral debulking (cup forceps, microdebrider or CO2 laser) to secure the airway and allow staging before definitive therapy; if a tracheostomy is unavoidable, place it high so the later resection preserves trachea. Emergency laryngectomy offers no survival advantage over tracheostomy with planned laryngectomy, and tracheostomy itself does not increase stomal recurrence (subglottic extension does). (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1576–1577)

**Expected outcomes for early glottic cancer**: RT local control about 81–90% for T1 (larynx preservation 90–98%) and 64–87% for T2; local control approaches 100% for mid-third cord lesions with surgery. T2 tumors with impaired mobility ('T2b') do worse with RT (about 51% vs 70% control in Harwood's series), and lesions >15 mm recur more often (26% vs 4%). Persistent edema more than 6 months after RT signals deep recurrence in about 45%. Overall 5-year relative survival is about 90% T1N0 and 75% T2N0, and second primaries (lung first) are the leading cause of death. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1577–1579; Ch 106, p 1596)

**Advanced glottic disease specifics**: T3 glottic tumors usually have low nodal risk unless transglottic; size >1.5 cm, subglottic extension and paratracheal/pretracheal nodes predict failure. T3 options: total laryngectomy, CRT, supracricoid partial laryngectomy, TLM in selected cases, or near-total laryngectomy (Pearson—preserves one arytenoid and part of cricoid to create a tracheopharyngeal speaking shunt, but the patient keeps a permanent stoma). T4 glottic: primary RT cures very few (2 of 25 T4N0 survived 5 years historically) and surgery outperforms CRT; treat the neck (occult risk about 20%) with ipsilateral levels II–IV plus paratracheal dissection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1579–1580)

**Open supraglottic laryngectomy (Ogura/Som) criteria**: removes all structures above the ventricle floor, preserving both true cords, both arytenoids, tongue base and hyoid. Indications: T1, T2 and selected T3 (pre-epiglottic space only) tumors. Contraindications: glottic involvement, impaired/fixed cord, thyroid or cricoid cartilage invasion, tongue-base involvement within 1 cm of the circumvallate papillae or deep tongue muscle, and poor pulmonary function (must tolerate aspiration). About 10% need completion laryngectomy for aspiration—age >65 is the main risk. Supraglottic cancer extends to the glottic level via the paraglottic space in 20–54% on whole-organ sections. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1580, Ch 108, p 1657)

**Key trial numbers**: VA Larynx (1991; 332 stage III–IV, two-thirds supraglottic): induction cisplatin/5-FU then RT in responders preserved the larynx in 64% with identical 2-year survival (68%), but only 39% had a fully functioning larynx. RTOG 91-11 (518 patients): 2-year larynx preservation 88% concurrent vs 75% induction vs 70% RT alone; at 5 years 84% vs 70.5% vs 66%; survival similar (54–56%); high-grade toxicity 82%. GORTEC induction TPF vs PF: 10-year larynx preservation about 70% vs 47% without survival difference. Treatment mortality of CRT is 2–4%, and treatment breaks erode efficacy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1584–1585; Ch 110, pp 1687–1688)

**Population signal against reflexive CRT**: NCDB analyses showed declining laryngeal cancer survival from the mid-1980s as nonsurgical treatment rose, and total laryngectomy was associated with better survival than CRT for stage IV disease; ASCO guidance states that extensive T3 or T4a tumors and/or poor pretreatment laryngeal function may achieve better survival and quality of life with primary total laryngectomy. In MD Anderson's T4 experience, 45% of organ-preservation survivors were tracheostomy-dependent and 23% aspirated. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1583, 1585)

**Partial laryngectomy salvage criteria (Biller)**: conservation surgery is precluded by subglottic extension >5 mm, cartilage invasion, contralateral cord involvement, arytenoid involvement beyond the vocal process, cord fixation, or a recurrence not matching the original lesion. Later criteria (Toma) allowed up to 10 mm anterior/5 mm posterior subglottic extension. Despite TLM and SCPL, about 70% of recurrent early glottic cancers still require total laryngectomy. Laryngeal cancer has the best salvage rate of any head and neck site (about 50%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1586, Ch 106, p 1610)

**Salvage laryngectomy complications and the neck**: meta-analysis shows about two-thirds develop a complication and 29% a pharyngocutaneous fistula. Adding chemotherapy to RT raises fistula from about 23% to 34%, and salvage within 1 year of treatment is a risk factor. Occult nodes are found in up to 28% of cN0 necks at salvage (more with rT4, supraglottic and transglottic recurrences), so elective neck dissection is advised except for recurrent T1–T2 glottic cancers originally staged T1–T2. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1586–1587)

**Stomal recurrence**: a grave complication arising from paratracheal nodes, thyroid invasion, tumor implantation or incomplete excision of subglottic spread—subglottic involvement is the strongest risk. Prevent it in subglottic primaries, glottic tumors with >1 cm subglottic extension, and T4 glottic tumors by ipsilateral thyroid lobectomy, bilateral paratracheal dissection and adjuvant RT including the upper mediastinum. Sisson's classification (stages I–IV, roughly: superior stoma without esophagus, superior with esophageal involvement, inferior stoma extending into mediastinum, lateral extension under the clavicle) guides treatment—aggressive mediastinal resection is generally not indicated for stage III–IV because of poor prognosis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1587)

**Malignant transformation numbers**: pooled data (Isenberg) show invasive cancer in about 3.7% without dysplasia, 10.1% with mild–moderate dysplasia, and 18.1% with severe dysplasia/CIS. A meta-analysis gives 14% overall with mean time to transformation 5.8 years, and about 7% of keratoses transform more than 10 years later—so surveillance is long term. Appearance and stroboscopy do not predict histology. WHO 2017 uses a two-tier low-grade/high-grade dysplasia system. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1570–1571, Ch 106, p 1615)

**Carcinoma in situ options**: excision preserving the lamina propria (microflap) or RT are both effective. Surgical recurrence is about 20% but repeated excision achieves control equivalent to RT, whereas RT gives about 93.5% local control. RT is favored for multiply recurrent or diffuse lesions, unreliable follow-up, or anesthesia risk. Vocal fold stripping is abandoned. In-office 532-nm pulsed KTP (or 585-nm pulsed dye) photoangiolysis targets sublesional vessels and allows bilateral anterior commissure treatment with little web risk, but only after an initial operative biopsy because no specimen is obtained. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1571–1572)

**SCC variants and behavior**: verrucous carcinoma—exophytic, pushing margins, no cytologic atypia, superficial biopsies often nondiagnostic, pure form does not metastasize (treat by conservative excision, no neck dissection; 5-year survival about 90%; reactive nodes from inflammation). Basaloid SCC—supraglottis/piriform sinus, aggressive with nodal and distant spread. Spindle cell (sarcomatoid) carcinoma—polypoid glottic mass, biphasic, can be mistaken for sarcoma; surgery preferred, RT alone ineffective. Adenosquamous—very aggressive, up to 75% nodal metastases, 5-year survival 15–37%. Papillary SCC—exophytic with severe atypia, better prognosis. NUT carcinoma—supraglottic, fatal within a year. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1589–1591)

**Survivorship numbers**: 5-year relative survival for laryngeal SCC is about 64%; N stage predicts survival more than T stage, ENE further lowers survival, and distant metastasis gives under 10% 5-year survival. Hypothyroidism risk is about 20% after RT, 50% after laryngectomy with ipsilateral lobectomy, and >65% with both—check TSH every 6–12 months. Low-dose chest CT screening is recommended for patients ≥50–55 with ≥20 pack-years (NCCN). (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, pp 1587–1588; Ch 106, p 1614)

**RT technique for early glottic cancer**: small opposed lateral fields about 5×5 to 6×6 cm, no elective nodal coverage. Typical schedules: Tis/T1 63 Gy at 2.25 Gy/fraction (or 66 Gy at 2 Gy); T2 65.25 Gy at 2.25 Gy, 70 Gy at 2 Gy, or 79.2 Gy at 1.2 Gy twice daily. Fractions of at least 2 Gy and overall time ≤ about 46 days improve control; Yamazaki's randomized T1 trial showed 92% vs 77% 5-year control with 2.25-Gy fractions. Adverse factors include impaired mobility, anterior commissure involvement, bulk, low hemoglobin, continued smoking, male sex and subglottic extension (erythropoietin is harmful). (Cummings 7e, Ch 106, pp 1609–1610; Ch 110, pp 1677, 1683)

**Surgery vs RT counseling points**: voice quality generally favors RT, while final larynx preservation tends to favor surgery (e.g., 92% vs 81% in Ton-Van's series; T2 RT failure about 1 in 3 in the Danish series). RT is unrepeatable, so surgery keeps RT in reserve for second primaries. Late RT risks include persistent edema, hypothyroidism, carotid stenosis (about 1 excess fatal stroke per 77 patients treated at 15 years) and radiation-induced malignancy (1–2%, 10–20 years later). No randomized trial compares endolaryngeal surgery with RT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 106, pp 1609, 1614–1615)

topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
text: **European Laryngological Society cordectomy types**: I subepithelial, II subligamental (removes epithelium, Reinke space and ligament), III transmuscular (through vocalis), IV total cordectomy (to perichondrium), V extended (adds contralateral cord/anterior commissure, arytenoid, ventricle/false cord, or subglottis), and the 2007 revision adds type VI for the anterior commissure. Types I–III are one-piece excisional biopsies. Total and extended cordectomies need TLM depth mapping. Subligamental resection when tumor reaches the ligament gives better voice than leaving tumor-adjacent ligament. (Cummings 7e, Ch 105, p 1578, Ch 107, pp 1617–1618)

topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
text: **TLM safety and complications**: keep FiO2 below 30%, use a laser tube with double saline-filled cuffs, wet towels over face/eyes, eyewear for staff, laser pedal for the surgeon only. Clip named vessels (superior laryngeal artery)—never rely on cautery—because delayed hemorrhage without a tracheostomy is the most dangerous complication. Consider tracheotomy for long cases with tongue-base edema risk, supraglottic bleeding risk, subglottic exposure, or poor pulmonary reserve. Exposed cartilage leads to granulomas until sequestra are removed. Extensive anterior commissure resection leaves a breathy, stiff voice. (Cummings 7e, Ch 107, pp 1629–1630)

**Supracricoid partial laryngectomy**: removes both true and false cords, both paraglottic spaces, the entire thyroid cartilage and at most one arytenoid, preserving hyoid, cricoid and at least one cricoarytenoid unit. With cricohyoidoepiglottopexy (CHEP)—for selected T2–T3 (and T1b) glottic cancers—local recurrence is about 4.5% for T2 and 10% for T3. With cricohyoidopexy (CHP, epiglottis and pre-epiglottic space also removed)—for supraglottic/transglottic tumors with glottic or pre-epiglottic involvement, decreased mobility, or limited thyroid cartilage invasion. ELS names these open partial horizontal laryngectomies type I (supraglottic), II (supracricoid), III (supratracheal). (Cummings 7e, Ch 108, pp 1634–1635, 1646–1647)

**SCPL contraindications**: subglottic extension >10 mm anteriorly or >5 mm posteriorly, arytenoid fixation, massive pre-epiglottic space involvement reaching the vallecula, extension to pharyngeal wall/vallecula/tongue base/postcricoid/interarytenoid region, and cricoid invasion. Distinguish cord fixation (thyroarytenoid invasion) from arytenoid fixation (cricoarytenoid joint invasion—a contraindication). Assess cord motion during phonation/deep breathing and arytenoid motion with a gentle cough. Apparent arytenoid immobility with some cord motion is 'pseudofixation' from tumor weight. Practical pulmonary test: climbing two flights of stairs without dyspnea. (Cummings 7e, Ch 108, pp 1634–1635, 1641)

**Primary TEP with immediate prosthesis**: primary puncture with immediate indwelling prosthesis (usually 8 mm long) is the method of choice in most centers—it stabilizes the party wall and avoids catheter-induced tract edema and repeated resizing. It can be done even with circumferential flap reconstruction provided the esophagus is not separated from the trachea. Delay the puncture 4–5 weeks only when the esophagus has been dissected off the trachea (e.g., gastric pull-up). Secondary puncture: within 10 mm of the mucocutaneous junction, with a trocar rather than a scalpel incision (avoids a too-wide tract). A short anterior cricopharyngeal myotomy at laryngectomy prevents PE-segment hypertonicity. (Cummings 7e, Ch 111, pp 1701–1704)

**Leak through vs around the prosthesis**: leakage through the device means valve failure (usually Candida/bacterial biofilm, mean device life 4–6 months in Europe)—clean, then replace. Consider probiotics or a magnet/Teflon valve (ActiValve) for frequent failures or aerophagia from negative esophageal pressure. Leakage around the device usually means the tract has shortened as edema resolved—downsize one length at a time (2–3 mm of play is normal). If still leaking, try a wider diameter or extended-flange device, silicone washer, purse-string suture, augmentation (e.g., bioplastic, fat), and finally surgical closure with later re-puncture (about 6 weeks). Treat reflux in every tract problem (2.3-fold risk of tract enlargement). (Cummings 7e, Ch 111, pp 1705–1708)

**Pulmonary and olfactory rehabilitation**: a stoma loses about 500 mL more water per day than nasal breathing. An HME recovers about 60% of this, reduces mucus and suctioning, and should be applied immediately after surgery in a peristomal adhesive housing. Hands-free speaking valves need a flat, nondeep stoma. Most laryngectomees are functionally anosmic despite an intact olfactory system because nasal airflow stops. The nasal airflow-inducing maneuver ('polite yawning'—lowering jaw/tongue with closed lips) restores smell in most. (Cummings 7e, Ch 111, pp 1704, 1712–1714)

**Lumen thresholds**: Tracheal tumors stay silent until the lumen narrows by about 75%. Exertional dyspnea appears when the lumen is under about 8 mm, and dyspnea at rest when it is under about 5 mm. Dyspnea that is inspiratory and worse lying flat points to a central airway lesion rather than lung disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1721)

**Flow-volume loops**: A plateau in the inspiratory limb suggests upper airway obstruction. Fixed obstruction gives a MIF50/MEF50 ratio near 1. Variable extrathoracic obstruction gives a ratio below 1 because inspiratory flow is reduced. Intrathoracic lesions mainly blunt expiratory flow, giving a ratio of 1 or more. A normal PFT does not exclude a tumor, and plain chest films detect only about one quarter to one half of tracheal tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1721)

**Histology changes selection**: Candidates with SCC need mediastinoscopy. Positive mediastinal nodes predict failure, so chemoradiation is used instead of resection. In ACC, positive nodes and even synchronous pulmonary metastases do not preclude resection, because the course is indolent. Resected SCC has a 5-year survival of about 39% versus 7% when unresectable. For ACC the figures are about 52% and 33%. Adjuvant RT of about 60 Gy is recommended, especially for positive margins. Higher doses add toxicity without survival benefit. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1719) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1723) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1728)

**Airway and release maneuvers**: Avoid paralytics and keep spontaneous ventilation until the airway is secured. A preoperative tracheostomy is harmful because the stoma interferes with the later anastomosis. After the airway is divided, ventilate by advancing the tube distally, jet ventilation, cross-field intubation of the distal airway, or ECMO. Suprahyoid laryngeal release (Montgomery) gains 2-3 cm and is preferred over suprathyroid release because it causes less dysphagia. Hilar/pericardial release gains about 2 cm for distal lesions. Carinal tumors involving more than about 4 cm of trachea are usually unresectable. (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1723) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1724) (Cummings 7e, Ch 112, p 1725)

**ATA 2015 sonographic patterns** (alternative to TI-RADS): High suspicion (>70-90% malignancy) is a solid hypoechoic nodule with irregular margins, microcalcifications, taller-than-wide shape, rim calcification with extrusion or ETE. FNA if 1 cm or larger. Intermediate (10-20%) is a solid hypoechoic nodule with smooth margins. FNA if 1 cm or larger. Low (5-10%) is an iso/hyperechoic solid or partly cystic nodule with an eccentric solid area. FNA if 1.5 cm or larger. Very low (<3%) is spongiform or partly cystic without suspicious features. FNA if 2 cm or larger, or observe. A pure cyst (<1%) needs no FNA. (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1743) (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1744)

**Surgeon US technique**: Normal glands (<40 mg) are not seen. An experienced sonographer lateralizes and assigns upper versus lower position for a solitary adenoma in 80-90% of cases. Adenomas are homogeneous and hypoechoic relative to thyroid. Inferior glands lie anterior to the RLN plane and superior glands posterior to it. A gland lying entirely deep to the posterior surface of the inferior thyroid artery or carotid is usually a superior gland. Reactive nodes from thyroiditis mimic adenomas but have an echogenic hilum with hilar blood flow. Suspected intrathyroidal adenomas can be confirmed with FNA PTH washout. (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1744) (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1745) (Cummings 7e, Ch 114, p 1746)

**Genetics**: About 25-30% of paragangliomas carry germline mutations, so genetic counseling or testing is offered to every patient. SDHD (PGL1) is the most common; it is autosomal dominant with maternal imprinting, so tumors develop only when the gene is inherited from the father. It gives about 75% penetrance by age 40 and multifocal tumors in about 56%. SDHB (PGL4) has later onset, is usually unifocal, and carries about a 33% malignancy risk plus thoracoabdominal PGL/pheochromocytoma and RCC risk. SDHC accounts for about 4%, and SDHAF2 causes PGL2. Other associations are VHL, RET/MEN2, NF1 and the Carney triad. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1757) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1758)

**Function and imaging**: Only 1-3% of head and neck PGLs are functional, and they secrete norepinephrine. These tumors lack PNMT, so excess epinephrine suggests an adrenal pheochromocytoma. Screen with plasma or urine metanephrines when tumors are multiple or familial or symptoms are present. Give alpha blockade, then beta blockade, before surgery on a secreting tumor. On MRI, tumors over 2 cm show salt-and-pepper flow voids. PGLs enhance and wash out faster than schwannomas, and the images alone are enough for diagnosis. Somatostatin-receptor imaging or 18F-DOPA PET screens for multifocal or metastatic disease, for example in SDHB carriers. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1758) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1759)

**Malignancy**: Classically, malignancy was defined only by metastasis to nodes or distant sites (lung, bone), not by mitoses or capsular invasion. Since WHO 2017, all paragangliomas are considered to have metastatic potential, and "metastatic paraganglioma" has replaced "malignant". Metastasis rates are about 6% for carotid, 10% for vagal, 5% for jugulotympanic, and up to 25% for laryngeal/orbital PGLs. NCDB 5-year survival is about 78% with regional spread and about 12% with distant spread. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1758)

**Bilateral tumors and baroreflex failure**: With bilateral tumors, resect the smaller side first and preserve at least one vagus. If one vagus is already paralyzed, operate on the functioning side only for documented growth, or consider RT. Bilateral carotid sinus denervation causes baroreflex failure 24-72 h after surgery, with labile hypertension and tachycardia. Treat acutely with nitroprusside or labetalol and long term with clonidine. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1760) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1761)

**Vagal paraganglioma**: Most arise from the nodose (inferior) ganglion about 2 cm below the skull base. Those arising from the jugular ganglion can be dumbbell-shaped through the jugular foramen. They displace the carotid anteriorly without splaying the ICA and ECA, and they cause vocal fold paralysis or Horner syndrome. Complete resection almost always sacrifices the vagus, so counsel about voice and swallowing rehabilitation. Use a transcervical approach for nodose tumors and a transmastoid-transcervical approach (with or without craniotomy) for higher lesions. Preoperative embolization is commonly advised for high vagal and jugular foramen tumors. (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1760) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1762) (Cummings 7e, Ch 115, p 1763)

**Hodgkin vs non-Hodgkin patterns**: HL peaks at ages 15-40. It spreads contiguously, rarely involves Waldeyer ring, preauricular or occipital nodes, and involves the mediastinum in more than 85%. Pruritus occurs in about 25%, and alcohol-induced nodal pain in under 1%. B symptoms are fever >38 C, drenching sweats, or >10% weight loss in 6 months. NHL often involves Waldeyer ring (asymmetric tonsil), preauricular nodes and extranodal sites. Indolent FL/SLL produces bilateral soft mobile 1-2 cm nodes that can wax and wane (FL regresses spontaneously in up to 20%). A dominant or necrotic node suggests transformation, so excise it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1775) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1777) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1781)

**Biopsy and specimen rules**: Excisional or incisional biopsy remains the preferred initial diagnostic method. FNA plus flow gives subtype accuracy of only about 50-70%, so FNA alone is not sufficient for a first diagnosis, though it is acceptable for relapse, SLL, or lymphoblastic lymphoma. Core biopsy (12-16 gauge, multiple cores) is diagnostic in about 78-95%. Send fresh tissue in saline (never on dry gauze, never fixed overnight), with the clinical question. Steroids before biopsy rarely ruin diagnosis if tissue is obtained within 24-48 h, except in lymphoblastic lymphoma. Withhold them for SVC syndrome alone, and give them only for life-threatening airway compromise. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1776) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1777)

**Staging**: HL uses Ann Arbor with Cotswolds modification: A/B symptoms, E for limited contiguous extranodal disease, and X for bulk (>10 cm, or mediastinal mass ratio >0.33 on CXR or >0.35 on CT). NHL uses Lugano, which drops the A/B suffix and counts tonsils, Waldeyer ring and spleen as nodal tissue. FDG PET/CT is the staging study of choice. It upstages 10-20% of HL and makes routine marrow biopsy unnecessary in HL. Indolent MZL/MALT and SLL may not be FDG avid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1778) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780)

**Treatment frameworks**: Early favorable HL is treated with 2 cycles of ABVD plus 20 Gy involved-field RT (GHSG HD10), and early unfavorable HL with 4 cycles of ABVD plus 30 Gy. Cummings gives 6 cycles of ABVD for advanced HL, with a 7-factor IPS for prognosis and interim PET to guide escalation or de-escalation. Current NCCN options for advanced HL also include brentuximab vedotin plus AVD and nivolumab plus AVD. Brentuximab vedotin targets CD30. DLBCL is the most common NHL and the most common extranodal head and neck lymphoma. It is treated with R-CHOP (with or without RT for limited stage), and prognosis follows the IPI: age >60, ECOG 2 or higher, stage III-IV, more than one extranodal site, high LDH. Double-hit (MYC plus BCL2/BCL6) disease does poorly. FL prognosis uses FLIPI. Burkitt and lymphoblastic lymphoma need an emergent oncology consult, CNS-directed chemotherapy, and tumor lysis precautions. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1778) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1779) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1780) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1783)

**Sinonasal lymphomas**: In Western patients these are mostly DLBCL of the maxillary sinus, which often invades the orbit and is EBV-negative. DLBCL here has a higher risk of CNS/leptomeningeal relapse, so intrathecal methotrexate or cytarabine prophylaxis is recommended. Extranodal NK/T-cell lymphoma, nasal type (formerly lethal midline granuloma) is more common in Asian and South American patients. It is angiocentric and necrotic, so multiple biopsies are often needed. It is virtually always EBV-positive (EBER in situ) and CD56-positive, and plasma EBV DNA tracks disease. More than 80% present at stage I-IIE. RT alone relapses in about 50%, so concurrent or sequential RT with asparaginase-based chemotherapy (e.g., SMILE) is used. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1784) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1785)

**Book specifics**: Hashimoto thyroiditis raises thyroid lymphoma risk about 70-80-fold. DLBCL makes up 60-70% of cases and MALT 10-20%. Up to one third show both, which is why open biopsy is often preferred. MALT is CD20-positive and CD5/CD10-negative, and PET is unreliable for staging it. Stage IE-IIE MALT is cured with involved-field RT alone (24 Gy is now as effective as the older 30-40 Gy) with 95-100% survival. DLBCL gets R-CHOP with or without RT, and surgery has no therapeutic role. (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1783) (Cummings 7e, Ch 116, p 1784)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Neck dose logic**: An elective dose of about 50 Gy in 2-Gy fractions controls the N0 neck in more than 90%, and gross nodal disease needs about 70 Gy over 7 weeks. Electively treat the neck when the risk of occult nodes is roughly 20% or more. In practice the threshold is often 5-10%. END and elective neck RT are equally effective, so choose the modality that matches treatment of the primary and avoids trimodality therapy. After RT for node-positive disease, reserve neck dissection for incomplete response. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1786) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1795)

**MD Anderson risk-grouped dosing**: Moderate-risk features include a close (<5 mm) or positive margin, an oral cavity primary, PNI, multiple nodes, and delay to RT; one of these calls for about 57.6 Gy. ECE or two or more moderate features is high risk and calls for 63 Gy. The total treatment package (surgery to end of RT) is itself prognostic, and accelerated delivery helps high-risk patients. In the pooled EORTC 22931/RTOG 9501 analysis, the benefit of adding cisplatin was confined to ECE and/or positive margins. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1796) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1797)

**Late neck effects**: Hypothyroidism develops in up to about 33% after lower-neck RT, usually within 1-2 years, so check TSH yearly. Significant carotid stenosis is found in 30-50% of irradiated necks, with about 5.6-fold stroke risk (higher after age 60 and beyond 10 years). Grade 3-4 subcutaneous fibrosis occurs in about 3% with standard RT and about 10% with chemoradiation. IMRT may roughly double radiation-induced second cancer risk (to about 0.75%) through low-dose bath and scatter. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1799)

**Key trials**: Intergroup 0099 established concurrent plus adjuvant chemoradiation for locally advanced NPC (3-year OS 78% vs 47% with RT alone). Induction TPF before concurrent cisplatin improved failure-free survival and OS. A network meta-analysis found the largest benefit with concurrent plus adjuvant chemotherapy, followed by induction plus concurrent. IMRT gives about 90-97% local control but distant metastasis (up to about 30%) is the main failure mode. Detectable plasma EBV DNA after RT identifies high relapse risk. (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1804) (Cummings 7e, Ch 117, p 1805)

**Sublevel decisions**: Level IIB involvement is mainly a risk for oropharyngeal primaries. For oral cavity and laryngeal primaries with a negative IIA, IIB can usually be skipped to spare the SAN. Include IA for floor of mouth, lip and anterior midface primaries. Pharyngeal wall cancers involve retropharyngeal nodes in about 44%, which may justify extending the dissection. For oral tongue cancer, add level IV to SND I-III because skip metastases occur. (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1808) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1817) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1823)

**Timing and types after RT**: Cummings describes a planned neck dissection 6-8 weeks after RT/CRT when residual risk is high. **Current view**: after the PET-NECK trial, PET-CT at about 12 weeks is the standard response check, and dissection is done only for incomplete or equivocal response, because PET before about 3 months is unreliable. A salvage dissection is early for persistent disease and late for recurrence. After CRT, nodal disease outside levels II-IV is rare, so SND (or a superselective one- or two-level dissection) is usually adequate. (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1812) (Cummings 7e, Ch 118, p 1826)

**SAN anatomy and morbidity**: The SAN crosses anterior to the IJV in about 70%, posterior in 27%, and through it in 3%. It pierces the SCM in about 82% of people. Shoulder dysfunction rates are about 60% after RND, 50% after MRND sparing only the SAN, and 30% when SAN, IJV and SCM are all spared. Shoulder droop is about 5% after SND II-IV versus 30% after SND II-V. Avoid local anesthetic for posterior triangle node biopsy so the nerve can be stimulated. Repair a transected SAN primarily or with a great auricular cable graft, and refer early for physical therapy to prevent adhesive capsulitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1836)

**Elective beats emergent**: Carotid rupture follows about 3-4% of RNDs, with about 50% mortality. Mortality of carotid ligation rises from about 14% when elective to 64% when emergent, so treat exposed carotid or a sentinel bleed proactively. In open control, ligate through separate incisions above and below the infected field. Endovascular embolization or covered stent is often first line. (Cummings 7e, Ch 119, p 1834)

**Mechanism clues**: Neck stab wounds injure the subclavian vessels more often than gunshots, because the knife slides downward over the clavicle. Transcervical (midline-crossing) gunshots carry very high vascular/aerodigestive injury rates. In children, stabbings predominate and aerodigestive injuries are more common than vascular ones. A hypoglossal deficit or Horner syndrome implies carotid sheath injury. About 30% of carotid injuries present with a neurologic deficit. Mandatory exploration is negative in 50-70%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1842) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1844) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1845)

**Guideline nuances**: ACR 2017 recommends CTA first for stable patients without life-threatening injury. Internal injury does not match the external zone in about 27% of cases, which supports the no-zone approach. The Western Trauma Association still advises exploration and/or endoscopy for symptomatic zone II wounds. If CTA is normal but aerodigestive injury is still suspected, obtain an esophagram: water-soluble contrast first, then barium if negative and suspicion persists. Flexible esophagoscopy misses injuries near the cricopharyngeus, and combining flexible with rigid endoscopy missed none in reported series. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1845) (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1849)

**Observation and repair timing**: Observed patients need physician examination at least three times per 24 h for 48-72 h, because most vascular injuries declare within 48 h. Repair laryngeal mucosal lacerations within 24 h. Simple tracheal lacerations can be closed without tracheostomy, but gunshot wounds to the trachea get a tracheostomy for about 6 weeks. Close esophageal injuries in two layers with drainage, and place a strap muscle flap between the tracheal and esophageal repairs to prevent TE fistula. Extensive injuries may need a lateral esophagostomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 120, p 1850)

**Cold nodule in Graves**: About 45% of palpable hypofunctioning nodules in a Graves gland are malignant. DTC is about twice as common in Graves disease and tends to be larger, more invasive and more often node-positive, so manage it aggressively. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1859)

**Drug and RAI details**: Rash, arthralgia or fever occur in about 5% on thionamides, and agranulocytosis in up to 0.2%. PTU causes hepatocellular hepatitis and ANCA vasculitis, and methimazole causes cholestatic hepatitis. The ATA limits PTU to the first trimester, thyroid storm, and methimazole intolerance. Stop thionamides about 3 days before and after RAI. RAI can cause a radiation thyroiditis flare 1-2 weeks later, hypothyroidism follows in 40-80% within a year, and RAI is absolutely contraindicated in pregnancy. Lithium and cholestyramine are adjuncts. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1860)

**Surgical indications and prep**: Absolute indications are severe thionamide reactions (agranulocytosis, hepatotoxicity) in a patient who cannot be blocked before RAI. Other indications are a gland >75 g, suspected or proven cancer, pregnancy plans or lactation, and moderate-to-severe ophthalmopathy. Prepare with 4-6 weeks of a thionamide and 7-10 days of inorganic iodine (Lugol/SSKI), started only after the thionamide. Beta blockade with iodine for 10-14 days is an alternative. Near-total thyroidectomy is favored over subtotal (3-6 g remnant) to avoid recurrence. If the nerve monitor loses signal on the first side, stage the second side. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1861)

**Acute suppurative thyroiditis**: Usually caused by S. aureus, streptococci or S. pneumoniae. It is commonest in children (suspect a piriform sinus fistula) and presents with severe pain, torticollis-like posture, high WBC, normal thyroid function and often normal ESR, which distinguishes it from de Quervain thyroiditis. Give antistaphylococcal and anaerobic coverage. Abscesses need drainage, sometimes partial thyroidectomy, with antibiotics for at least 2 weeks after drainage. Thyroid dysfunction is rare. (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1861) (Cummings 7e, Ch 121, p 1862)

**Pregnancy**: Nodules are found in 2-10% of pregnancies. Use US and FNA; avoid CT, and use MRI without gadolinium only if needed. For cytologically suspicious or proven DTC, surgery can usually wait until after delivery without affecting prognosis, even with nodal disease. If substantial growth occurs, operate in the second trimester, accepting higher maternal-fetal complication rates. RAI is contraindicated during pregnancy and breastfeeding. (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1895) (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1896)

**Pediatric DTC**: Nodules are uncommon in children (0.2-1.8%) but 16-25% are malignant, and more than 80% of these are papillary (diffuse sclerosing variant aggressive). At presentation more than 50% have nodal metastases (pre/paratracheal in 90% of node-positive cases), 18% local extension, and about 15% distant (often miliary lung) metastases. Multifocality (10-30%) favors total thyroidectomy with formal central dissection when nodes are present. Despite advanced presentation, 10-year survival approaches 100%. About 10% of pediatric thyroid cancers are MTC, so screen for RET. (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1895)

**Locally invasive disease**: Sacrifice the RLN only when the cord is already paralyzed and tumor invades the nerve. Otherwise peel tumor off and use RAI, which shows no survival difference from sacrifice; exclude benign causes (Graves, Hashimoto, Riedel) and lymphoma first. If the nerve is resected, reinnervate immediately (primary repair, graft or ansa transfer). Thyroid cartilage can be shaved if the inner perichondrium is intact. Tracheal shave or sleeve resection of 4-5 rings with primary anastomosis is standard; septal composite grafts can close window defects, and partial laryngectomy may be needed. (Cummings 7e, Ch 122, p 1890)

**Hypercalcemic crisis**: Start with saline volume expansion, taking care in cardiac patients, and stop calcium supplements and thiazides. Once the patient is volume replete, add a loop diuretic for calciuresis. Then give an IV bisphosphonate (osteoclast inhibition, profound drop). Calcitonin and glucocorticoids (useful in vitamin D or granulomatous causes) are adjuncts. Then plan definitive parathyroidectomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1902)

**Syndromic forms**: About 95% of MEN1 patients develop HPT, usually multigland and in the third or fourth decade. About 30% of MEN2A patients develop HPT. HPT-jaw tumor syndrome (CDC73/HRPT2) involves asynchronous parathyroid tumors, carcinoma in 15-20%, ossifying fibromas of the jaws, renal cysts and uterine lesions. Neonatal severe HPT is homozygous FHH, presents by 6 months, and needs urgent total parathyroidectomy. FHH itself is diagnosed by a Ca/Cr clearance ratio below 0.01 and is not operated on. (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1902) (Cummings 7e, Ch 123, p 1903)

**Medical specifics**: RAI worsens or triggers orbitopathy in at least 15% (38% in a Cochrane analysis), and oral prednisone for several weeks afterward reduces this. Selenium helps mild disease. Pulsed IV methylprednisolone (500 mg weekly for 6 weeks, then 250 mg weekly for 6 weeks) beats oral prednisone (80-100 mg) in efficacy and safety. Orbital RT (e.g., 20 Gy in 10 fractions) helps motility and soft tissue in early active disease, but avoid it in diabetics (retinopathy). Total and subtotal thyroidectomy do not differ in their effect on eye disease. Current EUGOGO (2021) first-line therapy for moderate-to-severe active disease is IV methylprednisolone plus mycophenolate. Teprotumumab (IGF-1R antibody, FDA-approved 2020) is an alternative that reduces proptosis but can cause hearing loss, so get a baseline audiogram. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1920) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1921)

**Endoscopic decompression details**: Avoid surgery in the active phase except for compressive optic neuropathy. The surgical sequence is decompression, then strabismus surgery, then eyelid surgery. Endoscopic medial wall and medial floor decompression reduces proptosis by about 3.2-5.1 mm. Preserve the inferomedial strut and a 10-mm periorbital sling over the medial rectus to limit diplopia. New diplopia occurs in 19-45% after endoscopic decompression, versus 0-15% with balanced medial-lateral decompression. The posterior limit is the annulus of Zinn thickening near the sphenoid face. Incise the periorbita posterior to anterior, and do not pack the nose. (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1921) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1922) (Cummings 7e, Ch 125, p 1923)

**Middle-ear transformer numbers**: The TM-to-footplate area ratio is about 20:1 (69 vs 3.4 mm2; about 26 dB), and the malleus-to-incus lever ratio is about 1.3:1 (about 2.3 dB). Theoretical gain is about 28 dB, but the real gain is about 20 dB. The maximum conductive loss, from ossicular discontinuity behind an intact TM, is about 60 dB. A pathologic third window lowers cochlear input impedance and produces air-bone gaps with normal or supranormal bone conduction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 128, p 1947) (Cummings 7e, Ch 128, p 1948)

**Dynamic ET endoscopy**: use an angled (30/45-degree) scope or a flexible scope aimed along the tube's lumen. Have the patient say 'ka-ka-ka' to see the levator lift the palate and rotate the torus medially. Then have them swallow or yawn to see the tensor open the anterolateral wall, normally from the nasopharyngeal end toward the isthmus. Grade mucosal inflammation from I to IV by how much it limits dilation. Always inspect the fossa of Rosenmüller (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, pp 1987–1988).

**Tubal tonsil and anterior thrust**: lymphoid tissue on the medial torus (tubal tonsil of Gerlach) can enlarge. A bulky lateral adenoid can trap the torus so that during a swallow it is pushed forward instead of rotating medially, which closes the valve just when it should open. This is a common cause of obstructive ETD and can only be seen on dynamic endoscopy (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, pp 1986–1988).

**BDET candidacy (Box 131.1)**: the patient must have all three of the following. (1) Obstructive symptoms for 3 months or more. (2) Symptoms persisting despite directed medical therapy. (3) Objective inflammatory pathology on dynamic endoscopy. The patient must also have at least one of: persistent OME or a TM with negative pressure on insufflation, or a consistent baro-challenge history (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, p 1990).

**BDET technique numbers**: the cartilaginous tube is about 25 mm long. The balloon stops at the isthmus and must never enter the bony tube, which lies next to the ICA. Inflate with saline to 10–12 atm for about 2 minutes. Use a shorter inflation when inflammation is heavy, to avoid creating a patulous tube (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, pp 1990–1991).

**BDET RCT result**: in the multicenter RCT, patients had chronic type B or C tympanograms and were randomized to balloon dilation or nasal steroids. At 6 weeks, 51.8% of the balloon arm had a type A tympanogram versus 13.9% of the medical arm. Crossover prevented between-group comparison beyond 6 weeks. Biopsies suggest that dilation crushes the inflamed lymphoid follicles, which are later replaced by thin scar under restored ciliated epithelium (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, p 1991).

**BDET risks**: false passage or mucosal tear can cause submucosal emphysema, including pneumomediastinum, which resolves with conservative care. Patulous ETD is also a risk. No carotid injury has been published, but carotid canal dehiscence has been reported in up to 6.3%. The FDA advises ET imaging beforehand, especially after skull-base or ear surgery, skull fracture, or with anomalous anatomy (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, p 1992).

**Aural fullness differential**: if fullness persists after a successful modified Valsalva, or after a tube or myringotomy, it is unlikely to be from current obstructive ETD. Think instead of TMJ or masticator myalgia (check the masseter, temporalis, and pterygoids with bimanual intraoral palpation), hydrops, third-window disease, or migraine (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, p 1989).

**Endoscopic lesion**: the anterolateral wall of the tube's valve is normally convex. In patulous ETD it has a longitudinal concave defect, usually near the 12 o'clock position and running the whole length of the valve. A concavity confined to the orifice is common and does not establish the diagnosis. Chronic allergy and reflux, with patchy mucosal atrophy, are more frequent associations than weight loss (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, pp 1988–1989, 1993).

**Sensitive bedside test**: run tympanometry in reflex-decay mode while the patient breathes through the ipsilateral nostril. It picks up impedance changes in time with breathing that are too subtle to see on otoscopy. Visible TM excursions are best seen in the posterosuperior quadrant (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, p 1989).

**Surgical ladder**: a tympanostomy tube helps up to 54% of patients, probably by mass loading the TM, but it can worsen symptoms. If temporary TM stiffening helps, a cartilage tympanoplasty gives a lasting effect. Options aimed at the tube itself are an off-label bone-wax shim through the isthmus (CT first to exclude ICA dehiscence, about 50% then develop an effusion), submucosal calcium hydroxyapatite injection, and valve reconstruction. Complete obliteration is a last resort because it causes chronic glue ear. Teflon injection was abandoned after cerebral thrombosis and deaths (Cummings 7e, Ch 131, pp 1994–1995).

**Middle-ear myoclonus**: spasm of the tensor tympani makes the TM flutter and causes a 'popping' objective tinnitus. It shows up as rhythmic oscillations on tympanometry. Dividing the tensor tympani tendon can relieve it, but the stapedius can be the culprit instead, and both may need to be addressed (Cummings 7e, Ch 130, p 1980).

**Topical aminoglycosides with an open middle ear**: per the AAO-HNSF consensus (2004, reaffirmed 2014), use non-ototoxic drops (fluoroquinolones) first when the TM is not intact. Reserve aminoglycosides for an acutely infected ear after quinolone failure, allergy, or resistant cultures, and warn the patient about ototoxicity. Vestibulotoxicity is more common than cochleotoxicity. Avoid acidifying or antiseptic drops through a perforation (Cummings 7e, Ch 139, p 2107).

**Drop-induced contact dermatitis**: suspect it when itching and clear otorrhea worsen on treatment, with an eczematous rash where the drops pool. Neomycin is the most common sensitizer (5–32% of chronic otitis externa), followed by framycetin and gentamicin. Aminoglycosides cross-react with each other. Preservatives such as benzalkonium and propylene glycol can also cause it, but steroid allergy is rare. Treat by stopping the drug and applying a topical steroid or calcineurin inhibitor (Cummings 7e, Ch 139, p 2107).

**Otomycosis**: fungi cause about 10% of infectious otitis externa, often after antibacterial drops or canal trauma. Aspergillus accounts for about 80–90% (A. niger, A. fumigatus, A. flavus), followed by Candida. Look for itch, malodorous otorrhea, and white or black hyphae in 'cottage cheese' debris. Treat with debridement and acidification or a topical antifungal, then keep the canal dry (Cummings 7e, Ch 139, pp 2107–2108).

**Regimen and sequelae**: start an antiviral early (e.g., valacyclovir 1 g three times daily for 7 days). Add prednisone about 1 mg/kg/day when there is facial palsy or SNHL, although high-quality evidence for either drug is lacking. Facial recovery is worse than in Bell palsy. Refer to ophthalmology if V1 or the cornea is involved. Postherpetic neuralgia is more common over age 60, and gabapentin is the preferred agent (Cummings 7e, Ch 138, p 2098).

**Eponymous immune syndromes with SNHL**: Susac syndrome is corpus callosum 'snowball' lesions, branch retinal artery occlusions, and progressive SNHL. Vogt-Koyanagi-Harada is an autoimmune attack on melanocytes, with vertigo, SNHL, panuveitis or retinal detachment, and later skin depigmentation. Kearns-Sayre syndrome (an mtDNA deletion) is SNHL with ophthalmoplegia, ataxia, heart block, and pigmentary retinopathy (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, pp 2091–2092).

**Crises of Tumarkin**: otolithic drop attacks. The patient suddenly loses postural control and falls without losing consciousness, often feeling pushed to the ground. They are attributed to high endolymphatic pressure acting on the otolith organs and usually signal advanced disease (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090).

**Bruns nystagmus**: seen in about 10% of vestibular schwannomas. Large CPA tumors compress the flocculus and brainstem, producing coarse, large-amplitude nystagmus on gaze toward the lesion (gaze-paretic) and fine nystagmus on gaze away (vestibular) (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090).

**Alexander's law**: in a peripheral vestibular lesion, nystagmus is stronger when the patient looks toward the fast phase and weaker when looking away. Dandy syndrome is oscillopsia from bilateral vestibular loss, iatrogenic or idiopathic (Cummings 7e, Ch 137, p 2090).

**Lateral (sigmoid) sinus thrombosis**: the classic picture is a 'picket-fence' fever (spikes above 39.4°C), headache, and raised ICP. Patients pretreated with antibiotics, especially children, often present instead with diplopia or other neurologic signs and few ear findings. Nearly all patients have another intracranial complication. Symptoms are worse when the dominant sinus is occluded (the right in about 60%). The Tobey-Ayer (Queckenstedt) test: compressing the contralateral jugular raises CSF pressure, but compressing the affected side does not (Cummings 7e, Ch 141, p 2153; Ch 137, p 2091).

**Imaging for sinus thrombosis**: on contrast CT, the empty delta sign is a non-enhancing lumen inside an enhancing sinus wall. MRI and MR venography are more sensitive.
