They also show how far the clot extends and reveal coexisting subdural empyema, cerebritis, or cerebellar abscess (Cummings 7e, Ch 141, p 2154).

**Managing sinus thrombosis**: every patient needs mastoidectomy. Drain a coexisting brain abscess first, then do the mastoidectomy. Anticoagulation is not routine; strongly consider it when the clot extends to the transverse or cavernous sinus or there are emboli. Do not give thrombolytics with an infected vessel wall. Ligate the IJ only for neck extension or septic emboli. Evacuating the clot has not improved outcomes. Needle-aspirate the sinus, and open it only if pus returns (Cummings 7e, Ch 141, p 2154).

**Otitic hydrocephalus**: reduced cranial venous outflow, usually from lateral sinus occlusion (sometimes extending to the transverse, petrosal, or cavernous sinus), raises ICP. It presents as severe diffuse headache and nausea. Visual loss can follow, so it needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical input (Cummings 7e, Ch 141, p 2154).

**Tympanosclerosis**: acellular hyaline and calcified deposits in the TM lamina propria (myringosclerosis, a horseshoe-shaped white plaque) or in the middle ear submucosa. It follows OME, AOM, or trauma. It occurs in about 20% of chronic otitis media surgeries and is much more frequent after grommets than after myringotomy alone (59% vs 13%). TM plaques rarely affect hearing. Middle-ear plaques, often in the attic around the malleus and incus heads, cause conductive loss by fixing the ossicles (Cummings 7e, Ch 140, p 2130).

**Stapes surgery in tympanosclerosis**: SNHL risk is higher than with other middle-ear disease, because extensive dissection is needed and labyrinthine erosion may coexist. Stapedectomy is best staged after the TM has healed; older one-stage series reported cochlear loss in 21% (Cummings 7e, Ch 140, p 2131).

**Attic ventilation**: the tensor fold is complete in 73% of ears. In those ears, the tympanic isthmus (next to the incus and stapes) is the only route by which air reaches the attic. If inflammation blocks the isthmus, the epitympanum loses ventilation, which leads to retraction and cholesteatoma. During chronic-ear surgery, open a complete tensor fold and clear the isthmus (Cummings 7e, Ch 144, p 2182).

**Sinus tympani depth (Marchioni CT types)**: type A is shallow, bounded by the facial nerve, and reachable endoscopically, through the facial recess, or by canalplasty. Type B is deep, extending medial to the facial nerve but not behind it, and needs angled endoscopic instruments or a facial recess approach. Type C extends posterior to the facial nerve and may need a retrofacial approach. Morphology is classified as classic, confluent (no ponticulus), or partitioned (Cummings 7e, Ch 144, p 2183).

**Terminology trap**: 'modified radical mastoidectomy' is not a synonym for canal-wall-down mastoidectomy. Classically it is the Bondy procedure: limited attic cholesteatoma is exteriorized by removing adjacent canal wall, the uninvolved middle ear is not entered, and the matrix is left on the ossicular heads as the cavity lining. The Körner septum (petrosquamous remnant) can be mistaken for the medial wall of the antrum (Cummings 7e, Ch 143, pp 2168–2169).

**Perforation hearing loss**: the loss grows with perforation size, is greatest at low frequencies, and varies inversely with middle ear plus mastoid air volume. That is why identical perforations can produce different losses, and why the loss worsens when otorrhea fills the space. About 0.5 mL of middle-ear air keeps ossicular coupling within 10 dB of normal. Repairs of perforations larger than 50% of the drum fail more often, and experienced surgeons close about 90% (Cummings 7e, Ch 142, pp 2156, 2161).

**Austin categories of conductive loss**: perforation alone causes loss proportional to its size. Perforation plus ossicular interruption causes about 38 dB. Total loss of the TM and ossicles causes about 50 dB, from phase cancellation. Interruption behind an intact TM causes the maximal 55–60 dB, because the intact drum reflects energy, adding about 17 dB. Interruption with oval window closure causes about 60 dB. An incudostapedial gap can falsely depress bone conduction by up to 10 dB, which recovers after repair (Cummings 7e, Ch 145, pp 2186–2188).

**Tuning-fork estimate of the air-bone gap**: a Rinne negative only at 256 Hz suggests a gap of about 20–30 dB. Negative at 256 and 512 Hz suggests 30–45 dB. Negative at 256, 512, and 1024 Hz suggests 45–60 dB (Cummings 7e, Ch 145, p 2188).

**CT grading of otosclerosis**: grade 1 is fenestral only. Grade 2 is patchy cochlear involvement: 2a basal turn, 2b middle or apical turns, 2c patchy involvement of the whole cochlea. Grade 3 is diffuse confluent involvement of the cochlear otic capsule. Active disease shows lucency at the fissula ante fenestram and a pericochlear 'halo' (double ring), which enhances on MRI (Cummings 7e, Ch 135, pp 2050–2051).

**Intraoperative problems**: the facial nerve is exposed in about 9% of cases. Retract it gently, never mobilize it. A prosthesis touching it is harmless. Check malleus fixation in every case, and if present, consider malleostapedotomy or a malleovestibulopexy prosthesis. For an obliterated footplate, drill to 'blue line' and saucerize. For a floating footplate, do not chase fragments into the vestibule. A gusher (0.03–0.2%) is managed with a tissue seal, completing the prosthesis, and considering a lumbar drain. If the chorda is stretched or torn, sectioning it gives fewer taste symptoms (Cummings 7e, Ch 146, p 2204).

**Postoperative complications**: SNHL occurs in under 1%. Treat suspected SNHL with steroids immediately. Reparative granuloma presents with hearing that improves and then falls at 1–6 weeks, with vertigo and a red posterosuperior TM. Treat with steroids and prompt removal. Vertigo with a positive fistula sign usually means the prosthesis is too long, so replace it with one about 0.25 mm shorter. Delayed facial palsy around day 5 is likely viral and responds to prednisone. Taste disturbance affects about one-third of patients and lasts 3–4 months (Cummings 7e, Ch 146, pp 2204–2205).

**Revision stapes surgery**: the air-bone gap closes to within 20 dB in 71–96%, with a 0–2% risk of profound SNHL. Primary failures are from displaced prosthesis (53%), incus erosion (26%, especially with wire-loop pistons), and bony regrowth (14%). Do revisions under local anesthesia so vertigo can be monitored, use a laser, and reconstruct an eroded incus with cement, a malleus-to-oval-window prosthesis, or a TORP (Cummings 7e, Ch 146, p 2206).

**Ménière disease with otosclerosis, and children**: uncontrolled Ménière disease is a contraindication to stapedectomy because of the risk of a dead ear. Avoid surgery when 500-Hz bone conduction is 45 dB or worse with high-frequency loss, because the saccule may be touching the footplate. In children, get a CT first to exclude a fundal IAC defect or X-linked gusher anatomy. Success is about 80%. Consider surgery after age 5 for bilateral fixation with an air-bone gap over 30 dB (Cummings 7e, Ch 146, p 2206).

**High-yield numbers**: facial paralysis occurs in 7% of fractures. Capsule-violating fractures carry 4–5 times the risk of facial palsy and 2–4 times the risk of CSF fistula. CSF fistula occurs in 17%. Meningitis risk is 1% without a fistula, 5–11% if a leak lasts under 1 week, and up to 88% if a leak persists indefinitely. In children, intracranial injury is more common (58%) and facial palsy less common (3%) (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, key points p 2207).

**Onset of facial palsy**: of facial nerve injuries examined before paralytics are given, 27% are immediate and 73% are delayed, appearing 1–16 days after injury. Delayed onset recovers completely in about 94%. Immediate onset in about 75% treated conservatively, and some immediate-onset cases are transections. Distinguish true delayed onset from delayed diagnosis in intubated patients, who should be managed as immediate onset (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, p 2211).

**Carotid and pneumolabyrinth**: carotid injury occurred in about 18% of fractures crossing the carotid canal versus about 5% when the canal was spared. However, angiography in asymptomatic carotid-canal fractures has shown low yield. Pneumolabyrinth on CT usually means profound deafness that does not recover. It is also associated with facial palsy, though the vertigo is transient in about 90% (Cummings 7e, Ch 147, pp 2210–2211).

**Genetic share of congenital loss**: In developed countries more than 70% of congenital hearing loss is genetic (about 30% environmental); of hereditary loss, roughly 70-80% is nonsyndromic. Nonsyndromic inheritance is about 75-80% autosomal recessive, ~15% dominant, 2-5% X-linked and ~1% mitochondrial. Naming: DFNA = dominant, DFNB = recessive, DFNX = X-linked, numbered by order of discovery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2282-2283)

**STRC (DFNB16)**: STRC encodes stereocilin, which links outer hair cells to the tectorial membrane; loss produces a flat, mild-to-moderate congenital recessive loss. STRC is the most common genetic cause of mild-to-moderate loss and the second most common genetic cause overall after GJB2. It sits in a region prone to copy-number variants, so any comprehensive test must include CNV analysis; a contiguous deletion that also removes CATSPER2 causes deafness-infertility syndrome in males. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2283)

**Dominant audioprofiles**: Dominant nonsyndromic loss is usually postlingual, progressive and milder than recessive loss, and several genes have signature audiograms: WFS1 (DFNA6/14/38) gives low-frequency loss; TECTA (DFNA8/12) gives a congenital, nonprogressive midfrequency 'cookie-bite' loss; KCNQ4 (DFNA2) gives progressive high-frequency loss through outer hair cell death. Recessive TECTA (DFNB21) instead causes severe-to-profound loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2283-2286)

**GJB2 numbers**: GJB2 causes up to 50% of severe-to-profound congenital recessive nonsyndromic deafness. Founder variants: 35delG in Europeans (about 2.5% carrier rate in the US Midwest), 167delT in Ashkenazi Jews (about 4% carriers), 235delC in Japanese. Truncating variants usually give moderate-to-profound loss; missense variants can be mild. Loss is usually symmetric and stable, temporal bone anatomy is normal (routine imaging not needed), there are no associated comorbidities, and implant results are very good. GJB2 and the adjacent GJB6 deletion can act together in trans (digenic). (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2283; Ch 149, p 2275)

**Usher syndrome types**: Usher = SNHL plus retinitis pigmentosa, often with vestibular loss; it accounts for 3-6% of congenital deafness and about half of combined deaf-blindness. Type 1: congenital severe-to-profound loss, absent vestibular function, RP in childhood (USH1B/MYO7A is 75% of type 1). Type 2: moderate-to-severe congenital loss, normal vestibular function, RP starting in the 3rd-4th decade (USH2A is the most common Usher form overall). Type 3: progressive loss with variable vestibular and RP onset. It presents as an apparent nonsyndromic loss (a 'nonsyndromic mimic'), so panels include Usher genes; a congenitally deaf child who walks late suggests type 1. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2288-2289)

**Waardenburg types**: WS1 (PAX3) is SNHL, white forelock, iris heterochromia and dystopia canthorum. WS2 (MITF, SNAI2) is WS1 without dystopia canthorum and with a higher rate of hearing loss (57-85% vs 36-67%). WS3 (Klein-Waardenburg, PAX3) is WS1 plus upper-limb hypoplasia or contractures. WS4 (Shah-Waardenburg) is WS plus Hirschsprung disease, usually recessive with EDNRB or EDN3 and dominant with SOX10. Hearing loss is usually profound, bilateral and stable, and temporal bone imaging is usually normal. The cause is absent strial melanocytes from a neural crest defect. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288)

**Stickler syndrome**: Dominant type II/XI collagen disorder (COL2A1, COL11A1, COL11A2), about 1 in 10,000. Diagnosis needs a congenital vitreous anomaly plus 3 of: myopia before age 6, retinal detachment or lattice degeneration, joint hypermobility, SNHL, or midline clefting. Robin sequence and cleft occur in 28-65%, often submucous. Hearing loss can be conductive (from ET dysfunction), sensorineural or mixed. The COL11A2 type has no eye findings because that gene is not expressed in the vitreous. Retinal detachment, in about 50%, is the most serious problem, so these children need ophthalmology follow-up. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2287)

**Jervell and Lange-Nielsen**: Recessive KCNQ1 (KVLQT1) or KCNE1 potassium-channel defect causing congenital bilateral severe-to-profound SNHL with long QT, syncope and sudden death. It is found in about 0.21% of congenitally deaf children (other estimates reach about 0.6%). Beta-blockers lower mortality from about 71% to 6%. The dominant long-QT form without deafness is Romano-Ward syndrome. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288)

**Pendred syndrome details**: Pendred is the most common syndromic hereditary SNHL (recessive, SLC26A4/pendrin, which can account for up to ~10% of hereditary deafness). The goiter appears in the 2nd decade and patients usually stay euthyroid. Most patients have a temporal bone anomaly on imaging (enlarged vestibular aqueduct, often with Mondini/IP-II). The perchlorate discharge test is positive when more than 10% of radioiodine washes out, but its sensitivity is low, so genetic testing is preferred. Nonsyndromic SLC26A4 loss is DFNB4. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2288)

**Alport syndrome**: Type IV collagen disease (COL4A5, X-linked in ~80%; COL4A3/4 autosomal) with hematuric nephritis progressing to ESRD in all males, progressive symmetric high-frequency SNHL detectable by late childhood, and eye lesions (anterior lenticonus, macular flecks). Diagnosis needs 3 of 4: family history of hematuria/renal failure, progressive high-frequency SNHL, the typical eye lesion, and glomerular basement membrane changes. Anterior lenticonus predicts ESRD before age 30. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2289)

**Branchio-oto-renal syndrome numbers**: Dominant, nearly full penetrance, 1 in 40,000, and about 2% of profoundly deaf children. Hearing loss occurs in ~90% (mixed 50%, conductive 30%, sensorineural 20%). Preauricular pits occur in 82%, auricular malformations in 32%, branchial fistulas or cysts are common, and renal anomalies occur in about 25%. Inner ear findings include cochlear hypoplasia, an enlarged vestibular or cochlear aqueduct, and a hypoplastic lateral semicircular canal. Genes are EYA1 (about 25% of cases), SIX1 and SIX5, so a child with ear pits and hearing loss needs a renal ultrasound. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2286)

**Mitochondrial syndromes**: Mitochondrial disorders are maternally inherited with no father-to-child transmission; severity tracks heteroplasmy. Hearing loss occurs in ~70% of syndromic forms. MELAS and MIDD (maternally inherited diabetes and deafness, 0.5-2.8% of diabetics) are caused by m.3243A>G and give progressive high-frequency SNHL from strial atrophy. MERRF causes hearing loss with myoclonus, ataxia and optic atrophy. Kearns-Sayre syndrome (large mtDNA deletions) causes ophthalmoplegia, retinopathy and heart block before age 20, with SNHL in 50%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2289-2290)

**Treatable metabolic causes**: Biotinidase deficiency (seizures, hypotonia, ataxia, rash, alopecia) causes SNHL in at least 75% of symptomatic untreated children. Biotin reverses the neurologic and skin findings but not established hearing loss or optic atrophy, so it must start early. Refsum disease (PHYH or PEX7; postlingual progressive SNHL, retinitis pigmentosa, neuropathy, ataxia, high CSF protein without extra cells) is diagnosed by serum phytanic acid and treated with diet and plasmapheresis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2289)

**Genetic testing yield and counseling numbers**: Comprehensive multigene panels (massively parallel sequencing) are now standard of care and diagnose about 40% overall, rising to about 60% in a newborn with bilateral congenital profound loss. Yield is higher with young age, early onset, symmetric loss and family history. For normal-hearing parents of one deaf child, the risk of a second deaf child is about 17.5%. If the familial variant is known, prenatal testing is possible by chorionic villus sampling (10-12 weeks) or amniocentesis (15-18 weeks). (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, pp 2290-2291)

**X-linked DFN3 and Mohr-Tranebjaerg**: X-linked nonsyndromic loss is under 2% of cases; the most common is DFN3 (POU3F4), with congenital mixed loss, apparent stapes fixation, a widened lateral IAC and a dilated vestibule. Stapedectomy causes a perilymph gusher, so it is avoided. Mohr-Tranebjaerg syndrome (TIMM8A, a mitochondrial import protein) is progressive postlingual deafness with dystonia, visual loss and intellectual disability that was first misclassified as nonsyndromic DFN1. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2286; Ch 149, p 2274)

**Chromosomal disorders and hearing**: About 75% of children with trisomy 21 have hearing loss (conductive, sensorineural or mixed). Trisomy 13 is usually profound deafness with cleft lip and palate. Turner syndrome (45,X) has frequent otitis media and common mild-to-moderate SNHL. About 20% of boys with Klinefelter syndrome (47,XXY) have mild SNHL. Loss in Turner and Klinefelter is often missed unless specifically tested. (Cummings 7e, Ch 149, p 2271)

**1555A>G numbers**: The m.1555A>G variant in the 12S rRNA gene (MTRNR1) is found in 17-33% of people with aminoglycoside-induced hearing loss and in about 2% of a US NICU cohort. Loss follows normal doses, can appear months after exposure, and starts in the basal outer hair cells. Without exposure, the same variant causes a later-onset, progressive, mild high-frequency nonsyndromic loss. (Cummings 7e, Ch 150, p 2286)

**Superior (anterior) semicircular canal BPPV**: accounts for only about 2% of BPPV and produces downbeating nystagmus with a torsional component (upper pole toward the upward ear), which can be provoked on standard Dix-Hallpike testing because each superior canal is coplanar with the contralateral posterior canal. Its direction is opposite to that of posterior canal BPPV on the same test. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2520)

**Maneuver details**: Epley clears posterior canal BPPV in more than 80%; the Semont (liberatory) maneuver also works but is harder to perform and somewhat less effective. Move head and body en bloc; avoid mastoid vibration in patients with prior retinal detachment or high myopia. Post-maneuver upright restrictions give at most a small benefit, and geotropic horizontal canal BPPV often clears by lying affected-ear-up for about 12 hours (forced prolonged positioning). (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2521)

**Events during repositioning**: posterior canal BPPV can convert to horizontal canal BPPV (usually resolves in days) or to apparent anterior canal BPPV; debris jamming at the common crus produces sustained pure torsional nystagmus because superior and posterior canal vertical components cancel. Persistent non-fatiguing horizontal positional nystagmus has been attributed to a 'light cupula,' a controversial entity that usually resolves within weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2520)

**Surgery for intractable BPPV**: posterior semicircular canal occlusion (plugging the canal lumen so it no longer senses angular acceleration) cured 94 of 97 reported cases, with transient postoperative hearing loss and permanent loss of that canal's function. Singular (posterior ampullary) neurectomy is effective but technically difficult, with hearing-loss risk reported up to 41%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2522)

**Superior division predominance**: the superior vestibular nerve is affected more often, possibly because it runs through a longer, narrower bony canal. Pathology shows vestibular nerve degeneration with sparing of end organs. Isolated inferior nerve neuritis may be missed because horizontal head impulse and calorics are normal. A small percentage later develop posterior canal BPPV, and attacks can recur. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2522)

**Steroids and antivirals**: in a placebo-controlled trial, valacyclovir had no effect. Methylprednisolone improved caloric recovery but pooled data show no proven benefit on symptoms, so evidence for steroids is weak (some limit use to starts within 3 days). Early ambulation is encouraged. If hearing loss accompanies the vertigo, treat and work up as sudden SNHL, including evaluation for a retrocochlear lesion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2522)

**Diagnostic criteria**: Cummings presents the AAO-HNS 1995 scheme, in which 'definite' Ménière disease needs 2 or more spontaneous vertigo spells of at least 20 minutes, audiometric hearing loss on at least one occasion, and tinnitus or fullness in that ear, 'probable' needs one definitive spell, 'possible' is vertigo without documented loss or fluctuating loss without definite spells, and 'certain' needs histopathology. **Current view**: the 2015 Bárány Society/AAO-HNS criteria, used in the 2020 AAO-HNS Ménière guideline, replace it. Definite disease is 2 or more spells lasting 20 minutes to 12 hours, audiometric low-to-mid-frequency SNHL in the affected ear on at least one occasion, and fluctuating aural symptoms. Probable disease is 2 or more spells of 20 minutes to 24 hours with fluctuating aural symptoms but no audiometric proof. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2525)

**AAO-HNS outcome reporting**: assess treatment no sooner than 24 months. The vertigo numeric value is post-treatment spells/month divided by pretreatment spells/month x 100 (Class A = 0, complete control, B 1-40, C 41-80, D 81-120, E >120, F = secondary treatment started). Hearing change is significant if the 4-tone PTA changes by more than 10 dB or word recognition by more than 15%. A 6-point functional level scale grades disability. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2526)

**Natural history and variants**: attacks most often last 2-3 hours. Vertigo stops spontaneously in about 57% by 2 years and 71% by 8 years, and only 1%-2% progress to profound deafness. Bilateral disease is roughly 19%-24%, familial in 10%-20%, and HLA-B8/DR3 and Cw7 are associated. Tumarkin otolithic crises (sudden drop attacks without loss of consciousness or vertigo) occur in 2%-6%. In Lermoyez syndrome, hearing and tinnitus worsen before the vertigo and then improve when it begins. The audiogram may be 'tent-shaped' (low-frequency fluctuating loss with a peak at 2 kHz), and diplacusis is common. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2525)

**Test performance**: caloric weakness occurs in 48%-74% (absent response in 6%-11%). Head impulse asymmetry in only 29%. ECochG SP/AP ratio is elevated in about 62% of patients but also in 21% of controls. cVEMP shows elevated thresholds, reduced amplitude and flattened tuning (normal best frequency about 500 Hz) but individual variation limits diagnostic use. Gadolinium MRI can show hydrops but is not part of diagnostic criteria. MRI's role is to exclude vestibular schwannoma or endolymphatic sac tumor. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2526)

**Medical and device therapy evidence**: salt restriction and diuretics remain reasonable first-line despite no placebo-controlled proof. Acetazolamide is no better than other diuretics. Betahistine was no better than placebo in a large European multicenter trial. The Meniett pressure device (needs a ventilation tube) helped only for the first 3 months versus placebo and is rarely used. A ventilation tube alone helps some patients. Intratympanic dexamethasone (typically 10 mg/mL, often repeated about every 3 months) gave complete vertigo control in 82% vs 57% with saline. Gentamicin was superior to dexamethasone in an RCT. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2527)

**Ablative/surgical outcomes**: titrated intratympanic gentamicin (single injection, repeat only if needed) controls vertigo in about 83%-90%, with profound loss around 3%-10%. Ablating caloric function as an endpoint caused severe-to-profound loss in 58%. Endolymphatic sac surgery has weak evidence (Thomsen sham-mastoidectomy trial, shunt no better than a tube). Vestibular nerve section controls vertigo in 85%-95% with hearing kept in 80%-90%. Labyrinthectomy gives the highest control and is favored when there is no useful hearing. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2528)

**Direction of evoked eye movements**: loud sound, positive canal pressure, or Valsalva against pinched nostrils excite the affected superior semicircular canal (upward slow phase, upper pole of the eye torting away from that ear). Negative canal pressure, Valsalva against a closed glottis, or jugular compression give the opposite movement. Patients may hear their eye movements, pulse, or a tuning fork on the lateral malleolus. Weber lateralizes to the affected ear. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2529)

**Imaging and objective tests**: standard 1-mm temporal bone CT overcalls dehiscence because of partial volume. Use 0.5-mm collimated scans reformatted in the plane of the superior semicircular canal (Pöschl) and perpendicular to it (Stenver), and never diagnose from CT alone. Supporting findings are lowered cVEMP thresholds, enlarged oVEMP amplitudes and bone conduction thresholds below 0 dB, producing an air-bone gap despite normal air conduction. 'Near-dehiscence' with these objective findings can be treated like true dehiscence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2530)

**Repair options**: middle fossa plugging is standard. Transmastoid plugging has more failures (better for vestibular than auditory symptoms) and suits patients who are poor middle fossa candidates. Round window plugging is generally not appropriate because it does not treat the third window, objective improvement is rare, and hearing often worsens. A tympanostomy tube can help mainly pressure-induced symptoms. Posterior canal dehiscence (at the jugular bulb) and lateral canal dehiscence (cholesteatoma, surgery) also occur. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2531)

**Cogan syndrome**: nonsyphilitic interstitial keratitis with Ménière-like vertigo and SNHL; eye and ear findings appear together or within 6 months. Typical form has interstitial keratitis; the atypical form (about 10%) has scleritis, episcleritis or other ocular inflammation and more systemic vasculitis. Aortitis (and other cardiopulmonary vasculitis) is the key systemic association; hearing loss is bilateral in about 44%, progressive and often profound, and loss of vestibular function causes oscillopsia. Treat early with prednisone 1 mg/kg/day, moving to steroid-sparing agents; infliximab can help refractory cases. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2531)

**Otosyphilis testing**: nontreponemal tests (VDRL, RPR) detect only about 70% of late disease, so use treponemal tests (FTA-ABS, MHA-TP), which detect 95% or more. Nontreponemal titers are used to follow treatment response. Lumbar puncture is positive in only about 5% and is not routinely required. Interstitial keratitis is present in about 90% of late otosyphilis, and Hutchinson's triad (SNHL, interstitial keratitis, notched incisors) marks late congenital syphilis. Hennebert sign and Tullio phenomenon are common in syphilis but not specific for it. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2532)

**Otosyphilis treatment**: Cummings treats early disease with IM benzathine penicillin 2.4 million units (with a short steroid course) and late disease like neurosyphilis with prolonged penicillin plus probenecid (for example 3 weeks). **Current view (CDC 2021)**: otosyphilis at any stage is treated as neurosyphilis, with aqueous crystalline penicillin G 18-24 million units/day IV for 10-14 days (or procaine penicillin plus probenecid), with ID consultation. Prednisone 40-60 mg/day for at least 2 weeks before taper is commonly added. Hearing, especially word recognition, improves in about 35%-50%. Early otosyphilis (within 2 years) tends to present as sudden SNHL, while late disease mimics Ménière disease and can appear decades after exposure. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2532)

**Ambiguity of diagnosis**: no audiometric profile distinguishes proven fistulas, inter-observer agreement at exploration is low, and beta-2 transferrin is insensitive for the tiny volumes involved. Natural fissures (fissula ante fenestram, round window niche to posterior ampulla) are common and of unclear significance. Many patients once labeled fistula actually have superior canal dehiscence. CT pneumolabyrinth supports a traumatic fistula, and definite traumatic cases can still resolve with conservative care. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2533)

**Labyrinthine fistula from cholesteatoma**: in one series of 375 chronic ear operations, 29 fistulas were found (13% of canal wall down cases); all had vertigo, but only 14 of 19 tested had a positive fistula (Hennebert) test. The lateral (horizontal) semicircular canal was the site in 76%, followed by oval window and promontory; close the fistula with cartilage, bone paste or fascia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2533)

**Labyrinthine concussion and blast**: injury without otic capsule violation causes short-lived vertigo and imbalance (days to weeks) and a noise-induced pattern of hearing loss with a 4-kHz notch. Nystagmus may beat toward the injured side in the first hours before reversing. Posttraumatic BPPV is common. Blasts (over 200 dB SPL) injure the inner ear more when the TM and ossicles stay intact. About 15% have dizziness. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2533)

**Diving inner-ear injuries**: alternobaric vertigo occurs on ascent (decreasing ambient pressure) in up to 26% of divers and lasts about 10-15 minutes. Inner ear barotrauma (usually on descent) gives hearing loss and tinnitus with vertigo in about 35%, managed like a fistula (bed rest, head elevation). Inner ear decompression sickness (especially deep mixed-gas diving) presents mainly with vertigo and needs urgent hyperbaric oxygen. Outcomes are best when it is started early (one study cites within 68 minutes). (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2534)

**Gentamicin bilateral vestibulopathy**: about 3% of patients given gentamicin develop vestibular injury (likely under-reported). Toxicity does not correlate with peak/trough levels or dose and is often noticed only after discharge, with oscillopsia on head movement and gait instability. Bedside dynamic visual acuity and head impulse testing during therapy can detect it, though signs lag about a week. No cause is found in about 31% of bilateral vestibular loss. Others include meningitis, autoimmune disease, cerebellar degeneration and bilateral Ménière disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2534)

**EVA vestibular features**: diagnosis is a vestibular aqueduct wider than 1.5 mm at its midpoint on CT (about the width of the lateral semicircular canal). Hearing loss begins in early childhood and often drops after minor head trauma; vestibular symptoms (episodic vertigo lasting hours, BPPV) often appear later, and VEMP thresholds are decreased. (Cummings 7e, Ch 167, p 2535)

**MSLT criteria for narcolepsy**: after an overnight PSG excludes other sleep disorders, an MSLT (20-minute nap opportunities) showing mean sleep latency of 8 minutes or less (normal about 15) plus sleep-onset REM in at least 2 naps (a SOREMP on the preceding PSG can count as one) supports narcolepsy. CSF hypocretin-1 deficiency defines type 1, whereas type 2 has normal hypocretin and no cataplexy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)

**Narcolepsy and RLS treatment**: narcolepsy is treated with sleep hygiene/scheduled naps, stimulants or modafinil for sleepiness, REM-suppressing tricyclics/SSRIs, and sodium oxybate (GABA-B agonist) for cataplexy. For restless legs/PLMD in children, give iron when ferritin is below 50 µg/L. Cummings also lists dopaminergic agents, gabapentin and benzodiazepines, but the current AASM (2024) RLS guideline favors iron and alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin, pregabalin) and advises against standard use of dopamine agonists because of augmentation. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)

**Parasomnia timing rule**: NREM parasomnias (sleep terrors, sleepwalking, confusional arousals, sleep-related eating) arise from slow-wave sleep in the first two-thirds of the night with amnesia for the event. REM parasomnias (nightmares, sleep paralysis, REM behavior disorder) cluster in the last third of the night with vivid recall. Sleep terrors (ages about 3-10) carry tachycardia/tachypnea. Confusional arousals lack an autonomic surge. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, pp 2796-2797)

**Kleine-Levin and idiopathic hypersomnia**: Kleine-Levin syndrome is episodic hypersomnia in adolescents (median onset 15 years, male predominance 2-3:1) with hyperphagia and hypersexuality, and symptom-free intervals. Idiopathic hypersomnia (daily sleepiness for at least 3 months by ICSD-3) differs from narcolepsy by normal hypocretin, no cataplexy and fewer than 2 sleep-onset REM periods, and responds less well to stimulants. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2796)

**Delayed sleep-wake phase disorder**: affects 5-10% of adolescents. Sleep onset is delayed 2-3 hours or more (often 2-6 a.m.) with normal architecture once asleep. Treat with sleep hygiene, chronotherapy that gradually advances bedtime, and melatonin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2796)

**Age-based sleep needs (AASM)**: 4-12 months 12-16 h including naps. 1-2 years 11-14 h. 3-5 years 10-13 h. 6-12 years 9-12 h. 13-18 years 8-10 h. RLS affects about 2% of children, often with family history and 'growing pains'. Rhythmic movement disorder (head banging, rocking) is usually benign and treated with a safe environment. (Cummings 7e, Ch 185, p 2795)

**CHAT trial**: 464 children aged 5-9 with OSA were randomized to adenotonsillectomy or watchful waiting. At 7 months, 79% of the surgery group vs 46% of the waiting group normalized (AHI <2). Surgery improved symptoms, behavior and quality of life, but not the primary attention/executive-function (NEPSY) endpoint. Normalization was less likely in Black children, obese children and those with higher baseline AHI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2804-2805)

**Cure rates and residual-disease predictors**: meta-analysis cure after adenotonsillectomy is about 60-66% (about 60% when cure = AHI <1). One multicenter series had only 27% with AHI <1. Predictors of residual OSA are age over 7, obesity, severe OSA and asthma. Persistence is 33-76% in obese vs 15-37% in nonobese children, and up to 80% of children with Down syndrome have persistent abnormalities. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2804)

**Medical and orthodontic options**: intranasal steroids (fluticasone, budesonide) and montelukast reduce AHI in mild OSA. Supplemental oxygen requires CO2 monitoring and is not a sole long-term therapy. Rapid maxillary expansion (expand over 3-4 weeks, then stabilize 6-12 months) helps children with a narrow maxilla, especially after adenotonsillectomy or with small tonsils. CPAP/BiPAP normalizes PSG in 86-100%, with 60-80% long-term adherence. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2804)

**Admission thresholds differ by guideline**: AAO-HNS recommends inpatient monitoring for AHI 10 or more and/or SpO2 nadir below 80%. AAP uses AHI 24 or more, nadir below 80%, or peak end-tidal CO2 of 60 mm Hg or more. Other risk factors: age under 3, pulmonary hypertension/cardiac disease, craniofacial syndromes, failure to thrive, hypotonia and morbid obesity. Respiratory complications occur in 16-27% of children with OSA vs up to 1.3% overall. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2805)

**Postoperative analgesia and fluids**: codeine and tramadol are contraindicated after tonsillectomy in anyone under 18 (FDA 2017), because CYP2D6 ultrarapid metabolizers build up toxic morphine. NSAIDs (ibuprofen) do not raise bleeding risk in Cochrane data, but ketorolac should be avoided (bleeding 4.4-18%). A single intraoperative IV dexamethasone dose is recommended. Rehydrate with isotonic fluid because hypotonic fluid plus high ADH causes potentially lethal hyponatremia. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2805-2806)

**Adenoidectomy-specific complications**: neck pain and stiffness after adenoidectomy reflect prevertebral inflammation. Pain lasting more than 2 weeks should raise concern for C1-C2 (atlantoaxial) subluxation (Grisel syndrome). Postobstructive pulmonary edema after relief of chronic obstruction is treated with oxygen, PEEP support, fluid restriction and diuretics. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, p 2805)

**Syndromic PSG and hematologic prep**: the AAP recommends PSG for all children with Down syndrome by age 4 (OSA in about 57%, most parents report no symptoms). Screen with PSG when starting growth hormone in Prader-Willi syndrome. Sickle cell patients get hydration and transfusion to hemoglobin about 10 g/dL before surgery, and type 1 von Willebrand disease is managed with desmopressin. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2801-2806)

**Syndromic causes of OSA**: craniofacial syndromes carry 40-50% SDB prevalence (craniosynostoses, Pierre Robin, Treacher Collins, craniofacial microsomia, 22q11). Achondroplasia (FGFR3, autosomal dominant) adds midface hypoplasia and foramen magnum stenosis. Mucopolysaccharidoses (Hurler/Scheie α-L-iduronidase, Hunter iduronate sulfatase) cause soft-tissue and tracheobronchial deposits where even tracheotomy may not secure the airway. Chiari malformation causes mixed central and obstructive apnea. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2801-2802)

**Epidemiology and screening numbers**: OSA affects 1-4% of children (snoring about 7.5%), peaking at 2-6 years. Boys are affected 50-100% more often and Black children about 3.5 times more. Only 20-30% of snoring children have a positive PSG. Clinical assessment alone is 30-81% accurate. The 22-item Pediatric Sleep Questionnaire has about 78% sensitivity and 72% specificity. Untreated primary snoring progresses to OSA in only 8-10% over 1-3 years. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2799-2804)

**Cummings abnormal pediatric PSG values**: obstructive AI or AHI above 1/h (1-4 mild, 5-10 moderate, above 10 severe). SpO2 nadir below 92%. Hypoventilation if peak end-tidal CO2 is above 53 mm Hg or end-tidal CO2 is above 50 mm Hg for more than 10% of sleep time. Without esophageal manometry, UARS is suggested by awakenings above 1/h, arousal index above 10/h or sleep efficiency below 80%. Nap studies, oximetry and home PSG are useful only when positive. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2802-2803)

**Pediatric residual OSA**: DISE (propofol, sevoflurane or dexmedetomidine +/- ketamine, Chan-Parikh, SERS or VOTE scoring) or sedated cine MRI finds the sites: adenoid regrowth, turbinate hypertrophy, lingual tonsils, macroglossia/glossoptosis, sleep-state laryngomalacia (about 3.9%, usually over age 2) and lateral wall collapse. Stage multilevel surgery in children because of scarring/stenosis risk. Lingual tonsillectomy reaches AHI <1 in only about 17% and AHI <5 in about 51%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 186, pp 2806-2807)

**Kasabach-Merritt phenomenon belongs to KHE/tufted angioma, not infantile hemangioma**: profound thrombocytopenia in an infant with a violaceous, infiltrative vascular tumor points to kaposiform hemangioendothelioma or tufted angioma. Diagnosis needs incisional biopsy; extensive or symptomatic lesions need antiangiogenic therapy, with sirolimus now a key agent. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, pp 3006-3007)

**Congenital hemangiomas are GLUT-1 negative**: RICH and NICH are fully formed at birth, lack GLUT-1 staining (unlike infantile hemangioma) and do not respond to propranolol or other medical therapy. RICH is observed; NICH may need laser or excision. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, p 3006)

**Functional complications that force early treatment**: subglottic lesions cause biphasic stridor; periocular lesions cause deprivation amblyopia or, if they distort the globe before about 6 months, astigmatic amblyopia; lip and neck-fold lesions ulcerate (brown crust, then pain and bleeding) and impair feeding; large parotid/scalp lesions can cause high-output heart failure. About 80% of salivary hemangiomas are parotid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, p 3007; Ch 205, p 3048)

**de Serres staging and imaging**: stage 1 unilateral infrahyoid, 2 unilateral suprahyoid, 3 unilateral supra- and infrahyoid, 4 bilateral suprahyoid, 5 bilateral supra- and infrahyoid. Higher stage means more complications and worse outcome. US or MRI (T2 bright, nonenhancing except septa, no feeding vessels) classifies macrocystic (cysts 2 cm or larger), microcystic or mixed. CT adds radiation without added information. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, pp 3012-3013)

**Sclerosants and their toxicities**: macrocystic disease responds to doxycycline, bleomycin, ethanol or sodium tetradecyl sulfate. OK-432 (Picibanil) is not available in the US. Rare major toxicities are pulmonary fibrosis with bleomycin and permanent nerve injury with ethanol. Skin blistering, fever and pain are common. Systemic sirolimus (mTOR inhibitor) is used for extensive microcystic disease. Up to 60% are detected prenatally, and prenatal lesions associate with chromosomal anomalies and may need EXIT delivery. (Cummings 7e, Ch 203, pp 3012-3015)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Van der Woude syndrome**: the most common syndromic cleft; autosomal dominant, caused by IRF6 (interferon regulatory factor 6, 1q32) mutations, with lower lip pits plus cleft lip and/or palate. About 10% of carriers lack lip pits, and cleft type can vary within a family. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, p 2837)

topic: Cleft Lip / Palate — ENT Surgical Fundamentals
text: **Rule of 10s for lip repair timing**: proceed with definitive lip repair when the infant is at least 10 weeks old, weighs 10 pounds and has hemoglobin of 10 g/dL. The Millard rotation-advancement is the most common unilateral repair; the Furlow double-opposing Z-plasty lengthens the soft palate and realigns the levator sling. (Cummings 7e, Ch 188, pp 2841-2846)

**Associated syndromes**: Stickler syndrome is the most commonly associated syndrome in Pierre Robin sequence (30-40% in this text, about 18% in other series, partly because mild forms are missed). Screen eyes for myopia/retinal detachment, plus hearing. Treacher Collins (autosomal dominant, malar hypoplasia, lower-lid colobomas, missing medial lower lashes, dysplastic ears) has Robin sequence/cleft palate in about 35%, often with severe OSA. (Cummings 7e, Ch 187, p 2818)

**EVA counseling**: hearing loss with enlarged vestibular aqueduct is often progressive and may drop suddenly after even minor head trauma (one series: 51% stable, 28% fluctuating). Advise avoiding head trauma, contact sports and rapid barometric changes such as scuba diving. Most bilateral EVA links to SLC26A4 (Pendred); the dilated endolymphatic sac is best seen on T2 MRI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 194, pp 2907-2915)

**Infectious lymphadenitis traps**: the PPD is positive in only about 50% of nontuberculous mycobacterial adenitis, so a negative PPD does not exclude it and should not be used to screen. Cat-scratch disease (Bartonella henselae, usually from a young cat) is confirmed by Bartonella titers and is typically self-limited. Fixed or matted nodes always need more workup; excise small or suspected malignant masses rather than taking a partial biopsy to avoid seeding. (Cummings 7e, Ch 202, pp 2999-3001)

**Why Sistrunk**: recurrence after simple cyst excision is about 46% vs 5.8% after a modified Sistrunk procedure (central hyoid plus tract toward the foramen cecum). Routine preoperative thyroid function testing or nuclear scans are no longer needed if ultrasound shows a normal thyroid. (Cummings 7e, Ch 202, p 3001)

**Pediatric salivary tumors**: vascular lesions (hemangioma, then lymphatic malformation) are the most common salivary masses in children. When they are excluded, a solid salivary tumor in a child is more likely malignant than in an adult. Mucoepidermoid carcinoma accounts for about half of pediatric salivary cancers, mostly in teenagers and mostly low grade. It is also the most common radiation-induced salivary tumor in children. Acinic cell is next. (Cummings 7e, Ch 205, pp 3047-3049)

**PFAPA**: the most common cause of recurrent fever in children. Fevers of 38.5-41°C last 3-6 days, recur every 2-8 weeks with well intervals, and come with aphthous stomatitis, pharyngitis or cervical adenitis. Corticosteroids such as prednisolone stop most attacks within 24 hours, NSAIDs do not help, and tonsillectomy is an option for selected children with severe pharyngitis. (Cummings 7e, Ch 201, p 2982)

**Autologous rib timing**: autologous framework requires enough rib cartilage, generally at age 8-9 or older. Nagata's two-stage technique needs more cartilage (chest circumference at the xiphoid of about 60 cm is a commonly used threshold), while Brent's uses three or four stages. High-density porous polyethylene (Medpor) frameworks can be placed earlier. (Cummings 7e, Ch 195, pp 2919-2922)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Vagal-complex eponyms beyond Vernet/Villaret/Collet-Sicard**: Avellis = ipsilateral palate and laryngeal paralysis with contralateral loss of pain/temperature below the neck (nucleus ambiguus/X plus cranial IX). Schmidt = X plus XI (vocal fold, palate, SCM, trapezius), usually a caudal medullary vascular lesion. Jackson = X, XI and XII (adds ipsilateral tongue atrophy). Tapia = X and XII with an intact palate and cricothyroid; classically from trauma or a malpositioned endotracheal cuff where the nerves cross near the internal carotid. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 2, 18, 30, 34)

**Melkersson-Rosenthal syndrome**: Triad of recurrent orofacial (lip) swelling, recurrent unilateral or bilateral facial paralysis, and fissured tongue (lingua plicata); a granulomatous process (orofacial granulomatosis/cheilitis granulomatosa) that may raise serum ACE. Treatment targets the palsy and edema; steroids and nerve decompression have limited success. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 22)

**Möbius syndrome**: Nonprogressive congenital facial diplegia, usually bilateral, with abducens palsy (loss of lateral gaze), often other cranial neuropathies, limb anomalies and pectoral/brachial muscle aplasia (Poland overlap). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 22)

**Benign lymphoproliferative mimics of neck lymphoma**: Castleman disease (giant/angiofollicular lymph node hyperplasia) has hyaline-vascular (radial capillaries into follicles) and plasma-cell histologic types and is treated by complete excision of the localized mass. Rosai-Dorfman disease (sinus histiocytosis with massive lymphadenopathy) is a benign self-limited histiocytic adenopathy with emperipolesis. Kimura disease is a chronic eosinophilic inflammatory mass of subcutaneous tissue, salivary glands and nodes, mostly in Asian men, with blood eosinophilia and high IgE. Distinguish from angiolymphoid hyperplasia with eosinophilia. Options include steroids, radiation and excision. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 6-7, 19, 30)

**Grisel syndrome**: Nontraumatic atlantoaxial rotatory subluxation (nasopharyngeal torticollis) in children after pharyngitis, adenotonsillitis, retropharyngeal or neck infection, otitis, or after adenotonsillectomy and other head and neck surgery. Presents with painful torticollis and needs C-spine imaging and spine consultation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 15-16)

**Thornwaldt (Tornwaldt) cyst**: A midline nasopharyngeal cyst from an infected/obstructed notochordal remnant (pharyngeal bursa) in the posterior nasopharyngeal vault, lined by respiratory epithelium. A benign midline lesion on imaging distinct from Rathke pouch remnants (craniopharyngeal canal through the sphenoid) and from NPC, which typically arises laterally in the fossa of Rosenmüller. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 44)

**Tolosa-Hunt syndrome**: Recurrent unilateral painful ophthalmoplegia (II, III, IV, V1, VI) from idiopathic granulomatous inflammation of the cavernous sinus/superior orbital fissure. A diagnosis of exclusion (rule out tumor, NPC extension, mucocele, sinusitis, aneurysm, thrombosis) that responds dramatically to systemic steroids and tends to recur. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 34-35)

**Plummer-Vinson (Paterson-Kelly) syndrome**: Iron-deficiency anemia, dysphagia from postcricoid/upper esophageal webs, atrophic glossitis and angular cheilitis, mostly in middle-aged women; treat with iron and dilation, and survey endoscopically because of increased postcricoid and esophageal carcinoma risk. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 1, p 26-27)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Malignant hyperthermia**: Triggered by volatile agents and succinylcholine in genetically susceptible patients (incidence about 1:10,000-1:50,000): uncontrolled intracellular calcium release produces rising end-tidal CO2, tachycardia, rigidity (masseter spasm is a warning), metabolic acidosis, hyperthermia and arrhythmias. Stop triggers and give dantrolene; known susceptible patients need a nontriggering anesthetic with a flushed machine. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 92)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Inhaled agents and nitrous oxide in ear surgery**: MAC is the alveolar concentration preventing movement to incision in 50% of patients; it falls about 6% per decade and is additive across agents. Nitrous oxide (MAC 104%) is 34 times more soluble than nitrogen and diffuses into closed air spaces, roughly doubling a compliant space in 10 minutes, so it can lift a tympanic membrane graft and raise ET cuff pressure; discontinue it before graft placement or avoid it. Desflurane is least soluble (fastest emergence, good in obesity) but pungent; sevoflurane suits inhalational induction. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 79-80)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Neuromuscular blockade and nerve monitoring**: Succinylcholine (onset 30-60 s, duration 5-10 min) is the only depolarizing relaxant; rocuronium (onset 60-90 s, 45-70 min) is the usual nondepolarizer. Block depth is followed by train-of-four. Neostigmine reversal must be paired with glycopyrrolate or atropine; sugammadex encapsulates rocuronium/vecuronium for rapid reversal, which allows paralysis for intubation yet a functioning EMG for facial or recurrent laryngeal nerve monitoring (caution in renal failure; it reduces oral contraceptive efficacy for 7 days). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 80-81)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Airway fire prevention numbers**: Use the lowest FiO2 that maintains saturation. K.J. Lee cites 21-40%, but current ASA guidance targets 30% or less. Avoid nitrous oxide, use laser-resistant or reflective-wrapped tubes, fill the cuff with methylene-blue-tinted saline, surround the field with wet pledgets, and use short bursts. If fire occurs, stop gas flow, remove the tube, extinguish and remove burning material (pour saline into the airway), re-establish ventilation by mask or reintubation, and then perform bronchoscopy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 4, p 91)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Prolonged PT or aPTT: the mixing study**: Isolated PT prolongation suggests factor VII deficiency, vitamin K deficiency or liver disease; aPTT or combined prolongation suggests multiple deficiencies or an inhibitor. A 1:1 mixing study that corrects indicates factor deficiency; failure to correct indicates an inhibitor. Acquired factor VIII inhibitor causes dangerous expanding hematomas (including neck/airway), while lupus anticoagulant prolongs the aPTT in vitro but causes thrombosis, not bleeding. Postpone elective surgery until clarified. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 113-114)

topic: Hemostasis / Coagulopathy / Antithrombotic Management in ENT
text: **Heparin-induced thrombocytopenia**: Platelet drop over 50% (or below 150,000) 5-14 days after heparin exposure (sooner with exposure within 100 days; delayed forms up to 30 days after stopping); incidence about 3-5% with UFH and under 1% with LMWH. It is prothrombotic (mostly venous). PF4 antibody ELISA is sensitive, serotonin release assay specific. Stop all heparin including flushes and coated lines; LMWH cross-reacts. Treat with a non-heparin anticoagulant (argatroban, bivalirudin; the book also lists lepirudin, since discontinued) and start warfarin only after platelet recovery, overlapping. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 5, p 115-117)

topic: Facial Pain / Headache vs Rhinogenic Disease
text: **Trigeminal neuralgia**: Brief electric-shock paroxysms (seconds to 2 minutes) in V2/V3 (V1 under 5%) triggered by chewing, talking, touch or cold air, with a normal neurologic exam; usually from superior cerebellar artery compression at the root entry zone, or MS demyelination in younger patients. Carbamazepine is first line (a response supports the diagnosis; about 75% are controlled medically), then oxcarbazepine, lamotrigine, baclofen or gabapentin. Procedures: percutaneous glycerol, radiofrequency or balloon rhizotomy, gamma knife, and microvascular decompression (most durable; not for MS). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 123-124, 133)

topic: Cranial Nerve Examination / Skull Base Localization
text: **Brainstem stroke syndromes**: Ipsilateral cranial nerve deficit with contralateral long-tract findings localizes to the brainstem. Weber (midbrain): ipsilateral CN III palsy with contralateral hemiparesis; Benedikt: CN III with contralateral chorea/tremor (red nucleus). Millard-Gubler and Foville (caudal pons): ipsilateral VI and VII palsy with contralateral hemiplegia (Foville adds gaze palsy). Medial medullary (Dejerine): ipsilateral tongue weakness with contralateral hemiplegia and loss of position sense. Lateral medullary (Wallenberg): ipsilateral face numbness, Horner, dysphagia and ataxia with contralateral body pain/temperature loss. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 125-126)

**Carotid-cavernous fistula**: Presents with pulsatile proptosis, chemosis, orbital bruit, retro-orbital pain, diplopia and visual loss (rarely epistaxis). Barrow type A is a direct high-flow ICA-cavernous sinus shunt (usually traumatic) treated by transarterial occlusion. Types B-D are low-flow dural shunts from ICA and/or ECA meningeal branches, half of which close spontaneously, and are treated transvenously via the inferior petrosal sinus if needed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 130)

**Spontaneous intracranial hypotension**: A CSF leak (usually spinal) produces orthostatic headache like a post-dural-puncture headache, low or unobtainable opening pressure, and diffuse pachymeningeal enhancement on contrast MRI that resolves with treatment; caffeine and hydration help, and persistent leaks need closure. Contrast with spontaneous skull-base leaks, which are typically associated with elevated pressure (idiopathic intracranial hypertension). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 134)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Pituitary adenoma subtypes and stalk effect**: Microadenomas are under 10 mm and macroadenomas over 10 mm; about two thirds secrete hormone (prolactin about 48%, GH 10%, ACTH 6%, TSH 1%). Prolactinomas are treated first with cabergoline or bromocriptine; other functioning and symptomatic tumors go to surgery. A nonfunctioning macroadenoma compressing the stalk raises prolactin (usually under 200 ng/mL) by removing dopamine inhibition. Apoplexy (hemorrhagic infarction) causes sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia and panhypopituitarism. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 6, p 134-135)

**Reading the flow-volume loop**: During inspiration extrathoracic airway pressure falls below atmospheric and the lumen narrows, while intrathoracic airways widen as pleural pressure drops. So a variable extrathoracic lesion (vocal fold paralysis, laryngeal mass) flattens the inspiratory limb with a normal expiratory limb. A variable intrathoracic lesion (distal tracheomalacia, tumor) flattens the expiratory limb. A fixed lesion (circumferential stenosis) flattens both. COPD gives a concave ('scooped') expiratory curve and restrictive disease a small loop with a normal FEV1/FVC. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 140-142)

**Sodium disorders**: Hyponatremia: classify by volume status (hypervolemic CHF/cirrhosis/nephrosis, hypovolemic losses, euvolemic SIADH/hypothyroidism), correct for hyperglycemia (add about 2 mEq per 100 mg/dL of glucose excess), give hypertonic saline only for symptoms (about 2 mEq/L/h for 2-3 h), and limit correction to 10-12 mEq/L in 24 h and 18 in 48 h; demeclocycline blocks ADH in malignant SIADH. Hypernatremia always implies a free water deficit; central and nephrogenic DI both give large volumes of dilute urine; replace free water slowly (no more than about 12 mEq/L/day). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 166-167)

**Potassium and magnesium**: The hyperkalemia ECG sequence is peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS, then arrest. With ECG changes or K over 6.5, give IV calcium gluconate first, then insulin plus glucose and bicarbonate to shift K intracellularly, then elimination (loop diuretic, binders, dialysis). Hypokalemia causes U waves and ileus. K.J. Lee's maximum repletion rate is about 40 mEq/h with cardiac monitoring, but usual rates are about 10 mEq/h peripherally and up to 20 mEq/h centrally. Hypomagnesemia (common with loop diuretics, alcohol, malnutrition, after parathyroidectomy) causes refractory hypocalcemia, so correct magnesium (1-2 g MgSO4 IV) before calcium will normalize. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 8, p 167-169)

**Penicillin allergy de-labeling**: About 10% of people report penicillin allergy, but only 5-10% of them are skin-test positive, about a third of those react on oral challenge (the gold standard), and roughly 90% tolerate penicillin; anaphylaxis occurs in under 0.015% of courses. A penicillin label raises rates of resistant infection, C. difficile and mortality. Cross-reactivity is about 1-5% with first-generation cephalosporins (older 10% figures reflect contaminated manufacturing) and negligible with third-generation agents. Distinguish adverse effects (nausea, diarrhea, headache) from true IgE reactions (urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 185)

**Aminoglycoside ototoxicity ranking**: Vestibulotoxicity runs streptomycin > gentamicin > tobramycin > amikacin, and among these systemic agents amikacin is the most cochleotoxic (neomycin, given orally or topically, is the most cochleotoxic aminoglycoside overall). Toxicity is dose-dependent, high frequencies are lost first, and type I vestibular hair cells in the cristae and maculae are targeted. Nephrotoxicity is usually reversible, ototoxicity usually not. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 177-178)

**Necrotizing fasciitis types**: Type 1 is polymicrobial (streptococci, staphylococci, enteric gram-negatives and anaerobes such as Bacteroides) and most common in the head and neck; type 2 is monomicrobial group A streptococcus (about 30% develop toxic shock); type 3 is Vibrio from marine injuries. Treatment is urgent debridement plus empiric vancomycin or linezolid with piperacillin-tazobactam or a carbapenem; add clindamycin for toxin suppression when toxic shock is suspected. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 186)

**Tetanus prophylaxis**: Unknown or fewer than 3 prior tetanus doses: give Tdap/Td for any wound and add tetanus immune globulin for contaminated or major wounds. With 3 or more doses: give a booster for clean minor wounds only if the last dose was over 10 years ago, and for other wounds if over 5 years ago; no TIG unless severely immunocompromised (including HIV). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 9, p 184)

**Systemic steroid equivalence and risks**: Approximate equipotent ratios: hydrocortisone 1, prednisone/prednisolone 4, methylprednisolone/triamcinolone 5, dexamethasone 25. K.J. Lee advises tapering courses longer than about 5 days, although clinically important HPA suppression is unlikely with courses under about 3 weeks. Intranasal fluticasone or mometasone does not cause it. Long-term risks include hypertension, hyperglycemia, posterior subcapsular cataract, glaucoma, osteoporosis, peptic ulcer, mood change and avascular necrosis of the femoral head (the most litigated complication). A short preoperative prednisone burst (about 30 mg daily for 4-7 days) reduces bleeding in polyp surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 191-192)

**Botulinum toxin mechanism**: The toxin's heavy chain mediates endocytosis into the presynaptic terminal and the light chain cleaves SNARE proteins (type A cleaves SNAP-25, type B cleaves synaptobrevin), blocking acetylcholine release and producing flaccid paralysis until collateral sprouting restores function in about 3 months. Seven serotypes (A-G) exist, and A and B are marketed. Type B (rimabotulinumtoxinB) starts faster, lasting shorter, stinging more and causing more dry mouth. ENT uses include adductor spasmodic dysphonia, sialorrhea, Frey syndrome, rhytids, hyperhidrosis and cricopharyngeal spasm. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 10, p 199)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **GPA workup and treatment**: Classic triad: necrotizing granulomas of the airway, systemic small/medium-vessel vasculitis and focal glomerulonephritis (rapidly progressive GN in about 75%). Rhinitis/crusting is the most common presenting symptom. Workup: cANCA/PR3 (supportive, not definitive), ESR/CRP, urinalysis for RBC casts or over 5 RBC/HPF, chest imaging and biopsy showing necrotizing granulomatous vasculitis. Induce remission with high-dose steroids plus cyclophosphamide or rituximab. Maintain with methotrexate, azathioprine or mycophenolate. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 219-220)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Relapsing polychondritis criteria**: Episodic painful chondritis (attacks resolve within about a week): auricular in about 50% with lobule sparing, nasal 15% (saddle nose), laryngotracheal 15% (airway collapse may need tracheostomy), nonerosive arthritis 50%, ocular 15%. McAdam criteria: bilateral auricular chondritis, nasal chondritis, laryngotracheal chondritis, seronegative nonerosive polyarthritis, ocular inflammation, cochleovestibular damage. Diagnose with 3 or more criteria, or 1 plus biopsy, or chondritis at 2 sites responding to steroids or dapsone. Treat with steroids, dapsone, colchicine or NSAIDs. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 221)

**Langerhans cell histiocytosis**: Clonal Langerhans cell proliferation (CD1a and S100 positive, Birbeck 'tennis racket' granules on EM) commonly presents in the temporal bone mimicking mastoiditis or chronic otitis with granulation, lytic lesions and facial palsy. Forms: eosinophilic granuloma (localized, older children/young adults, curettage or low-dose radiation), Hand-Schüller-Christian (triad of skull lesions, exophthalmos and diabetes insipidus in about 10%), and Letterer-Siwe (infants under 3, disseminated with hepatosplenomegaly, high mortality, chemotherapy). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 223-225)

**Eustachian tube dimensions and pressures**: The tube grows from about 17-18 mm and nearly horizontal at birth to about 35 mm at roughly 45 degrees in adults (cartilaginous anteromedial two thirds about 24 mm, bony one third about 11 mm, narrowest at the isthmus junction). It opens mainly by the tensor veli palatini (V3), assisted by the levator (X); in infants only the tensor is effective. Opening requires about 200-300 mm H2O; sustained -30 mm Hg for 15 minutes produces effusion; a differential of about 90 mm Hg can lock the tube shut (critical pressure, explaining descent barotrauma), and over about 100 mm Hg can rupture the TM; Valsalva generates about 20-40 mm Hg. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 13, p 239-240)

**When to mask**: Interaural attenuation is about 40-65 dB for supra-aural earphones, about 70 dB or more for inserts, and 0-10 dB for bone conduction. Mask the nontest ear for air conduction when the test-ear stimulus exceeds the nontest-ear bone threshold by 40 dB or more (70 dB with inserts), and for bone conduction whenever the test ear shows an air-bone gap over 10 dB. Use narrow-band noise for tones and speech-spectrum noise for speech. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 267)

**Degree scales and the AMA impairment formula**: Adults: normal to 25 dB HL, mild 26-40, moderate 41-55, moderately severe 56-70, severe 71-90, profound over 90; children use stricter limits (normal to 15 dB HL, slight 15-25). AMA monaural impairment = (average of 500, 1000, 2000, 3000 Hz minus 25) x 1.5%; binaural = (5 x better-ear % + poorer-ear %)/6. Percentages serve medicolegal purposes; descriptive terms better predict communication impact. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 276-278)

**Pseudohypacusis red flags and the Stenger test**: Clues: SRT better than PTA by over 10 dB, poor test-retest reliability (over 5 dB), acoustic reflexes at or within 5 dB of admitted thresholds, present OAEs (TEOAEs imply cochlear thresholds no worse than about 30-40 dB HL), a unilateral 'dead ear' without crossover responses, and half-word responses. The Stenger test (for interaural differences of at least 30 dB) presents a tone 5 dB above threshold in the good ear and 5 dB below admitted threshold in the poor ear; failure to respond is positive. False or exaggerated loss is about twice as common in children (typically about age 11, girls) and may signal psychosocial stress; ABR/ASSR estimates true thresholds. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 290-292)

**OSHA limits and hearing conservation**: OSHA permits 90 dBA for 8 hours with a 5-dB exchange rate (95 dBA for 4 h, 100 for 2 h, 105 for 1 h, 115 for 15 min or less), using time-weighted averages. Programs require exposure assessment (sound level meter, dosimeter), engineering/administrative controls, hearing protection, and baseline plus annual audiograms. Plugs and muffs attenuate about 20-40 dB, more at high frequencies. Musician plugs attenuate flatly. Shooters develop an asymmetric 4-kHz notch worse in the ear opposite the shoulder used to fire. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 14, p 294-295)

**VEMP technique and interpretation**: cVEMP measures an inhibitory saccular-inferior vestibular nerve reflex recorded from the tonically contracted ipsilateral SCM (P13 about 12 ms, N23 about 19 ms) using 500-1000 Hz tone bursts or clicks. It is unaffected by SNHL but abolished by even small conductive losses, may be absent in normal people over 60, and needs adequate SCM contraction. Asymmetry ratio = 100 x (larger - smaller)/(larger + smaller), normal up to about 40%. Normal threshold is about 90 dB nHL. Responses below 80 dB nHL or a present VEMP despite an air-bone gap suggest a third window (superior canal dehiscence). oVEMP (N10 from inferior oblique, best with gaze about 30 degrees up) reflects utricle-superior vestibular nerve function. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 15, p 309-312)

**Vascular anomalies compressing the airway**: Double aortic arch is a complete ring (larger right posterior arch) causing stridor, dysphagia and aspiration. Right arch with left ligamentum also forms a ring. Anomalous innominate artery compresses the anterior trachea. Aberrant right subclavian compresses the posterior esophagus only (dysphagia lusoria). At bronchoscopy, compressing a pulsatile anterior tracheal impression that dampens the right radial and right temporal pulses implicates the innominate artery. Dampening only the radial pulse implicates the subclavian. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 7, p 156-157)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Sarcoidosis head and neck patterns**: Laryngeal sarcoid is a pale, diffuse submucosal supraglottic (epiglottic) swelling. Sinonasal disease gives crusting and 'cobblestone' mucosa. Lupus pernio (violaceous plaques on nose, cheeks and ears) is pathognomonic. Löfgren syndrome is acute arthralgia, erythema nodosum and bilateral hilar adenopathy. Labs: elevated ACE, hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria. Biopsy shows noncaseating granulomas with Schaumann bodies. Chest staging 0-IV runs from no thoracic disease through hilar adenopathy and parenchymal involvement to fibrosis. Supraglottic lesions are observed unless obstructive. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 12, p 222-223)

**Calculating binaural hearing impairment**: average thresholds at 0.5, 1, 2 and 3 kHz for each ear. Monaural impairment = 1.5 x (PTA - 25 dB). Binaural impairment = [5 x (better-ear impairment) + (worse-ear impairment)] / 6, so the better ear is weighted five times more heavily. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 23, pp 448-449)

**Tuning-fork thresholds**: a negative Rinne at 256 Hz means an air-bone gap of at least 15 dB, at 512 Hz at least 25 dB, and at 1024 Hz at least 35 dB. Placing the fork on the teeth raises sensitivity by 5-10 dB. The maximal conductive component from stapes fixation is about 60 dB, and word recognition is usually 70% or better. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 23, p 445)

**Candidacy and contraindications**: a good candidate has an air-bone gap of at least 20 dB, a negative Rinne at 256 and 512 Hz (excellent if also negative at 1024 Hz) and discrimination of 70% or better. Always operate on the poorer-hearing ear first. Absolute contraindications are an only or better-hearing ear, TM perforation, active middle-ear infection, active Ménière disease and a prolapsed facial nerve. Relative contraindications include age under 18, poor eustachian tube function, an air-bone gap under 15 dB and occupations such as roofer, acrobat or scuba diver. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 23, pp 445-446)

**Steroid trial and responder definition**: give prednisone 60 mg/day for 4 weeks. A responder improves by 15 dB at one frequency or by 10 dB or more at two or more consecutive frequencies. Responders stay on full dose until hearing plateaus, then taper over about 8 weeks to a maintenance dose of 5-20 mg every other day. Nonresponders are tapered off. Second-line options are methotrexate, cyclophosphamide, etanercept and intratympanic steroids, although randomized trials showed no benefit from methotrexate maintenance or etanercept. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 23, p 447)

**Glasscock-Jackson classification**: for glomus tympanicum, type I is limited to the promontory, II fills the middle ear, III extends into the mastoid, and IV extends through the TM into the EAC or anterior to the ICA. For glomus jugulare, type I is small and involves the jugular bulb, middle ear and mastoid; II extends under the IAC; III reaches the petrous apex; IV extends beyond the apex into the clivus or infratemporal fossa (each type can have intracranial extension). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 24, p 454)

**SDH genetics and imprinting**: SDH loss causes pseudohypoxia, which upregulates HIF-1 alpha. SDHD (PGL1) and SDHAF2 (PGL2) are maternally imprinted, so the tumor appears only when the mutation is inherited from the father and can seem to skip a generation. SDHD carries the highest head and neck penetrance (91-98%) and causes multiple tumors. SDHB (PGL4) carries the highest malignancy risk (about 13-23%) and adrenal risk. Up to 30% of paragangliomas are familial, and about 10% are multicentric. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 24, pp 452-453)

**Functional tumors and malignancy**: 5% or fewer secrete catecholamines. Screen with plasma free or urine fractionated metanephrines (current Endocrine Society guidance, the book also lists urine VMA), because an unrecognized secreting tumor can cause a hypertensive crisis at induction. Levels must be about 5 times normal to cause symptoms. Prepare secreting tumors with preoperative alpha blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) before any beta blocker, and keep IV phentolamine for intraoperative crises. Malignancy occurs in 2-4%, is highest in vagal tumors, and is defined by metastasis to non-neuroendocrine tissue such as nodes, bone or lung, not by histology. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 24, p 452, 455)

**Facial nerve hemangioma vs schwannoma**: hemangioma is the second most common facial nerve tumor and is centered at the geniculate ganglion. It causes facial weakness out of proportion to its size, can present as sudden palsy, and rarely affects hearing. On CT a hemangioma shows an infiltrative, erosive lesion with stippled intralesional calcification and a ground-glass look; a schwannoma smoothly remodels bone. Resect hemangiomas early (a small geniculate lesion can often be peeled off the nerve), because the longer the preoperative weakness, the worse the result after grafting. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 24, pp 457, 459)

**Keros numbers and the weakest point of the skull base**: Keros type 1 olfactory fossa depth is 1-3 mm (second most common), type 2 is 4-7 mm (most common) and type 3 is 8-16 mm (rare, highest CSF-leak risk). The lateral lamella is weakest where the anterior ethmoid artery pierces it, about one-tenth as strong as the fovea. The fovea slopes about 15 degrees downward from anterior to posterior and from lateral to medial, so the posteromedial ethmoid roof is lowest. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 26, pp 485, 492)

**Ethmoid artery measurements**: the AEA leaves the orbit between the superior oblique and medial rectus about 24 mm behind the anterior lacrimal crest. The PEA is about 12 mm further back, and the optic canal about 6 mm behind that (the 24-12-6 rule). The AEA canal is dehiscent in about 40% and may hang in a mesentery below the skull base. The AEA marks the posterior limit of the frontal recess and is often in the posterior wall of a supraorbital ethmoid cell. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 26, pp 485-486, 491)

**Sphenoid pneumatization and wall dehiscence**: the sellar type, pneumatized past the tuberculum, is most common. The presellar type is next, and the conchal type is rare. Arrested pneumatization, a nonexpansile region of fatty marrow with sclerotic margins, is an incidental finding that can be mistaken for a skull-base lesion. The ICA is partly dehiscent in about 25% and the optic nerve in about 6%. The sphenoid ostium lies medial to the superior turbinate, about 1.5 cm above the choanal arch and about 7 cm from the anterior nasal spine at 30 degrees. The posterior septal artery crosses the rostrum below the ostium. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 26, pp 493-495)

**UPSIT scoring and bedside tests**: the UPSIT is a 40-item, self-administered, age- and sex-normed scratch-and-sniff test. Scores of 35-40 are normal, 19-34 microsmia, 6-18 anosmia, and 5 or less suggests malingering, because even an anosmic patient scores about 10 by chance. Confirm malingering with a trigeminal stimulant such as ammonia, which an anosmic patient still senses. In the alcohol sniff test a normal subject detects the pad at about 30 cm. Avoid topical anesthetic before testing (decongestant does not affect smell). Coronal MRI through the olfactory bulbs, tracts and frontal lobes is the study of choice for a suspected neural cause. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 27, pp 505-506)

**Guideline version difference and adjuncts**: K.J. Lee (citing the AAO-HNSF guideline) offers observation for mild disease with assured follow-up and antibiotics for moderate-severe disease (persistent or worsening symptoms or temperature over 38 C), which is the older 2007 framing. Since 2015 the guideline has offered watchful waiting regardless of severity, and the 2025 update recommends watchful waiting with assured follow-up for all uncomplicated ABRS, matching the site. Both agree that amoxicillin with or without clavulanate is first line (5-7 days in adults). In penicillin allergy, doxycycline or a respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin) is the alternative. Intranasal steroids, saline irrigation and analgesics are options for symptom relief. Oral corticosteroids are not recommended, and decongestants and antihistamines lack evidence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 28, p 510)

**Cavernous sinus thrombosis and SOF syndrome**: cavernous sinus thrombosis causes bilateral signs (chemosis, proptosis, ptosis, complete ophthalmoplegia, V1 pain or numbness, papilledema) with spiking fevers. MR venography, showing absent flow in the sinus, is the gold standard, and anticoagulation is controversial. Superior orbital fissure syndrome (CN III, IV, VI and V1, with a fixed dilated pupil) without vision loss needs emergent drainage. Canthotomy/cantholysis decompresses an orbit under acute pressure. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 28, p 512)

**Patient selection and field optimization for CRS surgery**: operate after appropriate medical therapy, with persistent CT or endoscopic disease; obtain the CT at least 4 weeks after starting medical therapy. Encourage smoking cessation because smoking worsens scarring. Give oral steroids for 5-7 days preoperatively in polyp patients. Reduce bleeding with head-up positioning, TIVA, controlled blood pressure and warm saline irrigation. Remove osteitic bone. Steroid-eluting frontal recess implants reduce polypoid recurrence. Image guidance is indicated for revision surgery, distorted anatomy and teaching. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 29, pp 521-522)

**Bent and Kuhn criteria (1994)**: diagnosis requires all 5 major criteria. These are type I hypersensitivity to fungi; nasal polyposis; characteristic CT (heterogeneous hyperattenuation, expansion or erosion); eosinophilic mucin without tissue invasion; and a positive fungal stain. The minor criteria support the diagnosis: asthma, unilateral predominance, bone erosion, positive fungal culture, Charcot-Leyden crystals and serum eosinophilia. An aspirate of eosinophilic mucin is the most sensitive specimen. On MRI the mucin is T1 iso-to-hypointense with a T2 signal void, and the mucosa enhances peripherally while the mucin does not. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 30, pp 531-533)

**Biopsy and imaging specifics**: frozen-section biopsy of the anteroinferior middle turbinate is about 85% sensitive and 100% specific, and multiple sites raise the yield. Silver (GMS) or calcofluor-white stains are needed because H&E and Gram stains miss fungi with sparse cytoplasm. A negative biopsy does not exclude disease when suspicion is high. Early noncontrast CT shows unilateral turbinate, septal or nasal-wall mucosal thickening. Periantral fat stranding (premaxillary, retromaxillary, PPF, orbit) is an early warning, and bone erosion is late. On contrast MRI, the 'black turbinate sign' is nonenhancing, necrotic mucosa. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 30, pp 536-537)

**Antifungal selection**: amphotericin B is empiric first-line and the drug of choice for Mucorales. The conventional form is about 1 mg/kg/day and the liposomal/lipid form about 5 mg/kg/day; lipid forms are less nephrotoxic, penetrate the CNS better and may improve survival. Voriconazole is first-line for Aspergillus and Pseudallescheria; keep troughs at about 1-5.5 mcg/mL. Mucorales are intrinsically resistant to voriconazole, and A. terreus is resistant to amphotericin. Posaconazole and isavuconazole are alternatives with Mucorales activity and are used orally for 3-6 months after control. Itraconazole is not effective. G-CSF, granulocyte transfusion and hyperbaric oxygen are adjuncts with limited evidence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 30, pp 538-539)

**Prognosis numbers**: overall mortality for acute invasive disease is about 50%. Poor prognostic factors are advanced age, palatal or facial involvement, ANC under 500, CRP of 5.5 mg/dL or higher, altered mental status, renal or liver failure and intracranial spread. Better outcomes come with reversible immunosuppression (DKA), surgical resection and liposomal amphotericin. In a large review, endoscopic debridement survival was 64% versus 54% for open surgery, and orbital exenteration did not improve survival. Plan scheduled second-look endoscopy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 30, pp 534, 537)

**Comparative success rates**: posterior packing fails in about 38% and carries multiple complications (alar necrosis, sinusitis, otitis, hypoxia, aspiration and cardiopulmonary events), so it calls for monitored admission. Transantral IMA ligation fails in 10-15%. TESPAL succeeds in 95-98%: incise anterior to the crista ethmoidalis, raise a medially based flap and cauterize or clip the SPA branches, usually with next-day discharge. Embolization succeeds in about 88% with about a 12% complication rate, including stroke and blindness from ophthalmic artery occlusion. When no single source is seen, both IMAs are embolized. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 31, pp 556-557)
