topic: Systemic Disease of the Nose / Sinuses
text: **Rhinoscleroma**: caused by Klebsiella rhinoscleromatis, it is endemic in Central America, Africa, India and the Middle East and often begins at epithelial transition zones (vestibule, subglottis). It progresses through catarrhal (honeycomb crusts), granulomatous (painless masses, septal destruction) and sclerotic (stenosis, stridor) stages. Mikulicz cells (vacuolated macrophages containing bacilli) and Russell bodies (plasma cells with inclusions) are diagnostic. Treat with long-term tetracycline or fluoroquinolone plus debridement. Rhinosporidiosis (Rhinosporidium seeberi, South Asia, stagnant water) forms friable 'strawberry' polyps studded with white sporangia, and it is treated by excision plus dapsone. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 31, pp 551-552)

**AJCC maxillary sinus T staging**: T1 is confined to the mucosa with no bone involvement. T2 erodes bone, including the hard palate or middle meatus, but not the posterior wall or pterygoid plates. T3 involves the posterior wall, orbital floor or medial wall, subcutaneous tissue, pterygoid fossa or ethmoids. T4a involves the anterior orbit, cheek skin, pterygoid plates, infratemporal fossa, cribriform plate, or sphenoid or frontal sinus. T4b involves the orbital apex, dura, brain, middle cranial fossa, cranial nerves other than V2, nasopharynx or clivus. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 32, pp 567-568)

**ENB staging and outcomes**: modified Kadish staging: A = nasal cavity. B = paranasal sinuses. C = beyond the sinuses. D = nodal or distant metastases. The Dulguerov TNM grades T2 by cribriform erosion, T3 by orbit or anterior cranial fossa without dura, and T4 by dura or brain. ENB is about 5% of sinonasal cancers. Neck metastases are present in about 5% at diagnosis and occur in up to 20% over a lifetime. Treat with resection (endoscopic when no major orbital, brain or skin involvement) plus 55-65 Gy adjuvant RT. Two-year survival is about 75% for Kadish A/B and 25% for C in this text. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 32, pp 566-567)

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Reconstructive ladder by defect**: small defects (under 1 cm) can be closed with acellular grafts, free mucosal grafts or fat. Medium defects (1-3 cm) or intradural/high-flow defects (an opened cistern) need vascularized local flaps. Large defects (over 3 cm) may need regional or free flaps. If the nasoseptal flap is unavailable, options are the posterior-pedicled inferior turbinate flap (posterior lateral nasal artery; short pedicle, best for sellar/clival defects) and the middle turbinate flap (planum, sella, fovea). Others are the endoscopically tunneled pericranial flap (supraorbital/supratrochlear vessels; anterior skull base), the temporoparietal fascia flap tunneled through the pterygoid region (risk to the frontal branch and IMA), and free flaps (RFFF, ALT). Leak rates are about 15% with free grafts versus 3-6% with vascularized flaps. Reharvesting a nasoseptal flap does not raise leak or flap-loss rates. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 32, pp 571-573)

**Balloon sinus dilation consensus**: balloon dilation requires both sinonasal symptoms and CT evidence of disease, and a CT before the procedure. It is not appropriate for headache or OSA without CRS or RARS criteria, or for symptoms without CT findings. It is appropriate for RARS with CT ostial occlusion, as an adjunct to ESS in CRSsNP, for persistent disease after prior surgery, and in frontal sinusitis. It improves short-term QOL in limited CRSsNP. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 33, p 584)

**International frontal sinus surgery classification (EFSS grades 0-6)**: grade 0 is balloon dilation with no tissue removal. Grade 1 removes recess cells not obstructing the ostium, grade 2 removes cells directly obstructing it, and grade 3 removes cells pneumatizing through the ostium without enlarging it. Grade 4 enlarges the ostium, grade 5 enlarges it from the lamina to the septum, and grade 6 is the common floor resection (Draf III/modified Lothrop). Trephination is for complicated acute frontal sinusitis, osteomyelitis or far-lateral or supra-agger disease. The osteoplastic flap with obliteration is reserved for failures, and late mucoceles are common after it. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 33, pp 591-592)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Sellar/suprasellar differential**: pituitary adenoma accounts for about 90% of sellar tumors (10-15% of intracranial tumors); micro- is under 10 mm and macro- over 10 mm, and a dumbbell shape comes from the diaphragma sellae waist. Prolactinoma is the most common functional adenoma (about 30% of all, 50-60% of functional) and is treated first with cabergoline or bromocriptine. Rathke cleft cyst (about 15% incidentally, rarely symptomatic, F:M 2:1) is a nonenhancing midline cyst followed with yearly MRI. Craniopharyngioma is bimodal (5-15 and 45-60 years) and suprasellar. The adamantinomatous type (90%, children) is cystic, T1-bright and calcified; the papillary squamous type (adults) is solid. Parasellar meningioma shows a dural tail in 60-70%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 34, pp 604-606)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Intraoperative carotid injury protocol**: apply immediate pressure with a pattie and harvest crushed muscle (neck or thigh) to pack over the tear until bleeding stops. Cover it with a nasoseptal flap and gentle packing, and go directly to angiography (pseudoaneurysm, need for endovascular sacrifice or stent). Use a 'rescue' nasoseptal flap incision when a leak is possible: cut only the posterior third of the superior incision to protect the posterior septal pedicle. Postoperative CSF leak is the most common complication. Tension pneumocephalus presents with rapid neurologic decline and is less common than after open surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 34, pp 609-610)

**Less common histologies to know**: secretory carcinoma (formerly MASC) carries the pathognomonic ETV6-NTRK3 translocation, which can be targeted with TRK inhibitors. Polymorphous adenocarcinoma (formerly PLGA) is the second most common minor-gland malignancy, usually on the hard palate. It shows perineural spread but rarely nodal spread and has a good prognosis. Epithelial-myoepithelial carcinoma is mostly parotid, locally aggressive and of low mortality. Acinic cell carcinoma is a mostly low-grade parotid tumor (occasionally bilateral) that recurs locally more than regionally. Low-grade MEC is associated with t(11,19) (CRTC1-MAML2), and Ki-67 and HER2 mark high grade. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 35, pp 624-625)

**Metastases to the parotid**: cutaneous SCC is the most common, followed by melanoma, with Merkel cell, sebaceous and eccrine carcinoma less often. About 5% of cutaneous SCCs metastasize to the parotid or neck, usually within 1 year. Risk factors are size over 2 cm, thickness over 4 mm, recurrence, PNI and a preauricular or ear primary. Parotid metastasis carries about a 25% rate of clinical and 35% of occult neck disease, so treat the neck. Primaries posterior to the EAC seldom drain to the parotid. Parotid plus neck disease has a worse prognosis than parotid disease alone. Primary MALT lymphoma (marginal zone B-cell, defined by lymphoepithelial lesions) is the most common extranodal salivary lymphoma and occurs mainly in Sjögren patients. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 35, pp 625-626)

**Infectious and granulomatous sialadenitis**: mumps (paramyxovirus) peaks at age 4-6, is bilateral and can cause orchitis, encephalitis and SNHL. HIV causes benign lymphoepithelial cysts, which occur only in the parotid because only it contains intraglandular nodes; treat with ART or sclerotherapy, but a solid mass carries about a 40% malignancy risk. HIV can also cause DILS (sicca). Atypical mycobacteria affect children 16-36 months old with violaceous skin and a negative CXR, and are treated by excision or curettage. Actinomycosis (sulfur granules, sinus tracts) needs IV penicillin G for 6 weeks. Cat scratch disease (Bartonella, Warthin-Starry stain) is treated with observation or azithromycin. Toxoplasmosis is treated with pyrimethamine, sulfadiazine and folinic acid. Heerfordt syndrome is parotitis, uveitis and facial palsy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 35, pp 619-620)

**Sjögren and radiation xerostomia therapy**: Sjögren syndrome (HLA-B8/DR3) is diagnosed with anti-Ro/SSA, anti-La/SSB and a lower-lip minor salivary gland biopsy. Treat with hygiene, saliva substitutes and the muscarinic agonists pilocarpine and cevimeline. MRI is the most sensitive test for MALT lymphoma, and any solid mass needs a biopsy. Irreversible radiation damage to salivary glands begins at about 25 Gy (serous acini are lost first). Amifostine (a free-radical scavenger) is a radioprotector, and palifermin promotes epithelial growth. Submandibular gland transfer to the submental space, shielded during RT, reduces xerostomia. Sialendoscopy helps RAI-induced sialadenitis. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 35, pp 620, 626-627)

**Motility disorders**: manometry is diagnostic. Achalasia (loss of Auerbach plexus; Chagas disease is a secondary cause) shows aperistalsis with poor LES relaxation, and the esophagram shows a dilated esophagus with an air-fluid level and a 'bird's beak'. Exclude pseudoachalasia from a GEJ tumor by endoscopy. Treat with pneumatic dilation or myotomy, or botulinum toxin in poor surgical candidates. Diffuse esophageal spasm gives simultaneous distal contractions with normal LES relaxation and a 'corkscrew' or 'rosary bead' esophagram, and is treated with nitrates or calcium channel blockers. Nutcracker esophagus is high-amplitude peristalsis causing chest pain. In scleroderma, the distal two-thirds are aperistaltic with a very low LES pressure and severe GERD, Barrett and stricture risk. Polymyositis weakens the striated upper esophagus and UES. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 36, pp 658-659)

**Endoscopic grading (Zargar) and pathophysiology**: grade 0 is normal and grade I is edema or erythema. Grade IIA shows hemorrhage, erosions, blisters or superficial ulcers, and grade IIB is circumferential. Grade IIIA shows focal deep gray-black necrosis, IIIB extensive necrosis, and IV perforation. Grades 0-IIA almost always heal, while most IIB and III lesions stricture. Endoscope within 12-48 h. Avoid the period of greatest wall weakness (about days 5-15), and the wall stays fragile for about 3 weeks. Alkali causes liquefactive necrosis with deep burns, whereas acid causes coagulative necrosis but can perforate the stomach. Oropharyngeal burns do not predict esophageal injury. Long-term SCC surveillance is needed. Ingestions are bimodal: accidental at age 1-5 and intentional (more severe) in adolescents and adults. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 36, p 661)

**Vesiculobullous and ulcerative disease (DIF patterns)**: pemphigus vulgaris (anti-desmoglein 3, age 50+) causes suprabasilar acantholysis with a 'tombstone' basal layer and intercellular IgG/C3 ('chicken-wire') on DIF. Mucous membrane pemphigoid is subepithelial with linear basement-membrane IgG/IgA/C3, threatens the eyes and larynx, and is treated with topical steroids, dapsone or systemic immunosuppression. Oral lichen planus shows Wickham striae, Civatte bodies, a T-cell band and fibrinogen on DIF. It is linked to hepatitis C and carries a 0-10% SCC risk (erosive form). Erythema multiforme is triggered mainly by HSV, and also by sulfonamides, anticonvulsants and quinolones, and progresses to SJS/TEN. Aphthous ulcers are minor (under 1 cm, heal within 2 weeks), major (over 1 cm, up to 6 weeks, posterior) or herpetiform (multiple, under 2 mm). Associations include Behçet, Crohn, celiac, PFAPA, Sweet syndrome and B12/folate deficiency. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 36, pp 649-650, 654)

**Imaging numbers**: on a lateral neck film, retropharyngeal soft tissue at C2 thicker than 5 mm in a child or 7 mm in an adult suggests retropharyngeal infection; look for an air-fluid level and the epiglottic thumbprint sign. Contrast CT is the best study. Clinical examination alone misidentifies the spaces needing drainage in about 70%, yet about 25% of explorations find no pus because CT cannot reliably separate phlegmon from abscess. In adults, exclude cystic metastatic adenopathy (oropharyngeal primary) that mimics an abscess. Pulse oximetry is often normal even when the airway is critical. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 37, p 679)

**Airway and medical-trial thresholds**: for an at-risk airway (submandibular, parapharyngeal or retropharyngeal spaces), use a humidified face tent, IV steroids, nebulized epinephrine and ICU observation if the airway is more than 50% of normal caliber. Perform tracheotomy for progression or less than 50% caliber. Awake fiberoptic intubation needs a glottis that will pass a 6-mm scope. Choose elective tracheotomy if edema is expected to last more than 48 h. A medical trial suits intranodal abscesses, phlegmon, most pediatric cases and abscesses under 2.5 cm in one space. Re-image or drain if there is no improvement in 48-72 h. Continue IV therapy for 24 h after symptoms resolve, then about 2 weeks orally. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 37, pp 680-681)

**Other thyroiditides**: painless (silent/postpartum, subacute lymphocytic) thyroiditis is autoimmune and painless, occurs in up to 5% of postpartum women, causes self-limited thyrotoxicosis and leaves about 20% permanently hypothyroid. Acute suppurative thyroiditis (Staph, Strep, Enterobacter) often follows a URI. In children, recurrent left-sided episodes suggest a pyriform sinus fistula, so after treatment (antibiotics, drainage) evaluate with barium swallow, CT or endoscopy. Drug-induced thyroiditis is caused by amiodarone (type 1 iodine-induced hyperthyroidism vs type 2 destructive thyroiditis), interferon-alpha, IL-2, lithium and minocycline. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 38, p 698-699)

**Riedel thyroiditis (invasive fibrous thyroiditis)**: a rare IgG4-spectrum fibrosing process related to sclerosing cholangitis and retroperitoneal fibrosis. It produces a woody, fixed, nontender goiter with progressive dysphagia, tracheal compression and possible RLN palsy, usually in a euthyroid patient. Its hallmark is fibrosis extending outside the thyroid, so it mimics anaplastic carcinoma or lymphoma and needs a biopsy. An isthmusectomy can relieve compression; avoid aggressive resection because planes are lost, and steroids can help. Hashimoto disease: TPO antibodies in 70-90%, about 20% hypothyroid at presentation, Hürthle cell metaplasia, and any discrete nodule or rapid growth needs FNA (lymphoma risk). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 38, pp 697-699)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Subsite prognosis**: head and neck melanoma does worse than trunk/extremity melanoma, and within the head and neck the scalp carries the worst outlook, followed by the ear, then the cheek, with the neck the most favorable (scalp > ear > cheek > neck). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 771)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Biopsy method**: never shave or needle-biopsy a suspected primary melanoma, since depth cannot be measured. A small lesion can be excised with 1-2 mm margins; for larger lesions an incisional or punch biopsy through the thickest part preserves the borders for margin planning and avoids disturbing lymphatic drainage before lymphoscintigraphy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 772)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Vertical EAC line rule**: primaries anterior to a vertical line drawn up from the external auditory canal (anterior scalp, temple, face, ear) put the parotid nodes and levels IB-IV at risk; primaries behind that line (posterior scalp, retroauricular) drain to levels II-V plus the postauricular and suboccipital nodes. A therapeutic neck dissection for anterior-site disease adds superficial parotidectomy; chin and neck primaries do not need it; posterior-site disease requires a posterolateral dissection including postauricular/suboccipital nodes. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, pp 777-778)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Sentinel node technique**: lymphoscintigraphy is done 1-24 h before surgery by intradermal injection of Tc-99m sulfur colloid or Tc-99m tilmanocept (binds CD206 on macrophages/dendritic cells), with planar imaging or SPECT/CT; if mapped the day before, reinject about 1 h preop. Isosulfan blue can be added; with a gamma probe, keep removing nodes (typically 3-4) until bed counts fall to 10% of the hottest excised node. Nodes get H&E plus IHC (HMB-45, S-100, Melan-A). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 778)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Desmoplastic melanoma**: pure desmoplastic tumors rarely spread to lymph nodes, so sentinel node biopsy is not recommended; mixed desmoplastic lesions follow conventional SLNB criteria. Because of strong neurotropism, excise with wide margins (2 cm or more if feasible) and give adjuvant radiation for locoregional control. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 780)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Radiation for melanoma**: indications are postoperative RT after resection of palpable nodal disease, elective nodal RT for T1b-T4 N0 patients who cannot have SLNB/neck dissection, regional recurrence after prior dissection, and high-risk primaries (T4, desmoplastic). Melanoma responds best to a hypofractionated schedule, eg 6 Gy fractions to 30 Gy. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 779)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Hereditary risk**: Familial atypical mole/melanoma syndrome is linked to CDKN2A on 9p21 (encoding p16INK4a and p14ARF). The book says lifetime melanoma risk approaches 100% in affected families, but CDKN2A carriers have a lifetime risk of roughly 30-70%, depending on region. Xeroderma pigmentosum is autosomal recessive, a nucleotide-excision-repair defect that cannot fix UV thymine dimers, causing about a 1000-fold skin cancer risk, often before age 10. Giant congenital nevi (over 20 cm) carry a lifetime transformation risk the book puts at about 10% (recent series suggest a few percent) and can occur with neurocutaneous melanosis. The book says up to 80% of melanomas arise in a preexisting lesion, but meta-analysis shows only about 30% arise from a nevus and about 70% arise de novo. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, pp 768-769)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Subtypes**: superficial spreading is most common (about 75%); nodular (10-15%) has no radial phase, grows vertically fast, is often ulcerated and thick when small; lentigo maligna melanoma (5-10%) follows years of radial growth on sun-damaged facial skin and becomes invasive once it reaches the papillary dermis; acral lentiginous (about 10%) is unrelated to sun and is the most common type in patients with darker skin. Acral and mucosal melanomas more often carry c-kit mutations (potential imatinib target) than BRAF. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 769)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Pathology and labs**: melanoma stains with HMB-45, S-100, Melan-A and vimentin and is cytokeratin negative; it is a 'great mimicker' and belongs in the differential of any undifferentiated tumor. Mitotic rate is still reported but was dropped from AJCC 8th T staging. LDH is a nonspecific metastasis marker and modifies the M category (eg M1a(1) = elevated LDH); obtain metastatic imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis or PET-CT plus brain MRI) for stage III/IV, and consider it for lesions >4 mm, ulceration, satellitosis, or recurrence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, pp 771-772, 775)

topic: Cutaneous Melanoma of the Head & Neck
text: **Systemic agents to recognize**: BRAF inhibitors (vemurafenib, dabrafenib) are paired with MEK inhibitors (cobimetinib, trametinib) for BRAF V600-mutant disease. Ipilimumab blocks CTLA-4, and pembrolizumab and nivolumab block PD-1. In the adjuvant setting after resection, nivolumab, pembrolizumab and (for BRAF V600) dabrafenib-trametinib are approved, and neoadjuvant pembrolizumab improved event-free survival over adjuvant therapy alone in resectable stage III-IV disease (SWOG S1801). Talimogene laherparepvec (T-VEC) is an intralesional, GM-CSF-producing oncolytic herpes virus for unresectable recurrent cutaneous or nodal disease. Dacarbazine gives only 10-20% responses. Targeted BRAF drugs are not immunomodulators (classic distractor). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, pp 779-780)

**Melanoma of unknown primary**: melanoma found in neck or parotid nodes with no identifiable primary (possibly a regressed lesion) is staged with a full metastatic workup and treated like stage III disease: neck dissection (with parotidectomy when the parotid basin is involved) This text adds postoperative hypofractionated radiation. Current NCCN care for resected stage III disease is adjuvant anti-PD-1 immunotherapy (or BRAF/MEK therapy for BRAF-mutant tumors), with RT reserved for high regional-recurrence risk because it improves regional control but not survival. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 43, p 783)

**Subglottic SCC**: rare (about 1%), usually poorly differentiated and advanced at presentation with stridor or dyspnea. It spreads to level VI (pretracheal/paratracheal) nodes and the superior mediastinum, so treatment must include level VI dissection plus hemithyroidectomy or total thyroidectomy (and corresponding radiation fields) to reduce peristomal/stomal recurrence. Staging: T1 subglottis only, T2 extends to cords with normal/impaired mobility, T3 cord fixation, T4a through cricoid or thyroid cartilage. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 791, 794)

**Verrucous carcinoma**: 1-2% of laryngeal cancers; exophytic, well-differentiated keratinizing tumor with pushing rather than infiltrative margins. It does not metastasize unless foci of conventional SCC are present, so treatment is surgical excision without neck dissection, and radiation is generally unnecessary. Superficial biopsies are often read as benign, so a deep, generous biopsy is needed. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, p 790)

**Distant spread and chest findings**: hematogenous metastases go most often to lung, then liver, then bone; lymphatic distant spread is to the mediastinum. Risk is higher with supraglottic or subglottic than glottic primaries, advanced stage, and neck disease. An isolated pulmonary nodule on staging CT is more likely a second primary lung cancer than a laryngeal metastasis. Pretreatment PET/CT changes management in 20-30% of advanced cases; MRI is more sensitive for cartilage invasion. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 787, 791)

**Dysplasia grading and risk**: mild dysplasia is confined to the basal third of the epithelium, moderate reaches two-thirds, severe exceeds two-thirds, and carcinoma in situ is full-thickness without basement membrane breach. Malignant transformation occurs in about 7-11% of mild/moderate dysplasia and about 18% of severe dysplasia (30% in older series), over a variable 3-10 years. Severe dysplasia and CIS behave alike clinically. Endoscopic excision is first-line. Radiation is an alternative for frail or multifocal disease. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, p 789)

**Nodal numbers**: 25-50% of supraglottic cancers have cervical nodes at presentation, rising with T stage (about 10% T1, 29% T2, 38% T3, 57% T4). Occult nodal rates are roughly 0% T1, 20% T2, 25% T3, 40% T4. Because drainage is bilateral, even early N0 supraglottic cancer gets bilateral level II-IV elective dissection or bilateral necks in the radiation field. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 790, 792-793)

**Outcome numbers**: radiation (60-70 Gy over about 6 weeks) achieves 90-98% local control for T1 and favorable T2 glottic cancer, but failure approaches 30% for T2 lesions with impaired cord mobility. Transoral laser microsurgery gives similar control (about 88% 5-year DFS for T1-T2), saves radiation for recurrence, but generally yields poorer voice; its contraindications include cord fixation or bilateral impaired motion, interarytenoid involvement, poor pulmonary status, and inadequate exposure. Occult nodal rates are under 5% for T1-T2 and 20-25% for T3-T4. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 790-792)

**Trial details**: the VA larynx study (1991) compared induction cisplatin/5-FU then RT (responders) versus total laryngectomy plus PORT; 2-year survival was equal (68%) and 64% of the chemo arm kept the larynx. Nonsurgical patients recurred more locoregionally, surgical patients more distantly, and T4, fixed-cord and gross cartilage-invasion tumors fared worse without surgery. RTOG 91-11 at 10 years: concurrent cisplatin-RT had the best locoregional control and larynx preservation, laryngectomy-free survival was better with both chemo arms than RT alone, yet overall survival did not differ (possibly from late toxicity). (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 793-794)

**Supracricoid laryngectomy specifics**: an option for select T3 tumors not suitable for transoral resection, reconstructed by cricohyoidopexy (CHP) or, when the epiglottis is spared, cricohyoidoepiglottopexy (CHEP). Contraindications are involvement of both arytenoids, subglottic extension reaching the cricoid, hyoid invasion, and posterior arytenoid mucosal invasion. Good pulmonary function is required. Open supraglottic laryngectomy is now mainly a salvage operation for T1-T2 N0-1 tumors with mobile cords, and nearly all patients aspirate initially. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, p 792)

**Recurrent laryngeal cancer**: about half of laryngeal recurrences can be salvaged. Suspect recurrence with new edema, worsening cord mobility, mass, ulceration, pain or dysphonia. Obtain PET/CT 10-12 weeks after therapy (earlier scans have more false positives) and confirm by biopsy, recognizing biopsy after chemoradiation raises chondritis risk. Salvage usually requires total laryngectomy because recurrences are insidious and multifocal. Select early failures may have conservation surgery. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 44, pp 795)

**Lip cancer numbers**: the lip is the most common oral cavity cancer site. More than 95% are SCC and about 95% arise on the lower lip, with a male predominance of roughly 20-35:1 for the lower lip and 5:1 for the upper lip. BCC is relatively more common on the upper lip, but SCC still predominates there. Regional metastasis occurs in about 10% and later than at other oral sites. Upper lip and commissure cancers carry 10-20% lower survival. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 816-817)

**Defect-size ladder**: realign the vermilion and close in four layers. Under one-fourth to one-third of the lip: V or wedge excision with primary closure. One-fourth to one-half: lip-switch flaps, Abbe when the commissure is spared and Estlander when the defect involves the commissure. One-half to two-thirds: Karapandzic flap (innervated, preserves sphincter but causes microstomia). Over two-thirds to total: Bernard-Burow or Gillies fan flaps, or free tissue transfer. Postoperative RT is indicated for T3-T4, perineural invasion, positive margins, or nodal metastases. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, p 817)

**Nodal pattern**: oral tongue SCC metastasizes most often to upper jugular nodes (about 73%), then submandibular (18%), middle jugular (18%), and submental (9%). About 25-33% of patients have clinically evident nodes and 20-25% occult nodes. Lesions of the midline dorsum or ventral tongue have greater bilateral risk and warrant bilateral neck dissection. Elective dissection should cover at least levels I-III. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 818-819)

**Extranodal extension and survival**: in oral tongue cancer, 5-year disease-specific/overall survival is about 88%/75% for pN0, 65%/50% for pN+ without ECS, and 48%/30% for pN+ with ECS. Overall, stage I-II 5-year survival is 60-75% versus 25-40% for stage III-IV. The rising incidence in young patients (4% in 1971 to 18% in 1993) has no clear risk-factor explanation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 817, 819)

**Mandible decision rules**: tumor reaching only gingiva is resected with periosteum as the deep margin. Tumor involving periosteum or minimal cortical erosion needs at least a marginal mandibulectomy (alveolar cuff or inner/outer cortex). Medullary invasion requires segmental mandibulectomy. An edentulous, atrophic mandible more often needs segmental resection because the remaining bone stock after a marginal cut risks fracture. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 818-819)

**Hypopharynx numbers**: over 90% are SCC. Pyriform sinus cancers dominate in the US (60-70%), while postcricoid cancers predominate in parts of Europe and are linked to Plummer-Vinson syndrome (iron deficiency anemia, dysphagia, webs, glossitis, angular stomatitis in women 30-50). About 60-75% have palpable nodes at presentation, medial pyriform wall tumors spread to the larynx and contralateral neck more than lateral wall tumors, distant metastasis develops in about 20%, and synchronous esophageal cancer has been reported in up to 20%, so esophagoscopy is important. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 827-828)

**Surgical options**: selected T1-T2 pyriform sinus cancers can undergo extended partial laryngopharyngectomy (Ogura), which keeps the cricoid and contralateral arytenoid/cord; small posterior pharyngeal wall tumors not fixed to prevertebral fascia can be removed via transhyoid or labiomandibular glossotomy approaches; postcricoid tumors usually need total laryngopharyngectomy (or laryngopharyngoesophagectomy). Reconstruction: primary closure if enough mucosa remains, pectoralis/RFFF/ALT patch for partial defects, tubed fasciocutaneous flap or free jejunum for circumferential defects, and gastric pull-up when resection extends below the thoracic inlet. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, p 828)

**WHO classification**: K.J. Lee uses the older numbering: type I keratinizing SCC (sporadic, tobacco/alcohol-related, about 25% in North America), type II nonkeratinizing (about 12%), and type III undifferentiated (lymphoepithelioma/Schmincke tumor, most common, about 63%, more frequent in younger patients). The current WHO system names these keratinizing SCC and nonkeratinizing carcinoma (differentiated or undifferentiated), plus basaloid SCC. Nonkeratinizing tumors are EBV-driven and endemic in southern China, Southeast Asia, North Africa and the Mediterranean, and Alaskan/Aleut populations, with HLA haplotypes and nitrosamines in salted foods as cofactors. Elevated IgA antibodies to viral capsid antigen or early antigen support diagnosis and screening. About 20% occur before age 30. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, p 829)

**Spread and failure pattern**: about 87% present with palpable nodes (20% bilateral), involving jugulodigastric, posterior triangle, and retropharyngeal nodes. Parotid nodes can be reached via Eustachian tube lymphatics, and low jugular/supraclavicular nodes carry a poor prognosis. Cranial neuropathies (especially III-VI) signal skull base or cavernous extension. CN XII and cervical sympathetic (Horner) involvement occur with further spread. NPC has the highest distant metastasis rate of any head and neck cancer (25-30%), now a leading cause of death. Concurrent chemoradiation raises 5-year survival from about 36-58% (RT alone) to 70-80%. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 829-830)

**Surgery in NPC**: reserved for radiation failures. Residual or recurrent nodal disease after radiation is managed with radical or modified radical neck dissection. Recurrent primaries can be resected by endoscopic nasopharyngectomy (limited lateral extension) or open approaches: Fisch infratemporal fossa, combined transpalatal/transmaxillary/transcervical, or maxillary swing. Re-irradiation with IMRT or protons is an alternative. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, p 830)

topic: Head & Neck Cancer Surveillance / Second Primaries
text: **Numbers to know**: second primary tumors (synchronous or metachronous) occur in about 5-10%, half in the head and neck and about 20% in the lung, with ongoing risk of about 4-5% per year, so surveillance continues for life. Distant metastasis occurs in about 15% overall (5-7% at diagnosis), more with higher N stage, number of nodes, ENE, advanced T stage, locoregional recurrence, and hypopharyngeal primaries; an isolated lung metastasis may be resected. New pain is a sensitive warning sign of recurrence. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 815-816)

**Soft palate cancer**: under 2% of mucosal head and neck cancers, usually on the oral surface so found early, but nodal risk exceeds 40% even for small midline lesions (clinical nodes up to 50%, bilateral 5-15%) to levels II-IV and retropharyngeal nodes. Second primary rates are high (about 13% synchronous, 26% metachronous). Larger tumors are usually treated with (chemo)radiation to avoid velopharyngeal insufficiency, with bilateral neck treatment in advanced cases. Surgical defects are best reconstructed with a thin radial forearm flap. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 45, pp 824-825)

topic: Radiation Therapy Principles for Head & Neck Surgeons
text: **Dose tiers to memorize**: about 50 Gy in 25 fractions sterilizes subclinical disease (eg, the elective N0 neck). 60 Gy/30 fx treats the postoperative bed and intermediate-risk nodal levels. 66 Gy/33 fx is used for close or positive margins. 70 Gy/35 fx treats gross disease with curative intent. Standard fractions are 1.8-2.0 Gy, 5 days a week over 6-7 weeks. 1 Gy = 1 joule absorbed per kg. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 47, p 842)

**Early glottic RT technique**: T1-2 N0 glottic cancer is treated with a small (about 5-6 cm square) field from the hyoid to the cricoid without elective nodal coverage or chemotherapy. Randomized data favor fraction sizes above 2 Gy; a common regimen is 63 Gy in 2.25 Gy fractions for T1N0 and 65.25 Gy in 2.25 Gy fractions for T2N0. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 47, p 844)

**Package time**: the interval from surgery to completion of postoperative radiation should ideally be 11 weeks or less, which in practice means starting the 6-6.5 week course about 4-5 weeks after surgery. Altered (accelerated) fractionation improves control in advanced disease when chemotherapy cannot be given, but adding it to concurrent chemotherapy adds toxicity without benefit. In the pooled RTOG 9501/EORTC 22931 analysis, level IV-V nodes from oral cavity or oropharynx primaries are among the features that merit considering chemoradiation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 46, p 838; Ch 47, pp 843, 846)

**Reirradiation**: surgery is preferred for in-field failures. When unresectable, reirradiation is potentially curative only in a minority (2-year survival about 10-30%). Recurrence under 1 year after the first course suggests radioresistance and poor candidacy, whereas a new primary in a field treated many years earlier is ideal. Typical practice treats gross tumor only (no elective volumes) to about 60-66 Gy with concurrent radiosensitizing chemotherapy, often hyperfractionated (eg, 1.2 Gy twice daily 6 hours apart to 60 Gy) to reduce late effects. After salvage surgery, adjuvant reirradiation with chemotherapy improved locoregional control and DFS but not OS, with about 40% grade 3-4 late toxicity at 2 years. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 47, pp 846-847)

topic: Systemic Therapy Foundations in Head & Neck Cancer
text: **Induction and concurrent evidence**: cisplatin/5-FU induction gives high response rates in untreated disease but only 5-15% in previously treated disease. Adjuvant chemotherapy after definitive therapy has been abandoned except in nasopharyngeal cancer. TAX 324 showed TPF induction beat PF (better PFS and OS), but DeCIDE and PARADIGM found no OS gain for TPF before chemoradiation versus chemoradiation alone, and the MACH-NC meta-analysis confirmed concurrent chemoradiation is superior to induction plus RT. Adding 5-FU or taxanes to concurrent cisplatin adds mucositis without benefit, so single-agent platinum is the concurrent standard. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 46, pp 834-837)

**RTOG 0129 benchmark**: HPV-associated oropharyngeal cancers had 3-year OS of 82.4% versus 57.1% for HPV-negative tumors; patients with HPV-positive disease and more than 10 pack-years of smoking have an intermediate, worse prognosis than nonsmokers. De-escalated therapy should be offered only on clinical trials; small, well-lateralized tonsil primaries with minimal nodal disease can receive ipsilateral-only radiation. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 47, pp 845-846)

**Molecular contrast (TCGA)**: HPV-negative HNSCC is defined by TP53 mutation (about 79%), CDKN2A/p16 loss (9p21 deletion), 11q13 amplification (cyclin D1, cortactin), and less often EGFR, FGFR1, NOTCH1, FAT1, CASP8/HRAS alterations. HPV-positive tumors have wild-type p53 (degraded by E6 with E6AP) and high p16 (because E7 inactivates Rb), frequent PIK3CA activation, and TRAF3 or CYLD inactivation, which occur only in HPV-positive tumors and mark a better-prognosis subgroup. Both share 3p and 8p loss and 3q and 8q gains. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 48, pp 849-854)

**Stage-based RT**: K.J. Lee gives radiation alone for T1N0 disease and cisplatin chemoradiation for T2N0 or higher, traditionally followed by three cycles of adjuvant chemotherapy. **Current view (NCCN)**: stage I (T1N0) gets RT alone, T2N0 gets RT with concurrent cisplatin considered for adverse features, and T1-2 N1 or any T3-T4 or N2-N3 disease gets concurrent cisplatin chemoradiation, preferably with induction gemcitabine-cisplatin, or with adjuvant chemotherapy. All patients receive coverage of levels II and V and the retropharyngeal nodes because subclinical nodal rates are high. NPC is the one head and neck site where adjuvant chemotherapy after chemoradiation has persisted. (K.J. Lee 12e, Ch 46, p 834, Ch 47, p 845)

**Window placement**: this chapter places the true vocal fold closer to the inferior border of the thyroid lamina than its midpoint (Cummings uses the midpoint rule but measures from a 'true inferior border', which gives a similar low window). A standard window is about 6 x 13 mm (5 x 10 mm in women), 3 mm above the inferior border and set back about 7 mm (men) or 5 mm (women) from the anterior midline. A higher window medializes the false fold or ventricle. Incise the inner perichondrium or medialization is limited. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Silastic Medialization Laryngoplasty for Unilateral Vocal Fold Paralysis", p 402)

**Timing**: in UVFP, framework surgery usually follows 6–9 months of observation. Go earlier for nerve transection, severe degeneration on LEMG, or malignancy-related paralysis, but wait about 1 month for fold atrophy, using temporary injection meanwhile. Best candidates have a phonatory gap of about 2–3 mm or more. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Principles of Laryngeal Framework Surgery", p 391)

**Rosen nine-lesion classification**: mid-membranous lesions are defined by morphology, stroboscopic wave, response to voice rest/therapy, and operative findings. The nine are nodules, subepithelial cyst, ligament cyst, subepithelial fibrous mass, ligament fibrous mass, polyp, reactive lesion, pseudocyst, and nonspecific vocal fold lesion. Nodules and reactive lesions respond to therapy; cysts, fibrous masses, and polyps do not. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Pathological Conditions of the Vocal Fold", p 25)

**Pseudocyst and NSVFL**: a pseudocyst is a translucent, blister-like superficial lesion caused by glottic insufficiency (contralateral scar, paresis); treat by excision plus correction of the insufficiency. A nonspecific vocal fold lesion persists after therapy even though the voice has normalized; by definition it needs no surgery, only follow-up. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Pathological Conditions of the Vocal Fold", p 28)

**Ligament vs subepithelial cyst**: a ligament-level cyst sits deep, is often seen better in abduction, markedly reduces the wave, and recovers more slowly than a subepithelial cyst or polyp. Dissect the epithelial cover off the cyst (medial side) before separating it from the ligament. Do not use subepithelial infusion for polyps, because it blurs the lesion margin. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Vocal Fold Cyst and Vocal Fold Fibrous Mass", p 166)

topic: Systemic / Granulomatous Disease Manifestations in ENT
text: **Laryngeal rheumatologic disease**: 25–53% of RA patients have laryngeal involvement, either cricoarytenoid arthritis (hypomobility) or 'bamboo nodes', which are transverse submucosal bands on the mid-fold. Treat bamboo nodes systemically first, with optional local steroid. Excision is difficult and scars. In SLE, laryngeal edema occurs in up to 28% and fold paralysis in 11%. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 53)

**Timing window**: most UVFP patients who will recover motion do so by about 8 months, so LEMG later than that is rarely useful. Prognostic LEMG is most valuable 2–6 months after injury. LEMG predicts non-recovery (absent reinnervation) better than it predicts good recovery. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 38)

**Nimodipine (off-label)**: in acute paralysis of less than 30 days with poor LEMG prognosis, nimodipine has been associated with more than 60% motion recovery versus about 30% in historical controls. About 30% need the dose stopped or reduced. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 39)

**Compensation patterns**: supraglottic hyperfunction can give a rough, pitch-locked voice that mimics primary MTD. A 'paralytic falsetto' raises F0 by about 85 Hz. Unmask the paralysis with 'unloading' tasks such as nasal humming, /u/, or inspiratory phonation, plus the ee-sniff maneuver. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 36)

**Exam pitfalls**: the interarytenoid gets bilateral RLN input, so slight adduction of a paralyzed fold does not prove partial innervation. Fold position does not predict lesion level (it reflects synkinesis). An anteriorly tipped arytenoid usually reflects PCA denervation, not dislocation. In a high vagal lesion the palate pulls toward the intact side. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 37)

**Etiology and low-yield tests**: causes are iatrogenic surgery about 46%, idiopathic about 18%, non-laryngeal malignancy about 14%, and intubation about 4%. Vinca alkaloid neuropathy is dose-related and recovers 4–6 weeks after the drug is stopped or reduced. Screening serologies, barium swallow, and thyroid scans have essentially no yield. Image the vagus/RLN path from skull base to upper chest with CT or MRI. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 34)

**Vocal fold paresis**: suspect it with loss of projection, vocal fatigue, and loss of upper range. Stroboscopic clues are mild bowing, incomplete closure, a prolonged open phase, increased amplitude, an asynchronous 'chasing' wave, false fold hyperadduction, and a capacious ventricle. A trial temporary injection that improves the voice supports the diagnosis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 39)

**Parkinson vs presbylaryngis**: PD can look identical (bowing in about 87%) but adds tremor and monotone. PD patients are poor augmentation candidates, so LSVT is primary therapy. Presbylaryngis is sex-specific: men mainly lose muscle (respond to augmentation), whereas women mainly thicken the lamina propria (pitch change, poor response). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic Insufficiency: Vocal Fold Paralysis, Paresis, and Atrophy", p 41)

**Expiratory Disproportion Index**: EDI = FEV1 (L) / PEFR (L/s) x 100. Values over 50 suggest clinically significant upper airway stenosis. Office topical anesthesia for airway exams: 4% lidocaine via the scope channel, with a maximum of about 300–400 mg (7–10 mL of 4% in a 70-kg adult). (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic and Subglottic Stenosis: Evaluation and Surgical Planning", p 46)

**Choosing a technique**: endoscopic treatment needs no malacia, cartilage collapse, or external compression, a stenosis no more than 2–3 cm long, an identifiable lumen, and a trach site away from the stenosis. A T-tube needs about 7–8 mm of normal airway below the folds. Open surgery is for failures, lengths over 3 cm, no lumen, or malacia. Post-trach stenosis usually appears 1–3 months after decannulation. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Glottic and Subglottic Stenosis: Evaluation and Surgical Planning", p 48)

**Endoscopic technique numbers**: make narrow CO2 radial cuts, keeping mucosal strips between them. Typical balloon diameters are about 12–14 mm (women) and 14–16 mm (men) with noncompliant balloons, inflated 30–60 s with the proximal end at least 5 mm below the folds. Inject triamcinolone 40 mg/mL into the intact strips, ideally before cutting. Mitomycin is 0.4 mg/mL for 4–5 min, with weak adult evidence. Avoid reintubating at the end. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Subglottic/Tracheal Stenosis: Endoscopic Management", p 294)

**Serial office steroid injection**: for idiopathic stenosis, give submucosal triamcinolone 40 mg/mL by percutaneous needle under endoscopic view or through a channeled scope. A typical series is monthly for about 6 injections, then every 3–4 months for a year if the lumen holds. Triamcinolone stays visible in tissue for months. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Awake Treatment of Laryngotracheal Stenosis", p 380)

**Timing and risk**: PGS appears 4–8 weeks after extubation. Risk rises sharply after about 10 days of intubation but has occurred after only 4 days, and is linked to large (8.0) tubes in men. In PGS the thyroarytenoid EMG is normal, whereas bilateral paralysis shows reduced recruitment, synkinesis, and large polyphasic potentials. About 50% of type 1 synechiae regain mobility after lysis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Posterior Glottic Stenosis: Endoscopic Approach", p 275)

**Staged widening**: wait about 9–12 months, or less with poor LEMG, then operate on the less mobile side. Start with posterior transverse cordotomy (3–4 mm into the false fold; a 2–3 mm notch gives a large airway gain) or medial arytenoidectomy. Reserve total arytenoidectomy, which has the most aspiration, for failures. Suture lateralization suits early paralysis (first 2 months), and repeat adductor botulinum toxin every 3–4 months is a nondestructive option. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Bilateral Vocal Fold Paralysis", p 264)

**Testing specifics**: dual-probe hypopharyngeal-esophageal impedance-pH (HEMII-pH) is abnormal with 6 or more proximal esophageal or 2 or more hypopharyngeal events. GI reports that use distal GERD norms may miss LPR. The Bravo capsule detects acid only. The oropharyngeal (Restech) probe does not directly measure reflux events. Barium swallow and EGD do not diagnose LPR. This chapter calls an RSI over 10 abnormal, but the validated cutoff is over 13. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Disease", p 64)

**PPI nuances**: about 36% of empiric-PPI failures still have nonacid LPR, so treatment failure does not exclude reflux. Taper PPIs, because about 25% get rebound acid hypersecretion. Alginates help nonacid reflux. Fundoplication chosen by full-column impedance helps about 80%. Consider Barrett screening even without heartburn. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Laryngopharyngeal Reflux Disease", p 63)

**Specific laryngitides**: inhaled steroids cause dysphonia in 5–50% of users (chemical irritation or Candida plaques that mimic leukoplakia); use a spacer, reduce the dose, and give antifungals. MRSA is a common bacterial cause. Idiopathic ulcerative laryngitis follows a URI with bilateral mid-fold ulcers and severe cough; it resolves in about 3 months, and early biopsy should be avoided. Antibiotics do not help acute viral laryngitis. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 52)

**Post-viral vagal neuropathy dosing**: give gabapentin starting at 100 mg three times daily and titrate to about 300 mg three times daily; success is about 37.5–80%. Amitriptyline, pregabalin, and tramadol are alternatives. TA-LCA botulinum toxin (about 2.5 U per side) can reduce refractory cough. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 56)

**Botulinum details**: a typical start for adductor LD is about 1 U per TA-LCA side, in a small volume (0.1 mL) under EMG with a prephonatory burst. For abductor LD, inject one PCA (5–7.5 U) and stage the other side after about 2 weeks because of airway risk. Supraglottic false fold injection (5–7.5 U per side) causes little breathiness but lasts only 8–10 weeks. Contraindications are pregnancy, breastfeeding, myasthenia, and aminoglycosides. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Botulinum Toxin Injection of the Larynx", p 344)

**SLAD-R outcomes**: selective laryngeal adductor denervation-reinnervation gives favorable voice in more than 90% long term. About 25% still have some breaks and a minority relapse. RLN section was abandoned because of recurrence and worse voice. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Nonsurgical Treatment of Voice Disorders", p 54)

**Airway laser checklist**: keep FiO2 at 30% or less (or the lowest level that keeps saturation safe) and avoid N2O. Use a laser-resistant tube rated for that wavelength, ideally double-cuffed and filled with methylene blue-tinted saline, and change it if the proximal cuff is breached. Place wet cottonoids over the cuff and wet towels on the face, and allow one pedal for the operator only. Run a SOOPS check (Saline, Oxygen, One pedal, Patient, Staff). CO2 settings for laryngeal work are typically 4–8 W intermittent or superpulse. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Anesthesia and Airway Management for Laryngeal Surgery: Surgeon's Perspective", p 85)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Ventilation for laryngeal surgery**: lesions in the anterior two-thirds can usually be done around a 5.0–5.5 microlaryngeal tube. Posterior lesions need an anteriorly displaced tube, intermittent apnea (with or without high-flow nasal O2), or jet ventilation. Supraglottic jet gives a clear field and less barotrauma but moves the folds. Subglottic (Hunsaker) jet is steadier but risks air trapping and pneumothorax if outflow is blocked. Jet cases need TIVA and transcutaneous CO2 monitoring. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Anesthesia and Airway Management for Laryngeal Surgery: Surgeon's Perspective", p 82)

topic: ENT Perioperative Anesthesia / Difficult Airway Planning
text: **Topical anesthetic toxicity**: the lidocaine maximum is about 3–5 mg/kg, roughly 300 mg (7.5 mL of 4%) in a 70-kg adult. Early toxicity is tinnitus, perioral and CNS symptoms, progressing to seizures and arrhythmia. Benzocaine sprays can cause methemoglobinemia (chocolate cyanosis, desaturation unresponsive to O2), treated with methylene blue 1–2 mg/kg IV. Fat for lipoinjection may contain insulin used in processing and can cause postoperative hypoglycemia. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Principles of Awake Laryngeal Procedures", p 322)

**Setup pearls**: position with neck flexion and head extension and no shoulder roll. Use the largest laryngoscope, angled telescopes, and a 400-mm microscope. Consent for lingual nerve hypesthesia (usually resolves in about 2 weeks) and about 1–2% risk of no improvement or worse voice. Voice rest is 2–14 days, then light 'airy' voice for 5–10 minutes per hour for 7–10 days. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Principles of Phonomicrosurgery", p 113)

**Material durations**: gelatin about 4–6 wk, CMC about 6–8 wk (FDA-cleared), micronized dermis about 2–3 mo, hyaluronic acid about 3–4 mo (with about 4% hypersensitivity edema at 2–3 days, treated with steroids), CaHA about 9–12 mo, fat potentially years. Teflon granulomas appear 5–10 years later. A gap under about 1 mm favors injection, and 2–3 mm or more favors framework surgery. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Principles of Vocal Fold Augmentation", p 148)

**Target and overcorrection**: inject at the vocal process level along the superior arcuate line, about 3–5 mm deep and lateral. For paralysis inject posteriorly first; for bowing inject at the mid-fold. Overinject about 0.1–0.2 mL beyond the best voice, since the carrier resorbs in 3–5 days; total volume is usually under 1 mL. Material in Reinke space can persist 6–18 months and may need removal. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Per-oral Vocal Fold Augmentation", p 330)

**Key numbers**: about 97% of patients smoke. Cessation halts progression but does not reverse it. Make the incision superolateral, ending about 3 mm short of the anterior commissure, and leave some gelatinous SLP. Pitch rises and the voice is transiently breathy, with recovery over about 6–8 weeks. Office KTP spots about 5 mm apart are an alternative. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Reinke's Edema", p 175)

**Glottic insufficiency link**: compensatory hyperadduction from glottic insufficiency often drives recurrence, so augment at the same sitting as excision. About 75% respond to PPI but about 21% recur. For recurrence, give botulinum toxin to the ipsilateral TA-LCA about 3 days before excision. If laser is used, leave a cuff of granuloma over the perichondrium. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Vocal Fold Granuloma", p 181)

**Adjuvant cidofovir**: inject intralesional cidofovir at about 2.5–5 mg/mL (higher concentrations scar), widely and superficially in a caudal-to-cephalad sequence, monthly for 3 or more sessions alongside staged excision. Adult RRP has a third onset peak around age 65. Avoid tracheotomy, which creates a new squamociliary junction for seeding. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Surgical Treatment of Recurrent Respiratory Papillomatosis of the Larynx", p 196)

**KTP treatment effect scale**: KTP-V angiolysis only, KTP-1 blanching with intact epithelium, KTP-2 crinkling, KTP-3 ablation without removal, KTP-4 ablation with tissue removal. With bilateral anterior disease, debulk one side and treat the other only to KTP-1 to avoid a web. Microdebrider: skimmer blade at about 800–1200 rpm. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Awake Laser Treatment for Benign Laryngeal Pathology", p 361)

**Ford sulcus types**: these are three distinct entities, not grades. Type 1 is a physiologic sulcus (often with atrophy, minimal dysphonia). Type 2 is sulcus vergeture, with epithelium adherent to the ligament along the fold. It is likely developmental and familial cases are all type 2. Type 3 is a focal epithelial-lined pit, likely ruptured cyst, often with cyst, fibrous mass, or mucosal bridge (diplophonia). Subepithelial hydrodissection maps the defect. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Vocal Fold Scar and Sulcus Deformities of the Vocal Fold", p 207)

topic: Transoral Laser Microsurgery for Laryngeal Cancer
text: **ELS cordectomy classification**: I subepithelial, II ligamental, III transmuscular, IV total, V extended (Va contralateral fold, Vb arytenoid, Vc ventricular (false) fold, Vd subglottis), VI anterior commissure. Take about 1–2 mm margins, orient the specimen on a tongue blade, and avoid frozen sections of the small laser specimen. Wait 6–12 months before augmenting the neocord. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Carcinoma of the Vocal Fold", p 306)

**AA specifics**: arytenoid adduction lowers, medializes, stabilizes, and lengthens the vocal process by rotating the arytenoid. Indications include a large posterior gap, lateralized fold, height mismatch, or MPT under about 5 s. Light suture tension suffices. AA has more postoperative airway edema than medialization alone and a rare piriform fistula. Cricothyroid subluxation is an adjunct that lengthens a short, flaccid paralyzed fold. Adduction arytenopexy is the option when the CA joint is fixed. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Arytenoid Adduction", p 423)

**Saccular cyst vs laryngocele**: a saccular cyst is mucus-filled, not air-filled. Anterior saccular cysts are small and protrude from the anterior ventricle; lateral cysts bulge the false and aryepiglottic folds. About 25% follow a URI. Confirm with fine-cut CT. Treat by endoscopic CO2 excision that removes the attached ventricular and false fold mucosa to prevent recurrence. (Operative Techniques in Laryngology 2024, Ch "Endoscopic Excision of Saccular Cyst", p 225)

**Caudal deviation techniques**: For caudal deformities, score the concave side along the axis of the bend to release cartilage memory. In the swinging-door maneuver the quadrangular cartilage is freed from the maxillary crest groove, an inferior strip is trimmed, and the cartilage swings to midline and is fixed to the nasal spine periosteum with a figure-of-eight absorbable suture. The doorstop variant skips the strip excision and sutures the cartilage onto the opposite side of the crest. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 1, p 5–6)

**Procedure hierarchy and evidence**: Procedures escalate from outfracture, to submucosal soft-tissue reduction (cautery, laser, radiofrequency, microdebrider), to submucosal bone plus soft-tissue resection, to full-thickness anterior resection. In long-term comparisons submucosal resection plus outfracture performed best at 6 years; microdebrider reduction kept 93% of patients improved at 10 years and outperformed bipolar radiofrequency over time. Total turbinectomy is reserved for tumor. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 2, p 11–14)

**SPA branching numbers**: The SPA supplies up to about 90% of nasal mucosa. It divides before leaving the foramen in about 42% of specimens (separate foramina), and medial to the crista ethmoidalis there are 2 or more branches in 97%, 3 or more in 67%, and 4 or more in 35% of people. The crista ethmoidalis lies within 1 mm of the foramen in 95% and sits just anterior or anteroinferior to it. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 3, p 19, 21)

**SPA ligation landmarks**: Make a vertical mucoperiosteal incision about 1 cm anterior to the attachment of the middle turbinate basal lamella to the palatine bone, elevate posteriorly sweeping inferior to superior, and find the artery just behind the crista; removing the crista with a 1-mm Kerrison (associated with fewer rebleeds) exposes the trunk before it branches. If lost, follow the middle turbinate attachment (the SPA is its main supply) or open the maxillary sinus to use the posterior antral wall as a landmark. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 3, p 20–23)

**Who should not get SPA ligation**: SPA ligation is not designed for bleeding driven by anticoagulant or antiplatelet therapy (better treated with limited cautery and resorbable packing) and gives little durable benefit in hereditary hemorrhagic telangiectasia. Early ligation for posterior epistaxis shortens hospitalization, lowers cost and risk; most patients can go home after about 12 hours of observation. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 3, p 19, 24)

**24-12-6 rule**: Along the frontoethmoid suture, the anterior ethmoid artery lies about 24 mm behind the anterior lacrimal crest, the posterior ethmoid artery about 12 mm further back, and the optic nerve about 6 mm behind the PEA, which is why cautery during external ligation must stop at the PEA. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 4, p 25, 31)

**Anterior ethmoid artery position**: The AEA runs between the bulla lamella and the middle turbinate basal lamella, usually one cell behind the frontal ostium, slanting from posterolateral to anteromedial in the ethmoid roof. It lies anterior to the bulla face only when a suprabullar recess exists. It hangs on a mesentery below the skull base in about 36% and is both suspended and dehiscent in about 16%. On coronal CT look for the notch in the lamina papyracea between the superior oblique and medial rectus on the first cut posterior to the globe. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 4, p 25–26)

**AEA injury and orbital hematoma**: A transected AEA can retract into the orbit and cause an expanding hematoma: decompress endoscopically if recognized intraoperatively, and perform lateral canthotomy and cantholysis when vision is threatened. Avoid monopolar cautery on the AEA or PEA (it can fracture the skull base and cause CSF leak), and clear disease by moving instruments in and out between skull base septations rather than sweeping across them. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 4, p 27–28, 32)

**Maxillary line and ostium height**: The maxillary line is the curved ridge where the uncinate attaches to the lacrimal bone; the natural ostium sits behind it at the junction of its lower third and upper two-thirds. With the uncinate intact, the level of the lower third of the middle turbinate approximates the ostium height. A 30-degree scope shows the ostium far more reliably than a 0-degree scope. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 6, p 41, 45–46)

**Maxillary roof as the height guide**: Keep the height of the maxillary sinus roof in view while working anterior to posterior: perforate the basal lamella with a J-curette at its inferomedial part, at roof height, near where the vertical and horizontal segments meet. On coronal CT count cells above the maxillary roof; a tall maxillary sinus with a short ethmoid roof means the skull base is close, and a high entry through the basal lamella leads into the posterior skull base and CSF leak. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 7, p 53–56)

**Basal lamella segments**: The middle turbinate basal lamella has a vertical (coronal) segment and a horizontal segment. Ideally remove the vertical segment fully but keep the horizontal segment: cutting through it destabilizes the turbinate and causes lateralization, while leaving too much of the vertical part pushes the dissection too high in the posterior ethmoid. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 7, p 51–53, 56)

**Bolger box**: If the superior turbinate cannot be used, define a box bounded by the superior turbinate medially, its basal lamella inferiorly, the ethmoid roof superiorly, and the orbit laterally. Draw a diagonal and enter the sphenoid medial and inferior to that line. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 8, p 63–64)

**Finding the natural ostium**: Trim the lower half of the superior turbinate with a through-cutter to reveal the ostium medial and posterior to it (spare the upper part, which carries olfactory fibers). Enter the ostium with a J-curette, fracture the sphenoid face laterally, and enlarge with Kerrison or mushroom punches, always working from known to unknown. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 8, p 61–63)

**Kuhn frontal cell types**: In the Kuhn scheme used by this atlas, frontal cells (seen in about 25–40% of dissections) sit above the agger nasi. Type 1 is a single cell above the agger nasi. Type 2 is a tier of two or more cells above it that stay below the frontal sinus. Type 3 is a single large cell extending into the frontal sinus and sharing its anterior or posterior wall. Type 4 is a rare isolated 'balloon' cell inside the sinus with no shared wall. The 2016 International Frontal Sinus Anatomy Classification (IFAC) has since replaced these types with agger nasi, supra-agger, supra-agger frontal, supra-bulla, supra-bulla frontal, supraorbital ethmoid and frontal septal cells. IFAC is the current system, but know both. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 9, p 70–73)

**Draf definitions as used in practice**: Draf I clears the anterior ethmoid, uncinate, and frontal recess cells below the frontal ostium without touching the ostium itself; Draf IIa removes all recess cells between the lamina and middle turbinate and opens the internal ostium; Draf IIb also removes the ipsilateral frontal floor from lamina to septum, including the anterior middle turbinate attachment; Draf III joins bilateral IIb openings by removing the upper septum and intersinus septum. Nearly all primary cases and many revisions are adequately treated with a IIa. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 9, p 67–69)

**Draf IIa sequence**: Start at the AEA (marks where the frontal dissection begins), switch to a 70-degree reverse-post scope, and find the dark 'transition zone' of the drainage path, nearly always medial and posterior to the posterior wall of the agger nasi. Remove the agger nasi posterior wall with front-to-back giraffe forceps, then its medial wall, then its cap (the single biggest widening move) with a frontal Kerrison (Bachert) back to the nasofrontal bone, then take the supraorbital ethmoid ledge back to the skull base. Finish by trimming the medial floor with a mushroom or Hosemann punch. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 9, p 76–78)

**Why a Draf IIa fails**: Persistent frontal disease after a complete IIa usually results from membranous stenosis, a lateralized middle turbinate (often a partially resected remnant), osteitis/neo-osteogenesis, or a prominent nasofrontal beak, which are the targets of extended (IIb/III) surgery. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 10, p 83, 85)

**Frontal sinus rescue procedure**: For frontal obstruction from a lateralized, partially resected middle turbinate, raise a medially based mucosal flap from the turbinate stump, remove the bony remnant (a Draf IIb), and advance the flap over the bare bone: in effect, a IIb with an advancement flap. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 10, p 91)

**Draf III selection**: Consider Draf III as a primary operation in eosinophilic CRS, AERD, and extensive polyposis (especially with lower airway disease), for recalcitrant or iatrogenic frontal disease, as salvage after failed osteoplastic obliteration, and as access for tumors (it reaches nearly all of the sinus except the far lateral orbital roof). Delay it in very active inflammatory disease still needing systemic steroids; with the outside-in technique the only anatomic contraindication is under 5 mm between the posterior table and the skin in front of the beak. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 11, p 94)

**Postoperative topical therapy**: After ESS start isotonic high-volume (240 mL) saline irrigation at 24–48 hours (hypertonic solutions cause more burning, headache, otalgia). Topical steroid sprays improve healing appearance and lengthen time to polyp recurrence; for severe polyposis add budesonide 0.5 mg/2 mL respule to 240 mL saline once or twice daily, which is off-label (discuss with the patient) and in limited studies has not suppressed the HPA axis. Perioperative systemic steroids improved endoscopic appearance but not symptoms in a randomized trial. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 12, p 103–104)

**Balloon sinus dilation basics**: A balloon catheter passed over a guidewire widens the natural maxillary, frontal, or sphenoid ostium without removing bone. It can be used alone (office or OR, under topical/local anesthesia) or as a hybrid with standard ESS. It cannot treat the ethmoids, which have no single ostium, so balloon-only treatment suits focal outflow disease such as recurrent acute rhinosinusitis or limited nonpolypoid CRS. Polyps, heavy osteitis, and extensive ethmoid disease are poor fits. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 13, p 105, 112)

**Balloon placement checks**: Confirm wire position before inflating. For the frontal sinus, a sharp spot of light that moves across the forehead means the true sinus, while a diffuse glow suggests an ethmoid or suprabullar cell. For the maxillary sinus, the wire must pass through the natural ostium. Dilating elsewhere creates an accessory ostium and recirculation. For the sphenoid (ostium about 1–1.5 cm above the choana, medial to the superior turbinate), transillumination is unreliable. Use fluoroscopy or navigation if there is doubt. Inflate to about 8–12 atmospheres. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 13, p 107–108)

**Skull base trajectory and carotid risk**: If the maxillary sinus height is more than twice the posterior ethmoid height (ratio above 2:1), a trajectory guided by the maxillary sinus tends to lead into the skull base rather than the sphenoid. Carotid dehiscence in the sphenoid appears in about 5–25% of radiographic/cadaveric studies, and with asymmetric sphenoids the intersinus septum usually inserts on one carotid canal. Use CT of 2–3 mm or thinner with reformats, and note lateral lamella depth, AEA course, Onodi cells, and a lateralized turbinate remnant. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 14, p 115–116)

**When a standard antrostomy is not enough**: A modified endoscopic medial maxillectomy (mega-antrostomy) removes most of the medial maxillary wall while keeping the nasolacrimal duct and the anterior inferior turbinate. It is used for maxillary disease that persists despite a good antrostomy and maximal medical therapy, with mucin or pus pooled on the floor, anterior, or lateral walls: cystic fibrosis, biofilm disease, heavy allergic mucin, polyps on the anterior wall/floor, prolapsed orbital fat after medial decompression, and mucosa stripped by prior Caldwell-Luc surgery. The wide opening improves irrigation delivery and office suctioning. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 15, p 123)

**Escalation for chronic sphenoiditis**: Sphenoidotomy for isolated sphenoid disease stays patent in more than 90% at up to 4 years, but sphenoid involvement in CRS needs revision in 34–65% of cases. Failures come from circumferentially denuded bone, too small an opening, and osteitis. The surgical ladder is standard sphenoidotomy, then sphenoid drill-out (both faces, rostrum and intersinus septum removed into one cavity), then radical sphenoidectomy/marsupialization with the floor drilled flush to the posterior wall. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 16, p 133–134)

**Endoscopic medial and inferomedial decompression**: Indications are proptosis (including cosmetic), exposure keratopathy, diplopia, and compressive optic neuropathy. Resect the middle turbinate, make a wide posterior maxillary antrostomy, complete sphenoethmoidectomy, then remove the lamina papyracea from the skull base to the orbital floor and from the maxillary line to the sphenoid face (the sphenoethmoid angle is the posterior limit), leaving a thin strip of lamina at the skull base. Downfracture the medial orbital floor medial to the infraorbital nerve, then incise the periorbita from posterior to anterior with a sickle/arachnoid knife and divide fibrous bands so fat prolapses. For severe disease, a balanced three-wall decompression adds an external lateral wall decompression. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 18, p 149–155)

**Decompression outcomes and diplopia**: Endoscopic decompression recesses the globe by about 3.5 mm on average (range 2–12 mm), and adding a lateral wall gives about 2 mm more. New or worse diplopia occurs in up to one-third, usually temporary. Preserving the inferomedial orbital strut lowers the risk, and persistent diplopia is treated with strabismus surgery 8–10 months later. Bilateral single-stage surgery is generally recommended. A balanced decompression helps avoid asymmetry. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 18, p 150, 155–156)

**Endoscopic vidian neurectomy**: Indicated for refractory vasomotor (and selected allergic) rhinitis with troublesome watery rhinorrhea after topical therapy, including intranasal anticholinergics, fails or is not tolerated. Make a wide antrostomy to the posterior wall, raise a lateral wall flap, remove the crista ethmoidalis and posterior maxillary wall, ligate the SPA, then divide the vidian nerve where its canal opens at the junction of the medial pterygoid plate and sphenoid floor, along with the more medial pharyngeal (palatovaginal) nerve that runs nearly perpendicular to it. Push bone wax into the canal to prevent regrowth. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 23, p 191–192)

**Andrews staging and endoscopic candidacy**: Andrews (a modification of Fisch): I, nasal cavity and nasopharynx; II, pterygopalatine fossa or maxillary, sphenoid, or ethmoid sinuses; IIIa, orbit or infratemporal fossa without intracranial spread; IIIb, IIIa plus small extradural parasellar disease; IVa, large extradural or intradural disease; IVb, cavernous sinus, pituitary, or chiasm. Most stage I, II, and selected IIIa tumors can be removed endoscopically. On imaging also look for a widened vidian canal and sclerosis of the pterygoid base (posterior extension) and inferior orbital fissure spread. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 24, p 202–205)

**Embolization timing and feeders**: Angiography of both carotid systems identifies feeders, most often distal internal maxillary branches, ascending pharyngeal, vidian, accessory meningeal, mandibular, and facial arteries. Embolize within 24 hours of surgery, because waiting allows collateral recruitment and revascularization; prior embolization makes revision cases harder. Even after embolization, clip the maxillary artery at surgery, because recanalized vessels can bleed heavily. (Many centers use a 24–48 hour window; the atlas favors within 24 hours.) (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 24, p 203, 206)

**Esthesioneuroblastoma staging and grading**: Kadish: A, nasal cavity only. B, nasal cavity plus paranasal sinuses. C, beyond the sinuses. Dulguerov TNM: T1, nasal cavity/sinuses sparing the sphenoid and highest ethmoid cells. T2, includes the sphenoid or reaches/erodes the cribriform plate. T3, orbit or anterior cranial fossa without dural invasion. T4, brain. Hyams grades I–IV rise with mitoses, pleomorphism, and necrosis and lose fibrillary matrix. Homer Wright rosettes mark low grade and Flexner-Wintersteiner rosettes high grade. Hyams grade was the strongest prognostic factor in one series (5-year survival about 80% for low grade vs 40% for high grade). This tumor makes up about 3–6% of sinonasal malignancies. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 25, p 212–213)

**Keros depths and AEA canal**: The cribriform plate is the lowest midline point of the anterior skull base, slung from the lateral lamellae that thicken laterally into the fovea ethmoidalis. Keros 1: cribriform 1–3 mm below the ethmoid roof. Keros 2: 4–7 mm. Keros 3: 8–16 mm (long, thin, vulnerable lateral lamella). Asymmetry is common. The AEA canal is partly or wholly dehiscent in about 40%. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 26, p 223–224)

**Intrathecal fluorescein technique**: The usual dose is 0.1 mL of 10% (non-ophthalmic) fluorescein diluted in 10 mL of the patient's CSF or preservative-free saline, injected slowly over about 10 minutes, often through a lumbar drain placed up to an hour before surgery with the patient briefly head-down. It is off-label for intrathecal use and requires consent; seizures and neurologic complications are dose-related. A blue-light filter helps reveal low-flow leaks. A patient-collected sample stays stable for beta-2 transferrin for about a week at room temperature. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 26, p 224–225; Ch 27 p 234–235, 237)

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Graft selection algorithm (cribriform)**: With a meningoencephalocele, reduce it with bipolar or coblation to the bony edge and use a rigid (bone) underlay to resist pressure. Without encephalocele: defects under 5 mm can be closed with a free mucosal graft or septal flap; those over 5 mm use free, pedicled, or synthetic grafts with or without a bone underlay. Always add tissue sealant plus absorbable and nonabsorbable packing. A split middle turbinate gives a composite bone-mucosa graft. Lay free mucosal grafts mucosal side toward the nose (ink that side) so a mucocele does not form beneath them. Endoscopic repair succeeds in up to about 98%. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 26, p 223, 225–228; Ch 27 p 239)

**Lumbar drain and acetazolamide after spontaneous repair**: Lumbar drain use ranges from 0% to 73%; reserve it for clear raised-pressure features or persistent high-flow leaks, and manage in a unit familiar with its risks (spinal headache, overdrainage with herniation, pneumocephalus, infection, retained catheter). Give long-term acetazolamide to patients with suspected IIH or high opening pressure, since recurrence or a second leak (0.5–9%) can appear up to 2 years later; consider VP shunting if refractory. Transient diabetes insipidus has been reported after sphenoid leak repair. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 27, p 240–241)

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **When to use a vascularized flap**: Free grafts work for small (under about 1 cm), low-flow defects without planned radiation or major arachnoid opening. Defects larger than about 2–3 cm and any high-flow leak (a cistern or ventricle opened) need a multilayer repair with a vascularized flap. The layers are a subdural inlay that forms the watertight 'bath plug' plus a pedicled onlay for blood supply; an extra extradural intracranial layer adds nothing, and sealants are not required. Repairs tend to fail at the dependent edge and at the top, where flaps migrate. Radiation, intraventricular extension, and obesity (raised ICP) predict failure. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 31, p 285–286, 290, 296)

topic: Endoscopic CSF Leak Repair / Nasoseptal Flap
text: **Nasoseptal flap reach**: A full flap (about 25 cm²) covers from the posterior frontal table to the sella and from lamina to lamina, or a full clivus. It reliably covers two neighboring skull base units (frontal, cribriform, sella/planum, clivus) but not three. Three designs: to the middle turbinate head for sella/planum only; to the mucocutaneous junction for ethmoid, clival, or frontal defects; and adding the nasal floor for extra width. Oversize the flap because contouring over angles uses up length, and in children under about 14 the flap may not be long enough (check the cranium-to-face ratio). (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 31, p 287, 289–290, 292)

topic: Endoscopic Pituitary / Anterior Skull Base Approach
text: **Internal carotid injury**: Carotid injury is the most catastrophic complication of endonasal skull base surgery. Temporize with controlled hypotension, packing or a crushed muscle patch, and transfusion, then go urgently to angiography for endovascular occlusion or stenting. Do not start extended endonasal cases without neurointerventional backup. A mini-Doppler, navigation, and landmarks (paraclival carotid canal, vidian canal leading to the anterior genu, eustachian tube as the lateral limit in the lower clivus) reduce the risk. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 30, p 275, 279–280, 283)
