**Frontal sinus trephination**: Indications include acute frontal sinusitis not drainable endoscopically or with orbital/intracranial spread, Pott puffy tumor, laterally based lesions, frontal recess neo-osteogenesis, type 3/4 frontal cells, osteoma or fibro-osseous lesions, and CSF leak; it also serves as an 'above-and-below' adjunct with irrigation (fluorescein or methylene blue) to show the recess from below. The usual route is a 1–2 cm medial infrabrow incision medial to the supraorbital bundle; enter through the sinus floor, not the anterior table (diploic veins raise the risk of osteomyelitis and intracranial spread when infected), saucerizing with a 4-mm cutting bur until the bone turns blue, then open 6–8 mm (5–15 mm for scopes and instruments). An 8F red rubber irrigation catheter stays 3–5 days. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 32, p 301–305)

**Osteoplastic flap with or without obliteration**: Now reserved for disease beyond endoscopic reach: refractory chronic frontal sinusitis, recurrent recess stenosis, extensive fibro-osseous lesions, posterior table defects with CSF leak, fractures involving the recess, and obstructing cells. Mapping the sinus with image guidance is more accurate than a 6-foot Caldwell template or transillumination. Through a coronal incision beveled parallel to the follicles, protect the frontal branch (deep to the temporoparietal fascia) by staying deep to that fascia laterally, then make a beveled osteotomy and hinge the anterior table. Obliterate only after removing every bit of mucosa under the microscope and drilling the bone, inverting recess mucosa and plugging the recess, then filling with fat. Hydroxyapatite cement is discouraged because of infection and revision. Mucosa can be left if less than half was disturbed. (Atlas of Endoscopic Sinus and Skull Base Surgery 2e, Ch 33, p 309–314)

**Coryllos anatomic types**: type I inserts at the tongue tip, type II just behind the tip (both 'anterior' tongue-tie), type III at the mid-to-posterior undersurface, and type IV is a broad submucosal band restricting the tongue base ('posterior' tongue-tie). Because every infant has a frenulum, liberal use of this scheme can label nearly any newborn as tongue-tied, so it should not drive surgery on its own. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3070)

**Functional scoring tools**: the Hazelbaker tool (HATLFF) grades seven tongue movements (lateralization, lift, extension, spread, cupping, peristalsis, snap-back) and is thorough but cumbersome; the Bristol Tongue Assessment Tool (BTAT) is a quicker four-item, 0–2 point screen in which low scores mean worse function. In children over about 3 years, measure tongue-tip protrusion past the lower incisors and the interincisal distance with the tongue tip held on the upper teeth. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3070)

**Epidemiology**: only an estimated 15%–44% of infants with ankyloglossia actually develop breastfeeding problems, and the prevalence appears to fall with age as the frenulum stretches or tears, so the diagnosis alone does not predict dysfunction. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, pp 3069–3071)

**Neonatal frenotomy safety**: performed without general anesthesia; minor bleeding is typical. Oral 24% sucrose is effective analgesia, whereas topical lidocaine or benzocaine should not be used in infants (FDA boxed warning for seizures and methemoglobinemia). Rare serious complications include hemorrhage with hypovolemic shock and submandibular swelling from injury to the Wharton ducts. Older children get a horizontal-to-vertical (diamond) frenuloplasty. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, pp 3072–3073)

**Maxillary frenulum and diastema**: a midline upper incisor gap normally narrows as the permanent canines erupt (around age 10); gaps under ~3 mm often close on their own (closure is 85%–99% likely at ≤1.5 mm and about 50% at ~1.85 mm). Labial frenectomy may be considered when the gap exceeds 2–3 mm after the lateral incisors erupt; timing relative to orthodontics is debated, and evidence for routine lip-tie release in infants is lacking. (Cummings 7e, Ch 207, p 3075)

**Risk factors for juvenile onset**: children with RRP are more often firstborn and vaginally delivered, and over half of their mothers have visible condylomas. A prolonged second stage of labor in first pregnancies and newly acquired maternal lesions (which shed more virus) are proposed explanations. US pediatric incidence is roughly 4.3 per 100,000. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, pp 3077–3078)

**Cesarean delivery is not recommended to prevent RRP**: even with active maternal condyloma, only about 1 in 231–400 exposed infants develops disease, cases occur after cesarean (suggesting some in utero transmission), and cesarean carries greater maternal risk and cost. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, p 3078)

**Presentation and misdiagnosis**: hoarseness or a weak cry is the first symptom (the vocal fold is the first site), followed by inspiratory stridor that becomes biphasic as disease grows. Children are often misdiagnosed with asthma, croup, allergy, nodules, or bronchitis, and infants can present in acute distress during an ordinary URI. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, p 3080)

**Tracheotomy is avoided when possible**: it is associated with distal tracheal spread (in one large series 92.5% of children with a tracheotomy developed lower-airway disease). If unavoidable, decannulate as soon as endoscopic control allows. Children who need tracheotomy tend to be diagnosed younger (registry mean 2.7 vs 3.9 years). (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, p 3080)

**Extralaryngeal spread** occurs in about 30% of children and 16% of adults, most often oral cavity, then trachea, then bronchi. HPV-11 is linked to distal spread. Pulmonary papillomas start as peripheral noncalcified nodules that cavitate (air-fluid levels on CT), carry a grave prognosis, and anecdotally raise malignant-transformation risk. Malignant transformation overall is rare (about 1.6% in one 244-patient series). (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, p 3080)

**When to add adjuvant therapy**: roughly 20% of patients eventually need it. Standard triggers are more than 4 surgeries per year, rapid regrowth with airway compromise, or distal multisite spread. Options described include intralesional cidofovir (off-label, most widely used historically, with heterogeneous evidence and a negative small RCT), interferon (growth and liver side effects), indole-3-carbinol, and bevacizumab (intralesional with KTP ablation, or systemic for distal/pulmonary disease). Celecoxib failed in a placebo-controlled trial. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, pp 3084–3089)

**Derkay staging**: a standardized severity score grades each airway subsite 0 (none), 1 (surface), 2 (raised), or 3 (bulky) and adds functional items (voice, stridor, urgency, interval since last surgery) to track disease and compare treatments. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, pp 3089–3090)

**Instrument choice**: the CO2 laser has been the most commonly used laser, but microdebrider cohorts show better voice, less OR time, lower cost, and less scarring/web formation. KTP and 585-nm pulsed-dye lasers are angiolytic options (including in-office). Leave a small amount of disease at the anterior commissure rather than creating opposing raw surfaces. HPV DNA has been found in laser plume, so smoke evacuation and masks matter. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, pp 3083–3085)

**HPV vaccine specifics**: the 9-valent vaccine (VLP-based, covers types 6 and 11) replaced the quadrivalent. The bivalent vaccine covers only 16/18 and so does not protect against RRP types. Efficacy is greatest before sexual debut, and adjuvant vaccination in established RRP appears to lengthen intersurgical intervals. (Cummings 7e, Ch 208, pp 3079–3080)

**Normal sizes**: the full-term neonatal subglottis is 4.5–5.5 mm in diameter (about 3.5 mm in preterm infants), and 4 mm or less is stenotic in a term baby. Because area scales with radius squared, dropping the radius from 4 to 3 mm cuts lumen area by about 40%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, p 3093)

**Congenital SGS** (no prior intubation or trauma) is the third most common congenital laryngeal anomaly after laryngomalacia and vocal fold paralysis but only about 5% of all SGS. Membranous type: circumferential soft-tissue thickening, narrowest 2–3 mm below the cords. Cartilaginous type: most often a thickened cricoid shelf. An elliptical cricoid is seen in trisomy 21. Presents as recurrent or prolonged croup, usually within 3 months. Under half need tracheotomy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, p 3093)

**Acquired SGS**: about 90% of acquired chronic SGS in infants follows intubation. Tube duration and size are the dominant risk factors. Severe injury has been seen after 1 week in neonates (17 hours in adults), though preterm infants tolerate weeks because their cartilage is pliable. Size the tube to leak at 20 cm H2O. Approximate ETT size: preterm 2.5, 0–6 mo 3.0, 6–12 mo 3.5, 1–2 yr 4.0, 2–3 yr 4.5. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, pp 3094–3095)

**Steroid and mitomycin adjuncts**: most data show no added benefit from intralesional steroid injection with dilation, and steroids can delay epithelialization and cause cartilage resorption, though injection remains common. Topical mitomycin-C helps in animal models and retrospective series, but the only double-blind RCT (after LTR) showed no benefit, and fibrinous debris after laser/mitomycin can acutely obstruct the airway. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, p 3100)

**Anterior cricoid split (ACS)**: divide the cricoid and first tracheal rings anteriorly (open or endoscopically with a sickle knife, sparing outer perichondrium, often followed by balloon dilation) for an infant who fails extubation. Keep intubated 5–7 days, then extubate with endoscopy. Requires adequate pulmonary function and is contraindicated with ongoing positive-pressure ventilator need. Success 35%–88%. Rarely used today. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, p 3100)

**Endoscopic posterior cricoid split with graft**: under spontaneous ventilation, divide interarytenoid scar and posterior cricoid lamina, then wedge a T-shaped costal cartilage graft between the cut ends with flanges tucked into submucosal tunnels. No stent is needed, and extubation or decannulation is tried after 2–3 days. Used for posterior glottic stenosis, SGS, and bilateral vocal fold immobility. (Cummings 7e, Ch 209, p 3100)

**Diagnostic threshold**: collapse of more than 50% of the lumen at end expiration on dynamic airway study is considered diagnostic. In primary malacia the cartilage-to-membranous wall ratio falls from about 4.5:1 to near 2:1. Bronchomalacia coexists in about 30%, and reflux is present in about half (up to 78% in severe cases). (Cummings 7e, Ch 210, p 3112)

**Natural history and aortopexy**: most improve within 6–12 months and resolve by about age 2. Aortopexy (sutures from ascending aorta near the innominate takeoff to the posterior sternum) is chiefly indicated for one or more BRUEs, mostly with esophageal atresia or vascular compression. Pooled success is about 80%. Untreated GERD raises aortopexy failure, so fundoplication is often done first or concurrently. (Cummings 7e, Ch 210, p 3113)

**Airway stents in children**: stents are a last resort, used only for severe refractory malacia after vascular repair and not as primary therapy. Reviews report stent-related mortality around 12%. Metal stents epithelialize in 6–8 weeks, become nearly impossible to remove, and can erode into vessels (FDA advisory in 2005 against metallic stents in benign airway disease). Silicone tube stents are removable but migrate and impair clearance. (Cummings 7e, Ch 210, pp 3113–3114)

**Esophageal atresia/TEF** (about 1 in 3500): EA with distal TEF 85%, isolated EA 8%, H-type TEF 4%, EA with proximal TEF 3%, double fistula <1%. Up to 50% have other anomalies (VACTERL, CHARGE, cardiac most common). Suspect when a 10F catheter will not pass beyond 10 cm. Gastric air on x-ray implies a distal fistula. Tracheomalacia is a consistent feature after repair, and long-gap EA is defined as >3 cm or two vertebral bodies. (Cummings 7e, Ch 210, p 3111)

**Imaging limits**: only about 11% of airway foreign bodies are radiopaque, and 89% of children with an ingested foreign body have a normal exam. Low-dose airway CT ('virtual bronchoscopy') has very high negative predictive value (100% in one series) for selected stable, equivocal cases. Barium swallow is not indicated and makes esophageal extraction harder. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, pp 3122–3123)

**Three clinical phases**: an initial choking/gagging event, then an asymptomatic interval as reflexes fatigue (the trap that delays diagnosis), then complications such as obstruction, pneumonia, or erosion. Prolonged cough or wheeze unresponsive to bronchodilators/steroids, or recurrent pneumonia, should prompt evaluation. About 90% of airway foreign bodies lodge in the bronchi. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, pp 3121–3124)

**Observation for coins**: an asymptomatic child with a smooth mid- or distal esophageal object for under 24 hours and no esophageal disease may be watched for 8–16 hours and re-imaged; about 25%–30% of such coins pass on their own. Remove sooner for batteries, sharp objects, objects >24 hours, or symptoms. Coronal orientation on AP film suggests esophagus, but this rule is not absolute; a lateral film confirms location behind the trachea. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, pp 3123–3124)

**Symptoms do not track injury**: in a large pediatric series 12% of asymptomatic children had severe esophageal injury while 82% of symptomatic children had none, and in another series 61% of children without oral lesions still had esophageal injury. Nonetheless, unintentional ingestion without symptoms rarely causes significant injury; endoscopy is reserved for oral lesions, marked symptoms, or intentional ingestion. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, p 3129)

**Initial ED rules**: Give no activated charcoal (it does not bind caustics), do not induce vomiting, and place no blind NG tube (perforation risk). If dilution is used, limit it to 15 mL/kg. Household bleach (pH about 7) is usually only an irritant and can be observed. Endoscopy is best done 12-48 hours after ingestion. Later endoscopy is riskier, especially from about day 5 to day 15, when the wall is weakest. A flexible scope is preferred, the endoscopist usually stops at the first circumferential burn, and tracheoscopy is considered if esophageal injury is found. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, pp 3128–3129)

**Steroids and late care**: a meta-analysis (10 studies, 572 patients) found steroids do not reduce stricture after grade II burns. Strictures are dilated with reassessment every 2–3 weeks; late presenters (>48 hours) are imaged with water-soluble contrast rather than scoped. Laundry detergent pods can cause CNS depression and respiratory distress that warrant ICU care and airway protection. (Cummings 7e, Ch 211, p 3129)

**EoE criteria and endoscopy**: diagnosis needs at least 15 eosinophils per high-power field on esophageal biopsy. Endoscopy may show white exudates, edema, linear furrows, rings, and strictures, but these are nonspecific. The book also lists PPI non-response. Note that the 2018 international consensus dropped the PPI-trial requirement, and PPI is now treated as a therapy. (Cummings 7e, Ch 212, p 3136)

**Reflux testing**: combined pH/multichannel intraluminal impedance is preferred because it detects acid and nonacid reflux. The lipid-laden macrophage index on BAL (100 cells scored 0–4, >100 abnormal) has poor sensitivity and specificity for reflux aspiration. Pepsin in airway samples appears more specific. Upper GI series shows anatomy (malrotation, hernia), not reflux disease. (Cummings 7e, Ch 212, p 3136)

**Infant reflux treatment**: regurgitation peaks at 4–6 months and resolves with growth. Hydrolyzed or elemental formula trials are more effective than acid suppression in infants. Thickening reduces visible regurgitation but not reflux episodes. Prone sleeping is contraindicated (SIDS). Metoclopramide/domperidone are not recommended (extrapyramidal and cardiac risk), and erythromycin's prokinetic effect fades from tachyphylaxis. Stop empiric acid suppression if there is no clear benefit. (Cummings 7e, Ch 212, pp 3136–3138)

**Reflux and laryngomalacia**: GER is reported in up to 90% of infants with laryngomalacia, and half of infants with stridor in one study had LPR, but a systematic review of 1295 neonates found no causal link. The association may reflect airway-obstruction pressures rather than reflux causing the malacia. BRUEs are generally not caused by reflux. (Cummings 7e, Ch 212, pp 3136–3137)

**Technique and early care**: palpate the suprasternal notch for an anomalous vessel, avoid a low tracheotomy, place stay sutures on each side of a vertical tracheal incision (labeled LEFT and RIGHT and taped to the chest), and confirm the tube tip is above the carina. Do the first tube change on postoperative days 3–7, then remove stay sutures. Routine changes every 2–4 weeks. (Cummings 7e, Ch 213, pp 3142–3144)

**Cincinnati decannulation criteria**: tolerates downsizing. Caps during all waking hours. Completes a 48-hour inpatient capping trial. DL/bronchoscopy shows no obstructing lesion. Capped sleep study shows AHI <10, obstructive index <5, and end-tidal CO2 >50 mm Hg for under 25% of sleep. Wait 2–4 months off the ventilator first (AAO-HNS 2013). Failure after attempted decannulation is still 5%–21%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 213, p 3145)

**Complication burden**: early complications about 15% (pneumothorax, accidental decannulation, plugging). Late complications in about 63%, granulation most common, plus tracheoinnominate and tracheoesophageal fistula. About 15% of children with tracheotomies die while cannulated, but tube-specific mortality is 0.5%–3.6%. Surveillance bronchoscopy every 6–12 months finds new lesions in 30%–45%. Tracheocutaneous fistula follows decannulation in 13%–57%. (Cummings 7e, Ch 213, pp 3144–3145)

**Associated findings**: tracheobronchomalacia is found in about a third of cleft patients, and TEF in 12%–56%; other midline defects should prompt evaluation for VACTERL, Pallister-Hall, or Opitz-Frias (Opitz G/BBB) syndromes. Avoid strong downward pressure when palpating the interarytenoid notch, which can create a false cleft. Refer to neurology when aspiration exceeds what the anatomy explains. (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, p 3148)

**Staged management for type I–II**: give a 4–6 month trial of thickened feeds, positioning, and reflux/pulmonary optimization; about half of type I (91%–100% in some series) succeed without surgery. Interarytenoid injection augmentation (0.2–0.6 mL) helps more than 70% at least temporarily (about 3 months average) and predicts success of formal repair. Endoscopic repair is the gold standard for definitive closure (success 75%–100%). (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, pp 3148–3151)

**Open repair for deep clefts**: most type III and all type IV clefts need open repair, usually anteriorly via midline thyrotomy, cricoidotomy, and tracheofissure (good exposure, low RLN risk), with two- or three-layer closure and an interposed graft. Consider tracheostomy to avoid prolonged positive pressure, and ECMO/bypass for distal extension. About half of type IV repairs have complications (dehiscence most common), and mortality for large type IV clefts is 44%–76%. The Sandu–Monnier modification splits types III and IV into a/b subtypes; limited type IIIa clefts can be repaired endoscopically. (Cummings 7e, Ch 214, pp 3151–3152)
